(3) Pregnancy test (lithium category D — Ebstein cardiac anomaly first trimester). (4) CBC (baseline). (5) ECG if > 40 yo or cardiac history. Then trough lithium levels every 1–3 days during titration, every 1–3 months once stable.
Why is lamotrigine titrated slowly when used as a mood stabilizer?
To minimize the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN, which is life-threatening. Rapid titration is the major risk factor. Teach client to stop the medication immediately and seek care for any rash — especially with fever, blistering, or mucosal involvement. Lamotrigine is best for bipolar depression (less effective for mania).

Lithium

The gold standard mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder. Narrow therapeutic index requires careful monitoring, hydration, and consistent sodium intake.

Lithium carbonate (Lithobid, Eskalith)

Mood stabilizer prototype

Mechanism unclear; stabilizes neuronal membranes and alters intracellular signaling. Effective for both acute mania and maintenance.

Uses

  • Acute mania
  • Maintenance therapy for bipolar I and II
  • Prevention of recurrent mood episodes
  • Augmentation of antidepressants in depression

Therapeutic levels

  • Acute mania: 0.8–1.4 mEq/L
  • Maintenance: 0.6–1.2 mEq/L
  • Toxicity: > 1.5 mEq/L
  • Severe toxicity: > 2.0 mEq/L (medical emergency)

Side effects (therapeutic range)

  • GI upset (nausea, diarrhea — usually improves)
  • Fine hand tremor
  • Polyuria, polydipsia
  • Weight gain
  • Cognitive dulling

Toxicity signs

  • Early (1.5–2.0): N/V, diarrhea, coarse tremor, slurred speech, lethargy, confusion
  • Severe (> 2.0): Hyperreflexia, seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse, death

Long-term concerns

  • Thyroid: Hypothyroidism (check TSH q6–12 months)
  • Renal: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, CKD with long-term use (check BUN/Cr q6–12 months)
  • Cardiac: Conduction abnormalities (baseline ECG if > 40 yo)
  • Pregnancy: Category D — Ebstein cardiac anomaly in 1st trimester

Critical client teaching

  • Maintain consistent fluid intake (2–3 L/day) — dehydration → toxicity
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake — low sodium → ↑ lithium retention → toxicity
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors — ↑ lithium levels
  • Take with food (decreases GI upset)
  • Report: vomiting, diarrhea, fever — risk of dehydration → toxicity
  • Monitor for thyroid symptoms (cold intolerance, weight gain, fatigue)

Lithium toxicity treatment

  • Mild toxicity: hold lithium, hydrate, monitor levels
  • Severe toxicity: hemodialysis (most effective treatment)

Anticonvulsant Mood Stabilizers

Several anticonvulsants are effective mood stabilizers. They work by stabilizing neuronal membranes through sodium channel modulation or GABA enhancement.

Valproic acid / divalproex (Depakote)

First-line for acute mania, especially with rapid cycling or mixed episodes.

Uses

  • Acute mania, mixed episodes, rapid cycling
  • Bipolar maintenance
  • Seizure disorders
  • Migraine prophylaxis

Adverse effects

  • Hepatotoxicity — baseline LFTs; monitor
  • Pancreatitis — severe abdominal pain, elevated amylase/lipase
  • Thrombocytopenia — check CBC
  • GI upset, sedation, weight gain
  • Hair loss
  • Teratogenicity: Category X — neural tube defects, severe — AVOID in pregnancy

Levels

  • Therapeutic: 50–125 mcg/mL
  • Toxic: > 175 mcg/mL

Lamotrigine (Lamictal)

Best for bipolar depression

More effective for bipolar depression than mania.

Uses

  • Bipolar I maintenance
  • Bipolar depression
  • Seizure disorders

Adverse effects

  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome — life-threatening rash; very slow titration required
  • Headache, dizziness, ataxia
  • Nausea

Nursing actions

  • Slow titration over 6+ weeks to reduce SJS risk
  • Hold and report ANY rash
  • ↓ dose with valproate (valproate ↑ lamotrigine levels)

Carbamazepine (Tegretol)

Used when other agents fail. Many drug interactions.

Uses

  • Bipolar disorder, mania
  • Seizure disorders
  • Trigeminal neuralgia

Adverse effects

  • Agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia — baseline CBC; monitor
  • Stevens-Johnson Syndrome — HLA-B*1502 testing in Asian descent before initiation
  • SIADH/hyponatremia
  • Sedation, ataxia

Interactions

  • Potent CYP450 inducer — ↓ OCPs (pregnancy risk), warfarin, many other drugs
  • Auto-induces own metabolism (levels may decrease over time)

Atypical Antipsychotics for Bipolar

Several atypical antipsychotics are FDA-approved for bipolar disorder — acute mania, depression, and maintenance.

Atypical antipsychotics

Multiple indications

Examples used in bipolar: olanzapine (Zyprexa), quetiapine (Seroquel), risperidone, aripiprazole (Abilify), ziprasidone, lurasidone (Latuda), cariprazine.

Uses in bipolar

  • Acute mania (most atypicals)
  • Acute bipolar depression (quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine, olanzapine + fluoxetine)
  • Maintenance therapy

Common adverse effects

  • Metabolic syndrome: Weight gain, hyperglycemia, dyslipidemia (olanzapine and clozapine worst)
  • Sedation (quetiapine, olanzapine)
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • EPS — less than typical antipsychotics but possible (risperidone has more)
  • Tardive dyskinesia with long-term use
  • Increased mortality in elderly with dementia-related psychosis (BBW)

Nursing actions

  • Baseline weight, fasting glucose, lipids — monitor regularly
  • AIMS exam for tardive dyskinesia
  • Educate about long-term metabolic risk
  • Quetiapine has dose-dependent effects (low dose for sleep/depression, higher for mania)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder

A nurse is caring for a client with bipolar I disorder who has been taking lithium for 6 months. The client reports the past 2 days of vomiting and diarrhea due to gastroenteritis. The client's current lithium level is 1.8 mEq/L. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Recognition of Toxicity

  • Lithium level of 1.8 mEq/L is in the toxic range (therapeutic: 0.6–1.2 maintenance, 0.8–1.4 acute mania)
  • Toxicity precipitated by dehydration from vomiting and diarrhea
  • Decreased fluid → ↑ lithium concentration → toxicity

Toxicity Manifestations to Assess

  • Coarse tremor, slurred speech
  • Confusion, lethargy, ataxia
  • Hyperreflexia, muscle twitching
  • Severe N/V, diarrhea (worsened by GI illness)
  • Severe (> 2.0): seizures, coma, cardiovascular collapse

Nursing Actions

  • HOLD next lithium dose
  • Notify provider immediately
  • IV fluid replacement (NS) for hydration
  • Monitor lithium level every 6–12 hours
  • Severe toxicity (> 2.0): prepare for hemodialysis (most effective treatment)
  • Monitor vital signs, neurologic status, intake/output

Client Education for Preventing Recurrence

  • Maintain 2–3 L fluid intake daily
  • Maintain consistent sodium intake
  • When vomiting/diarrhea/fever/heavy sweating: hold lithium and notify provider
  • AVOID NSAIDs and ACE inhibitors
  • Carry a medical alert
  • Schedule routine lithium levels and follow up

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 9.1

A nurse is reviewing the medication record of a client taking lithium. Which of the following should the nurse identify as a concerning interaction?

  1. Acetaminophen 500 mg PRN for pain
  2. Ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for arthritis
  3. Multivitamin once daily
  4. Loratadine 10 mg daily for allergies
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Acetaminophen is safe to use with lithium.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) decrease renal clearance of lithium, leading to elevated levels and toxicity. Avoid NSAIDs or use cautiously with monitoring.
  • C. A standard multivitamin is not contraindicated.
  • D. Loratadine is safe with lithium.

Exercise 9.2

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed lithium. Which of the following statements indicate understanding? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "I will drink 2–3 liters of fluid each day."
  2. "I will take this medication with food."
  3. "I will use a low-sodium diet to prevent weight gain."
  4. "I will get my blood drawn periodically to check levels."
  5. "I will stop taking lithium if I feel better."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, D

  • A. Correct — CORRECT — Adequate hydration is essential to prevent lithium toxicity. Dehydration concentrates lithium and increases risk.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — Taking lithium with food reduces GI upset.
  • C. INCORRECT — Sodium restriction increases lithium retention and toxicity risk. Maintain a CONSISTENT sodium intake.
  • D. Correct — CORRECT — Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and requires routine level monitoring (q3–6 months once stable; more often during titration).
  • E. INCORRECT — Discontinuing mood stabilizers without medical guidance increases relapse risk and worsens outcomes.

Exercise 9.3

A client taking valproic acid for bipolar disorder reports severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. Which of the following should the nurse suspect?

  1. Constipation
  2. Pancreatitis
  3. Hepatotoxicity
  4. Thrombocytopenia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Constipation does not typically cause severe pain radiating to the back.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — Valproate can cause acute pancreatitis, which presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. This is a serious adverse effect requiring immediate evaluation.
  • C. Hepatotoxicity typically presents with jaundice, fatigue, and elevated LFTs — not severe back pain.
  • D. Thrombocytopenia presents with easy bruising and bleeding, not abdominal pain.

Exercise 9.4

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed lamotrigine for bipolar maintenance. Which of the following teaching points is most important?

  1. "Take this medication on an empty stomach."
  2. "Report any rash to the provider immediately."
  3. "Lamotrigine will work within 24 hours."
  4. "You can discontinue this medication when you feel stable."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Lamotrigine can be taken with or without food. This is not the priority teaching.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — Lamotrigine can cause Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, a life-threatening rash. ANY rash warrants immediate evaluation. Slow titration (6+ weeks) is used to reduce this risk.
  • C. Mood stabilizers take weeks to reach therapeutic effect.
  • D. Mood stabilizers should be continued long-term to prevent relapse.

Exercise 9.5

A client taking carbamazepine for bipolar disorder reports a sore throat and fever. Which of the following should the nurse do first?

  1. Administer acetaminophen for the fever
  2. Obtain a CBC
  3. Increase fluid intake
  4. Continue the current dose and recheck in 1 week
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Symptomatic treatment is important but does not address the priority concern.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — Carbamazepine can cause agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia. A sore throat and fever can be early signs of infection due to neutropenia. The priority is to check the CBC to assess for blood dyscrasias.
  • C. Hydration is supportive but not the priority assessment.
  • D. These symptoms require immediate evaluation, not delayed monitoring.

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 10

Psychotic Disorders

Psychotic disorders (schizophrenia, schizoaffective) are treated with first-generation (conventional) antipsychotics like haloperidol and second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics like risperidone, olanzapine, and clozapine. First-gen agents cause more EPS; second-gen cause more metabolic effects.

Psychotic Disorders — Overview

Antipsychotics target schizophrenia’s positive and negative symptoms — the generation determines both coverage and side effects.

Antipsychotic therapy — overview

Positive vs negative
  • Used primarily for schizophrenia spectrum disorders — acute exacerbations with partial remissions
  • Positive manifestations (hallucinations, delusions, bizarre behavior) vs negative (social withdrawal, flat affect, anergia, low motivation)
  • Goals: suppress acute episodes, prevent recurrence, and maximize functioning

First-Generation (Conventional)

Strong on positive symptoms — but movement disorders and NMS define the risk profile.

First-generation antipsychotics — action & uses

Haloperidol
  • Block dopamine (D₂), acetylcholine, histamine, and norepinephrine receptors; prototype chlorpromazine (low-potency), haloperidol (high-potency)
  • Control mainly positive manifestations
  • Uses: acute/chronic psychosis, bipolar mania, Tourette syndrome, severe agitation

Extrapyramidal symptoms & tardive dyskinesia

EPS / TD
  • Early EPS: acute dystonia, akathisia, and parkinsonism — treat with anticholinergics (benztropine, diphenhydramine)
  • Tardive dyskinesia (late): involuntary tongue/face movements (lip-smacking) — may be permanent; use the lowest dose, switch to an atypical, or give valbenazine
  • Evaluate for TD at 12 months, then every 3 months

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome & other effects

NMS — emergency
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: high fever, muscle rigidity, autonomic instability, altered LOC — a medical emergency → stop the drug, cool, hydrate, give dantrolene/bromocriptine
  • Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), sedation, orthostatic hypotension
  • Agranulocytosis (report fever/sore throat), QT prolongation/dysrhythmias; contraindicated in dementia and Parkinson’s

Second-Generation (Atypical)

Cover both symptom types with fewer movement effects — but metabolic effects and clozapine’s blood counts take center stage.

Atypical antipsychotics

Risperidone / olanzapine
  • Block dopamine and serotonin receptors; prototypes risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole, ziprasidone
  • Treat both positive and negative manifestations with fewer EPS — generally first-line
  • Metabolic effects: weight gain, hyperglycemia/new diabetes, and dyslipidemia — monitor weight, glucose, and lipids

Clozapine

Agranulocytosis monitoring
  • Reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia
  • Agranulocytosis risk requires regular WBC/ANC monitoring — report fever/sore throat
  • Also watch for seizures, myocarditis, and significant metabolic effects

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Active Learning Scenario

System Disorder

A nurse is caring for a client with schizophrenia who has been taking haloperidol for 2 weeks. The client now exhibits severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia (104°F), altered mental status, and diaphoresis. The blood pressure is fluctuating. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: System Disorder.

Recognition — Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

  • Tetrad: hyperthermia, severe rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability
  • Life-threatening neurologic emergency
  • Most often within 2 weeks of starting a typical antipsychotic; can occur with atypicals and abrupt discontinuation of dopamine agonists
  • Mortality 10–20% if untreated

Differential — Distinguish from Serotonin Syndrome

  • NMS: "lead pipe" rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability
  • Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, neuromuscular hyperactivity, plus autonomic and mental status changes
  • Both: hyperthermia and altered mental status — clinical context matters

Immediate Nursing Actions

  • DISCONTINUE the antipsychotic immediately
  • Notify the provider STAT — transfer to ICU
  • Cooling measures (cool blankets, IV fluids, ice packs)
  • IV fluid resuscitation
  • Continuous monitoring of vital signs, cardiac rhythm, mental status
  • Anticipate: dantrolene (muscle relaxation), bromocriptine (dopamine agonist)
  • Monitor CK (rhabdomyolysis); BUN/Cr (renal function); electrolytes

Follow-up After Recovery

  • Switch to a different (preferably atypical) antipsychotic
  • Avoid the offending agent for life
  • Educate client and family about NMS warning signs

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 10.1

A nurse is caring for a client receiving haloperidol who develops sudden severe neck spasm and tongue protrusion. The nurse should anticipate administering which of the following medications?

  1. Benztropine IM
  2. Haloperidol IM
  3. Lithium PO
  4. Naloxone IM
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — CORRECT — These are acute dystonic reactions, which respond to anticholinergic medications. IM benztropine (or diphenhydramine) is administered for rapid relief.
  • B. Haloperidol is the cause of the reaction. Giving more would worsen the symptoms.
  • C. Lithium is a mood stabilizer, not appropriate for acute dystonia.
  • D. Naloxone reverses opioids, not antipsychotic side effects.

Exercise 10.2

A nurse is caring for a client receiving clozapine for treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Which of the following is the priority assessment?

  1. Daily weight
  2. Fasting glucose
  3. WBC and ANC
  4. Liver function tests
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Weight monitoring is important but not the priority for clozapine.
  • B. Glucose monitoring is important due to metabolic effects but not the priority.
  • C. Correct — CORRECT — Clozapine causes agranulocytosis (life-threatening). Weekly WBC/ANC for 6 months, then biweekly, then monthly is required (REMS program). The medication cannot be dispensed without a current count.
  • D. LFTs are monitored but not the priority for clozapine.

Exercise 10.3

A nurse is monitoring a client on long-term antipsychotic therapy. Which of the following findings indicate tardive dyskinesia? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Lip smacking
  2. Tongue protrusion
  3. Choreoathetoid movements of the extremities
  4. Severe muscle rigidity and hyperthermia
  5. Acute torticollis
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C

  • A. Correct — CORRECT — Repetitive involuntary movements of the face, especially lip smacking and tongue protrusion, are hallmarks of TD.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — TD commonly involves the tongue and face.
  • C. Correct — CORRECT — Slow, twisting movements of arms, fingers, and toes are part of TD.
  • D. These describe NMS, not TD. TD is a movement disorder without autonomic instability.
  • E. Acute torticollis is acute dystonia, not TD. TD develops over months/years.

Exercise 10.4

A nurse is teaching a client newly prescribed risperidone. Which of the following statements indicates the need for further teaching?

  1. "I will have my weight and blood sugar monitored regularly."
  2. "I can stop taking this medication when I no longer hear voices."
  3. "I will avoid alcohol while taking this medication."
  4. "I will report any uncontrolled muscle movements."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Correct understanding — atypicals require metabolic monitoring.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT (indicates further teaching needed) — Antipsychotics must be continued long-term to prevent relapse. Abrupt discontinuation often leads to symptom return.
  • C. Correct understanding — alcohol increases sedation and risk.
  • D. Correct understanding — risperidone has the highest EPS risk among atypicals.

Exercise 10.5

A nurse is assessing a client newly prescribed an atypical antipsychotic. Which of the following baseline assessments are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Weight, BMI, waist circumference
  2. Fasting glucose
  3. Fasting lipid panel
  4. AIMS exam
  5. Pulmonary function tests
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, D

  • A. Correct — CORRECT — Baseline anthropometrics are essential for monitoring metabolic side effects.
  • B. Correct — CORRECT — Baseline glucose is needed; atypicals can cause new-onset diabetes (BBW).
  • C. Correct — CORRECT — Dyslipidemia is a known effect of atypical antipsychotics.
  • D. Correct — CORRECT — Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale screens for tardive dyskinesia; reassess every 3–6 months.
  • E. Not routinely indicated for antipsychotic monitoring.

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 11

Medications for Children and Adolescents Who Have Mental Health Issues

Mental health medications in children and adolescents focus on ADHD (CNS stimulants like methylphenidate and amphetamines; non-stimulant atomoxetine), anxiety and depression (select SSRIs), and conduct/aggression. All psychotropics in pediatrics carry heightened black-box warnings.

TL;DR · One-glance summary

ADHD stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) — Schedule II, monitor weight/height/sleep, take in AM. Atomoxetine — non-stimulant alternative, no abuse potential. SSRIs in pediatrics: fluoxetine and escitalopram FDA-approved; black box for suicidal ideation. Atypicals for severe behavioral issues.

ADHD stimulants

  • Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta, Daytrana patch): Schedule II
  • Amphetamines (Adderall, Vyvanse, dextroamphetamine): Schedule II
  • AE: Appetite suppression (weight loss/growth delay), insomnia, tachycardia, hypertension, irritability
  • Teaching: Give in AM (avoid evening dose); take with food; monitor weight/height; "drug holidays" sometimes used
  • Contraindicated: Cardiac structural abnormalities; severe anxiety

Non-stimulants & antidepressants

  • Atomoxetine (Strattera): SNRI; non-controlled; 1–3 weeks for onset; black box for suicidal ideation
  • Clonidine, guanfacine: Alpha-2 agonists; help with ADHD + tics; sedating
  • SSRIs for pediatric depression/anxiety: Fluoxetine (8+ yo), escitalopram (12+ yo) — FDA approved
  • Black box warning: Heightened suicide risk in children — close monitoring required

Other pediatric psychotropics

  • Atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, aripiprazole) for autism-related irritability, Tourette
  • Lithium and anticonvulsants used cautiously
  • Always consider non-pharm interventions first (behavioral therapy)

Pediatric MH — additional

  • Desipramine, nortriptyline (TCAs): Sometimes used cautiously for ADHD or depression in adolescents; baseline ECG (cardiac monitoring); narrow TI in overdose
  • Lithium use in children: Approved > 7 yo for bipolar; close monitoring of levels
  • Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine): Prodrug — must be metabolized to be active; less abuse potential than other amphetamines
  • Strattera (atomoxetine): Non-stimulant; 1–3 weeks to onset; black box for suicidal ideation; hepatotoxicity risk
  • Guanfacine (Intuniv), clonidine (Kapvay): Alpha-2 agonists; help with ADHD impulsivity, sleep, Tourette's; sedating; rebound HTN if stopped
  • Eating disorders: Fluoxetine FDA-approved for bulimia; do not initiate antidepressants if active anorexia (risk of seizures with electrolyte imbalances)
A child started on methylphenidate (Concerta) for ADHD. What are the four key monitoring/teaching points?
(1) Give in the morning — late dosing causes insomnia. (2) Monitor weight and height — appetite suppression can cause growth delay; consider "drug holidays" on weekends/summers. (3) Monitor cardiac status (HR, BP) — contraindicated in structural heart abnormalities. (4) Schedule II controlled substance — written Rx, no refills, secure storage. Vyvanse (lisdexamfetamine) is a prodrug → less abuse potential than other amphetamines.
When would atomoxetine (Strattera) be chosen over a stimulant for ADHD — and what are its key downsides?
Chosen when: stimulants contraindicated (cardiac issues, severe anxiety), history of substance abuse, or tics/Tourette syndrome. Mechanism: SNRI; not a controlled substance. Downsides: takes 1–3 weeks for onset (vs. stimulants in 30 min), black box warning for suicidal ideation, and risk of hepatotoxicity (teach client to report jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain).
Which two SSRIs are FDA-approved for pediatric depression — and what is the critical safety counseling?
Fluoxetine (Prozac): approved age 8+. Escitalopram (Lexapro): approved age 12+. Black box warning: heightened risk of suicidal ideation in children/adolescents, especially in first 4 weeks. Counsel parents to watch for worsening mood, agitation, new suicidal thoughts. Schedule weekly follow-up initially. Therapy is most effective combined with psychotherapy.

Pediatric Mental Health — Overview

Medications for children and adolescents treat ADHD, depression, anxiety, and related disorders — always alongside behavioral and family therapy.

Principles of pediatric psychopharmacology

Start low, monitor closely
  • Dose by weight; start low and titrate slowly, and reassess frequently as the child grows
  • Monitor growth (height/weight) with stimulants and assess for increased suicidal ideation when starting antidepressants
  • Combine medication with behavioral, school, and family interventions for best outcomes

CNS Stimulants

First-line pharmacologic treatment for ADHD. They raise norepinephrine and dopamine levels to improve attention and impulse control; best combined with behavioral therapy.

Methylphenidate, amphetamines

Schedule II · ADHD

Methylphenidate, dexmethylphenidate, dextroamphetamine, and amphetamine mixtures. Therapeutic effects begin rapidly.

Complications

  • Insomnia, restlessness — give last dose before 4 p.m.
  • Decreased appetite, weight loss, growth suppression — monitor height/weight against baseline
  • Cardiac effects (palpitations, hypertension, dysrhythmias); possible psychotic manifestations

Contraindications & interactions

  • History of substance use disorder, hypertension, cardiovascular disease, anxiety
  • MAOIs → hypertensive crisis (separate by 14 days)
  • High abuse potential; Schedule II handling/refill rules

Non-Stimulant ADHD Medications

Alternatives when stimulants are unsuitable (substance-use risk, intolerable effects) or insufficient.

Atomoxetine

Selective NRI · non-stimulant
  • Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor; not a controlled substance; maximal effect can take up to 6 weeks
  • Complications: appetite/weight/growth suppression, suicidal ideation (monitor), and hepatotoxicity (report jaundice, dark urine, RUQ pain)
  • Contraindicated with hepatic disorders; MAOIs → hypertensive crisis

Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists — Guanfacine, clonidine

Non-stimulant
  • Centrally acting; used for ADHD and tic disorders
  • Sedation and hypotension/bradycardia; rebound hypertension if abruptly stopped — taper
  • Monitor blood pressure and pulse; extended-release forms are not interchangeable mg-for-mg with immediate-release

Antidepressants in Youth

SSRIs and TCAs treat pediatric depression, anxiety, and OCD; both require close monitoring for increased suicidal ideation early in therapy.

SSRIs — Fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine

First-line
  • Selectively inhibit serotonin reuptake; for depression, anxiety, OCD
  • Increased suicide risk in children/adolescents — assess for depression and monitor closely, especially early
  • Serotonin syndrome risk with other serotonergic drugs; taper to discontinue

Tricyclic antidepressants — Desipramine

Second-line for ADHD
  • Block reuptake of norepinephrine/serotonin; used for ADHD (less effective than stimulants) and depression
  • Increased suicide risk, orthostatic hypotension, anticholinergic effects, sedation, weight gain
  • Cardiac toxicity in overdose; concurrent MAOIs are dangerous

Second-Generation Antipsychotics

Used for irritability/aggression in autism spectrum disorder and for conduct and bipolar disorders in youth.

Risperidone (and other atypicals)

Atypical antipsychotic
  • Block serotonin and dopamine receptors; for autism-related irritability, conduct disorder, bipolar disorder
  • Metabolic effects (weight gain, diabetes, dyslipidemia — monitor), EPS, sedation, elevated prolactin
  • Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants; start low and titrate

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse working in a pediatric mental health clinic is caring for a client who has a new prescription for risperidone for the treatment of conduct disorder. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify at least four adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Identify at least four nursing interventions to prevent or minimize the adverse effects of this medication.

Complications

  • New onset of diabetes mellitus or loss of glucose control in clients who have diabetes
  • Weight gain
  • Hypercholesterolemia
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Anticholinergic effects (urinary hesitancy or retention, dry mouth)
  • Agitation
  • Dizziness
  • Sedation
  • Sleep disruption
  • Tremors
  • Agranulocytosis, neutropenia
  • Hyperprolactinemia

Nursing Interventions

  • Obtain the client's fasting blood glucose prior to and periodically throughout treatment.
  • Instruct the client to report indications of diabetes mellitus including increased thirst, urination, and appetite.
  • Advise clients to follow a healthy, low-caloric diet.
  • Recommend regular exercise.
  • Monitor weight throughout treatment.
  • Monitor cholesterol and triglycerides, especially if weight gain is more than 30 lb.
  • Monitor blood pressure with first dose and instruct client to change positions slowly.
  • Encourage the client to sip fluids throughout the day.
  • Monitor and report manifestations of an infection (a sore throat).
  • Monitor and report gyneocomastia and amenorrhea.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 11.1

A nurse is teaching the guardians of a child who has a new prescription for desipramine. The nurse should include that which of the following adverse effects is the priority to report to the provider?

  1. Constipation
  2. Suicidal thoughts
  3. Photophobia
  4. Dry mouth
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Constipation is an anticholinergic effect of desipramine; increase fluids — but another effect is the priority.
  • B. Correct — The greatest risk is injury from a suicide attempt. Desipramine (a TCA) can cause suicidal thoughts/behaviors; guardians should monitor and report increased depression or suicidal ideation.
  • C. Photophobia is an anticholinergic effect; wear sunglasses — but another effect is the priority.
  • D. Dry mouth is an anticholinergic effect; use fluids/hard candy — but another effect is the priority.

Exercise 11.2

A nurse is teaching an adolescent client who has a new prescription for clomipramine for OCD. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include to minimize an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Wear sunglasses when outdoors.
  2. Check your temperature daily.
  3. Take this medication in the morning.
  4. Add extra calories to your diet.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Wearing sunglasses outdoors decreases photophobia, an anticholinergic effect associated with TCA use.
  • B. Daily temperature checks are not necessary with a TCA.
  • C. Take a TCA at bedtime rather than morning to prevent daytime sleepiness.
  • D. A low-calorie diet helps prevent weight gain, an adverse effect of TCAs — extra calories would worsen it.

Exercise 11.3

A nurse is caring for a school-age child who has a new prescription for atomoxetine. The nurse should monitor the client for which of the following manifestations as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Kidney toxicity
  2. Liver damage
  3. Seizure activity
  4. Adrenal insufficiency
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Atomoxetine can cause urinary retention, but not kidney toxicity.
  • B. Correct — Liver damage is an adverse effect of atomoxetine. Monitor for jaundice, upper abdominal tenderness, dark urine, and elevated liver enzymes.
  • C. Bupropion increases seizure risk at high doses; seizure activity is not an atomoxetine effect.
  • D. Atomoxetine can cause suicidal ideation and mood swings; adrenal insufficiency is not an effect.

  2. Leave the patch on for 9 hr.
  3. Apply the patch to the child's waist.
  4. Use opened tray within 6 months.

Answer: B

  • A. Transdermal methylphenidate is applied once per day.
  • B. Correct — Transdermal methylphenidate is worn for 9 hr/day.
  • C. The patch is applied to the child's hip, not the waist.
  • D. Use an opened tray within 2 months, not 6.

Exercise 11.5

A nurse is teaching the guardians and their school-age child about a new prescription for lisdexamfetamine. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching? (Select all that apply.)

  1. An adverse effect of this medication is CNS stimulation.
  2. Administer the medication before bedtime.
  3. Monitor blood pressure while taking this medication.
  4. Therapeutic effects of this medication will take 1 to 3 weeks to fully develop.
  5. This medication raises the levels of dopamine in the brain.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, C, E

  • A. Correct — CNS stimulation (insomnia, restlessness) is an adverse effect.
  • B. Incorrect — Administer in the morning to reduce insomnia, not at bedtime.
  • C. Correct — Monitor blood pressure due to potential cardiovascular effects.
  • D. Incorrect — Therapeutic effects begin immediately and last 10 to 12 hr (not 1-3 weeks).
  • E. Correct — Lisdexamfetamine, a CNS stimulant, raises norepinephrine and dopamine levels in the CNS.

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 12

Substance Use Disorders

Substance use disorders are treated with deterrents, replacement therapies, and withdrawal management. Alcohol: disulfiram, naltrexone, acamprosate. Opioids: methadone, buprenorphine, naltrexone, naloxone (overdose reversal). Tobacco: nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion.

Substance Use Disorders — Overview

Withdrawal can be dangerous; medications ease it and support long-term abstinence.

Substance use disorders — overview

Tolerance & withdrawal
  • Tolerance requires more substance for the same effect; withdrawal/abstinence syndrome occurs when blood levels of a dependent substance fall
  • Withdrawal severity varies by substance and can include GI, neurologic, cardiovascular changes, and seizures
  • Pharmacologic care supports safe withdrawal and maintains abstinence

Alcohol Use Disorder

Benzodiazepines carry clients through withdrawal; disulfiram and naltrexone support staying sober.

Alcohol withdrawal

Benzodiazepines
  • Withdrawal begins 4–12 hr after the last intake and lasts 5–7 days: nausea, tremors, restlessness, elevated vital signs, diaphoresis, and possible tonic-clonic seizures
  • Alcohol withdrawal delirium (2–3 days after cessation) is a medical emergency
  • Benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, lorazepam) ease withdrawal and prevent seizures; provide thiamine and fluids

Abstinence maintenance

Disulfiram / naltrexone
  • Disulfiram (aversion therapy): causes acetaldehyde syndrome if alcohol is consumed (nausea, flushing, hypotension → can be fatal) — avoid all alcohol-containing products; effects persist 2 weeks
  • Naltrexone (opioid antagonist): reduces alcohol craving — ensure the client is opioid-free first
  • Acamprosate: reduces the dysphoria/anxiety of abstinence

Opioid & Nicotine Use

Replacement and antagonist therapy for opioids; craving-blockers for nicotine.

Opioid use disorder

Methadone / buprenorphine
  • Methadone (replacement): prevents withdrawal in maintenance programs
  • Buprenorphine (often with naloxone): safer with less respiratory-depression risk and can be office-prescribed
  • Clonidine eases withdrawal symptoms

Opioid overdose reversal

Naloxone
  • Naloxone is the opioid antagonist that reverses respiratory depression, coma, and other toxicity
  • Given IM, subcutaneous, IV, or intranasal
  • Short half-life — repeat doses may be needed as it can wear off before the opioid

Nicotine cessation

Bupropion / varenicline
  • Bupropion: reduces craving and withdrawal — avoid in clients at increased seizure risk
  • Varenicline: a nicotinic receptor agonist that reduces craving and relapse — monitor blood pressure and mood/behavior
  • Nicotine replacement (patch, gum, lozenge) supports gradual withdrawal

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has tobacco use disorder about a new prescription for varenicline to promote smoking cessation. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify at least three adverse effects.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify at least two teaching points.
  • EVALUATION OF MEDICATION EFFECTIVENESS: Identify a client outcome to indicate medication effectiveness.

Expected Pharmacological Action

Varenicline is a nicotinic receptor agonist that promotes the release of dopamine to simulate the pleasurable effects of nicotine.

Therapeutic Uses

Varenicline is indicated to reduce nicotine cravings and block the desired effects of nicotine in clients who have tobacco use disorder.

Complications

  • New-onset hypertension
  • Loss of glycemic control in clients who have diabetes mellitus
  • Nausea
  • Vomiting
  • Insomnia
  • New-onset depression
  • Suicidal thoughts

Client Education

  • Clients who are commercial truck or bus drivers, airplane pilots, or air traffic controllers should not take varenicline.
  • Take medication after a meal.
  • Titrate as prescribed to minimize adverse effects.
  • Notify the provider if adverse effects occur.

Evaluation Of Medication Effectiveness

  • The client will maintain smoking cessation.
  • The client will report reduced cravings for nicotine.

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 12.1

A nurse is providing teaching for a client who is withdrawing from alcohol and has a new prescription for propranolol. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Increases the risk for seizure activity
  2. Provides a form of aversion therapy
  3. Decreases cravings
  4. Can increase blood pressure
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Seizure activity is a potential effect of alcohol withdrawal itself, not of propranolol.
  • B. Disulfiram, not propranolol, provides aversion therapy.
  • C. Correct — Propranolol is an adjunct medication used during alcohol withdrawal to decrease cravings and reduce autonomic symptoms.
  • D. Propranolol is an antihypertensive that can lower (not increase) blood pressure.

A charge nurse is planning a staff education session to discuss medications used during the care of a client experiencing alcohol withdrawal. Which of the following medications should the charge nurse include in the discussion? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Lorazepam
  2. Diazepam
  3. Disulfiram
  4. Naltrexone
  5. Acamprosate

Answer: A, B

  • A. Correct — Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine, is used to manage acute alcohol withdrawal.
  • B. Correct — Diazepam, a benzodiazepine, is used to manage acute alcohol withdrawal.
  • C. Incorrect — Disulfiram is used to maintain abstinence, not to treat withdrawal.
  • D. Incorrect — Naltrexone is used to maintain abstinence, not to treat withdrawal.

Answer: B

  • A. Constipation, rather than diarrhea, is a common adverse effect of clonidine.
  • B. Correct — Dry mouth can be an adverse effect of clonidine.

Exercise 12.4

A nurse is teaching a client who has tobacco use disorder about nicotine replacement therapy. Which of the following statements by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

  1. "I should avoid eating right before I chew a piece of nicotine gum."
  2. "I will need to stop using the nicotine gum after 1 year."
  3. "I know that nicotine gum is a safe alternative to smoking if I become pregnant."
  4. "I must chew the nicotine gum quickly for about 15 minutes."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — The client should avoid eating or drinking (especially acidic beverages) right before chewing nicotine gum, as this reduces absorption.
  • B. Nicotine gum is generally used for up to ~12 weeks, not 1 year.
  • C. The client should avoid all nicotine products, including gum, during pregnancy.
  • D. Chew slowly and intermittently ("chew and park"), not quickly.

Exercise 12.5

A nurse in an acute mental health facility is caring for a client who is experiencing withdrawal from opioid use and has a new prescription for clonidine. Which of the following actions should the nurse identify as the priority?

  1. Administer the clonidine on the prescribed schedule.
  2. Provide ice chips at the client's bedside.
  3. Educate the client on the effects of clonidine.
  4. Obtain baseline vital signs.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Administering clonidine on schedule, providing ice chips for comfort, and educating the client are all important actions — but not the priority.
  • D. Correct — Assessment is the first step of the nursing process. Baseline vital signs are needed before giving clonidine (which lowers blood pressure and heart rate).

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 13

Chronic Neurologic Disorders

Chronic neurologic disorders include Parkinson disease (levodopa/carbidopa, dopamine agonists), Alzheimer disease (donepezil, memantine), multiple sclerosis (interferon beta, glatiramer), myasthenia gravis (neostigmine, pyridostigmine), epilepsy (phenytoin, valproate, gabapentin), and migraine (triptans, ergot alkaloids).

Chronic Neurologic Disorders — Overview

Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s, and seizures — therapy manages symptoms and slows decline.

Chronic neurologic medications — overview

Symptom management
  • Cover Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and seizure disorders
  • Therapy manages manifestations and improves quality of life; many of these drugs have narrow margins and important interactions

Parkinson’s Disease

Restore the dopamine–acetylcholine balance — levodopa/carbidopa is the cornerstone.

Levodopa/carbidopa

Dopamine replacement
  • Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and converts to dopamine; carbidopa prevents its peripheral breakdown so more reaches the CNS
  • Adverse: nausea, dyskinesias, orthostatic hypotension, and psychosis (visual hallucinations); “wearing-off” effects over time
  • Avoid high-protein meals and vitamin B6 (pyridoxine), which reduce levodopa’s effect; take with food initially for nausea

Other anti-Parkinson’s agents

Dopamine agonists
  • Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole, bromocriptine): activate dopamine receptors — can cause sleep attacks/impulse-control issues
  • COMT inhibitors (entacapone) and MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline) extend levodopa’s effect
  • Anticholinergics (benztropine) and amantadine help tremor and dyskinesias

Alzheimer’s & Seizure Disorders

Cholinesterase inhibitors for memory; antiepileptics with their signature toxicities.

Cholinesterase inhibitors & Alzheimer’s

Donepezil
  • Prevent breakdown of acetylcholine → more ACh at receptors; donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine for Alzheimer’s; neostigmine for myasthenia gravis
  • Excessive muscarinic stimulation (cholinergic effects): salivation, diaphoresis, diarrhea, bradycardia — atropine is the antidote
  • Memantine (NMDA antagonist) is also used for moderate-to-severe Alzheimer’s

Phenytoin

Narrow therapeutic range
  • A first-line antiepileptic for many seizure types; narrow therapeutic range (monitor levels)
  • Gingival hyperplasia (good oral hygiene/dental care), sedation, and ataxia
  • Many interactions; decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness

Other antiepileptics

Valproate / carbamazepine
  • Valproic acid: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and teratogenicity (neural tube defects) — monitor LFTs
  • Carbamazepine: bone marrow suppression and hyponatremia — monitor CBC/sodium
  • Levetiracetam, lamotrigine (watch for Stevens-Johnson), gabapentin, and phenobarbital

Status epilepticus

Emergency
  • Prolonged or repeated seizures without recovery — a medical emergency
  • IV benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam) are first-line to stop the seizure
  • Protect the airway, give oxygen, and follow with a longer-acting antiepileptic

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is planning care for a client who has tonic-clonic seizures and a new prescription for phenytoin. Considering the adverse effects and nursing interventions, what should the nurse include in the plan of care? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item to include the following:

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects and two medication interactions.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Include two interventions that relate to the two adverse effects, and two interventions that relate to the two medication interactions.

Therapeutic Uses

Phenytoin is a hydantoin medication that suppresses partial seizure and primary generalized seizure activity in the affected neurons.

Complications

  • CNS effects
  • Gingival hyperplasia
  • Teratogenic birth defects
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, and glucocorticoids
  • Causes stimulation of hepatic medication-metabolizing enzymes
  • Alcohol (acute use), diazepam, cimetidine, and valproic acid increase phenytoin levels.
  • Carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and chronic alcohol use decrease phenytoin levels.
  • Additive CNS depressant effects can occur with concurrent use of CNS depressants.

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client to refrain from alcohol and other medications that cause CNS depression, such as barbiturates.
  • Encourage the client to use dental floss and massage gums daily.
  • Instruct the client to avoid pregnancy and use an alternate form of contraception.
  • Monitor INR if on warfarin and blood glucose levels if taking a glucocorticoid.
  • Monitor therapeutic effects of warfarin and glucocorticoids.
  • Never abruptly discontinue antiepileptic medications.
  • Advise clients to avoid use of alcohol and other CNS depressants
  • Monitor blood phenytoin levels

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 13.1

A nurse in the post-anesthesia recovery unit is caring for a client who received a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent and has muscle weakness. The nurse should expect a prescription for which of the following medications?

  1. Neostigmine
  2. Naloxone
  3. Dantrolene
  4. Vecuronium
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Neostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, reverses the effects of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents.
  • B. Naloxone reverses the effects of opioids.
  • C. Dantrolene acts on skeletal muscle to reduce metabolic activity (used for malignant hyperthermia).
  • D. Vecuronium is itself an intermediate-acting nondepolarizing blocking agent.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 13.2

A nurse is providing information to a client who has early Parkinson's disease and a new prescription for pramipexole. The nurse should instruct the client to monitor for which of the following adverse effects of this medication?

  1. Hallucinations
  2. Increased salivation
  3. Diarrhea
  4. Discoloration of urine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Pramipexole (a dopamine agonist) can cause hallucinations.
  • B. Increased salivation is an adverse effect of cholinesterase inhibitors, not pramipexole.
  • C. Constipation, not diarrhea, is an adverse effect of pramipexole.
  • D. Discoloration of urine is associated with COMT inhibitors (e.g., entacapone), not pramipexole.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 13.3

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for levodopa/carbidopa for Parkinson's disease. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. Increase intake of protein-rich foods.
  2. Expect muscle twitching to occur.
  3. Take this medication with food.
  4. Anticipate relief of manifestations in 24 hr.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Avoid high-protein foods, which can reduce levodopa absorption and effectiveness.
  • B. Muscle twitching (dyskinesia) should be monitored and reported, not expected as normal.
  • C. Correct — Take levodopa/carbidopa with food to reduce GI upset.
  • D. Therapeutic relief develops gradually over weeks to months, not 24 hr.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 13.4

A nurse is preparing to administer a medication to a client who has absence seizures. The nurse should expect to administer which of the following medications to the client? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Phenytoin
  2. Ethosuximide
  3. Gabapentin
  4. Carbamazepine
  5. Valproic acid
  6. Lamotrigine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, E, F

  • A. Incorrect — Phenytoin is prescribed for partial (focal) and tonic-clonic seizures.
  • B. Correct — Ethosuximide's sole indication is absence seizures.
  • C. Incorrect — Gabapentin is prescribed for partial seizures.
  • D. Incorrect — Carbamazepine is prescribed for partial and tonic-clonic seizures.
  • E. Correct — Valproic acid is effective for absence seizures (broad-spectrum).
  • F. Correct — Lamotrigine is effective for absence seizures (broad-spectrum).

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 13.5

A nurse is reviewing a new prescription for oxcarbazepine with a client who has partial seizures. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "Use caution if given a prescription for a diuretic medication."
  2. "Consider using an alternate form of contraception if you are using oral contraceptives."
  3. "Chew gum to increase saliva production."
  4. "Avoid driving until you see how the medication affects you."
  5. "Notify your provider if you develop a skin rash."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, D, E

  • A. Correct — Use caution with diuretics, which can compound the risk of hyponatremia associated with oxcarbazepine.
  • B. Correct — Oxcarbazepine reduces oral contraceptive effectiveness; use an alternate method.
  • C. Incorrect — Chewing gum to increase salivation is not indicated for this medication.
  • D. Correct — Avoid driving until CNS effects (dizziness, drowsiness) are known.
  • E. Correct — Report any skin rash; it can signal a serious hypersensitivity reaction.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 14

Eye and Ear Disorders

Eye disorders include glaucoma (treated with beta blockers, prostaglandin analogs, cholinergics, alpha agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), allergic conjunctivitis, and infections. Ear disorders are primarily otitis externa (topical antibiotic-steroid drops) and otitis media (oral antibiotics).

Glaucoma Medications

Most are eye drops — punctal occlusion is the key technique to limit systemic effects.

Beta blockers

Timolol
  • Timolol decreases aqueous humor production to lower IOP
  • Apply gentle pressure on the nasolacrimal duct for 30–60 seconds after instilling to minimize systemic absorption
  • Systemic effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm) — caution in asthma/COPD and diabetes; monitor pulse

Alpha₂ agonists & prostaglandin analogs

Brimonidine / latanoprost
  • Brimonidine (alpha₂ agonist): decreases production and increases outflow — first-line for POAG; causes stinging/dry mouth
  • Latanoprost (prostaglandin analog): increases outflow — causes permanent brown iris pigmentation and eyelash growth
  • Teach not to rub the eyes; report changes

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors & osmotics

Acetazolamide / mannitol
  • Acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor): reduces aqueous humor production via diuresis — a nonantimicrobial sulfonamide (sulfa-allergy caution)
  • Mannitol (osmotic): rapidly lowers IOP in acute angle-closure glaucoma to prevent blindness
  • Cholinergic agonists (pilocarpine) constrict the pupil to improve outflow

Ear Disorders

Otic agents soften cerumen and treat infection — and watch for ototoxic systemic drugs.

Otic medications

Antibiotic/steroid drops
  • Cerumenolytics soften and help remove earwax
  • Otic antibiotic/steroid drops treat otitis externa; warm drops to body temperature before instilling
  • Be aware of ototoxic medications (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, high-dose aspirin) — report tinnitus or hearing changes

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a provider's office is teaching a client who has a prescription for ciprofloxacin/hydrocortisone about the medication and how to prevent otitis externa. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify two therapeutic effects of the medication.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two potential adverse effects.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify two actions to prevent otitis externa.

Therapeutic Uses

The bactericidal effects of ciprofloxacin and the anti-inflammatory effect of hydrocortisone decreases pain, edema, and erythema in the ear.

Complications

  • Rash
  • Dizziness, lightheadedness, tremors, restlessness, and convulsions

Client Education

  • Keep foreign bodies out of ear canal.
  • Avoid manual measures to remove cerumen.
  • Dry ear canal after bathing or swimming using a towel.
  • Avoid use of ear plugs except for swimming.

Exercise 14.1

A nurse is instructing a client who has a new prescription for timolol how to insert eye drops. The nurse should instruct the client to press on which of the following areas to prevent systemic absorption of the medication?

  1. Bony orbit
  2. Nasolacrimal duct
  3. Conjunctival sac
  4. Outer canthus
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Pressing on the bony orbit will not prevent systemic absorption.
  • B. Correct — Pressing on the nasolacrimal duct (inner canthus) prevents the drug from draining into systemic circulation.
  • C. Pressing on the conjunctival sac will not prevent systemic absorption.
  • D. Pressing on the outer canthus will not prevent systemic absorption.

Exercise 14.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for brimonidine ophthalmic drops and wears soft contact lenses. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. "This medication can stain your contacts."
  2. "This medication can cause your pupils to constrict."
  3. "This medication can absorb into your contacts."
  4. "This medication can slow your heart rate."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Rifampin (not brimonidine) can stain soft contact lenses.
  • B. Brimonidine can cause mydriasis (dilated pupils), not constriction.
  • C. Correct — Brimonidine can absorb into soft contact lenses; remove lenses before instillation and wait before reinserting.
  • D. Beta-adrenergic blockers (timolol) can slow heart rate, not brimonidine.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 14.3

A nurse in an emergency department is reviewing the medical record of a client who is being evaluated for angle-closure glaucoma. Which of the following findings are indicative of this condition?

  1. Insidious onset of painless loss of vision
  2. Gradual reduction in peripheral vision
  3. Severe pain around eyes
  4. Intraocular pressure 12 mm Hg
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B. Insidious painless vision loss and gradual peripheral vision reduction describe open-angle glaucoma.
  • C. Correct — Angle-closure glaucoma has a sudden onset with severe pain around the eyes that can radiate over the face.
  • D. An IOP of 12 mm Hg is within the expected reference range (10-21 mm Hg).

NCLEX® Connection: Physiological Adaptation — Illness Management

Exercise 14.4

A nurse is teaching a client about preventing otitis externa. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. Clean the ear with a cotton-tipped swab daily.
  2. Place earplugs in the ears when sleeping at night.
  3. Use a cool water irrigation solution to remove earwax.
  4. Tip the head to the side to remove water from the ears after showering.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Do not insert anything (including swabs) into the ear; this can damage the canal and push debris inward.
  • B. Earplugs are recommended when swimming, not routinely when sleeping.
  • C. Cool water irrigation is not used; it can cause vertigo and is not for routine wax removal.
  • D. Correct — Tip the head to remove water after showering/swimming to keep the canal dry and prevent otitis externa ("swimmer's ear").

NCLEX® Connection: Health Promotion and Maintenance — Health Promotion/Disease Prevention

Exercise 14.5

A nurse in a provider's office is instructing a guardian of a toddler how to administer ear drops. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "Place the child on the unaffected side when you are ready to administer the medication."
  2. "Warm the medication by gently rolling it between your hands for a few minutes."
  3. "Gently shake medication that is in suspension form."
  4. "Keep the child on their side for 5 minutes after instillation of the ear drops."
  5. "Tightly pack the ear with cotton after instillation of the ear drops."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, D

  • A. Correct — Position the child on the unaffected side so the affected ear is accessible and upward.
  • B. Correct — Warm the medication by rolling between the hands; cold drops can cause vertigo/discomfort.
  • C. Correct — Gently shake medications in suspension form to mix.
  • D. Correct — Keep the child on their side for 5 minutes so the drops reach the eardrum.
  • E. Incorrect — Pack the ear loosely with cotton, not tightly.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 15

Miscellaneous Central Nervous System Medications

Miscellaneous CNS medications include centrally-acting skeletal muscle relaxants for muscle spasm (cyclobenzaprine, methocarbamol, baclofen, dantrolene) and migraine therapies. Most cause significant CNS depression.

Miscellaneous CNS Medications — Overview

Paralytics for surgery, relaxants for spasticity, and bladder agents — a grab-bag of neuromuscular drugs.

Miscellaneous CNS agents — overview

Neuromuscular
  • Neuromuscular blocking agents relax muscles during anesthesia, intubation, and ECT
  • Muscle relaxants/antispasmodics treat spasticity (MS, cerebral palsy, spinal cord injury)
  • Bladder agents treat urinary retention or overactive/neurogenic bladder

Neuromuscular Blocking Agents

They paralyze without sedating — so airway support is mandatory, and malignant hyperthermia is the emergency.

Succinylcholine (depolarizing)

Malignant hyperthermia
  • Mimics acetylcholine, causing sustained depolarization → rapid, short-acting paralysis for intubation
  • Malignant hyperthermia (muscle rigidity, extreme fever): a life-threatening emergency → stop the drug, cool, give 100% O₂ and dantrolene
  • Hyperkalemia — avoid in severe burns, major trauma, or upper-motor-neuron injury; postoperative muscle pain is common

Nondepolarizing blockers

Vecuronium / rocuronium
  • Block acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction (pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium, cisatracurium)
  • Cause paralysis without loss of consciousness or pain relief — sedation/analgesia must be provided separately; support ventilation
  • Aminoglycosides and tetracyclines intensify the blockade; reverse with cholinesterase inhibitors (neostigmine)

Muscle Relaxants & Bladder Agents

Centrally and peripherally acting relaxants for spasticity, plus the two bladder drugs.

Centrally acting muscle relaxants

Baclofen / diazepam
  • Baclofen enhances GABA in the CNS to reduce spasticity (MS, cerebral palsy, spinal cord injury) — do not stop abruptly (seizure risk)
  • Diazepam, cyclobenzaprine, and tizanidine also relieve spasms (tizanidine: hepatotoxicity — monitor LFTs)
  • CNS depression with all of them — avoid alcohol/other depressants and hazardous activities; risk of dependence with long-term use

Dantrolene

Direct-acting
  • A peripherally acting relaxant that blocks calcium release in skeletal muscle to inhibit contraction
  • Uses: spasticity and treatment of malignant hyperthermia
  • Monitor liver function (hepatotoxicity); watch for muscle weakness and sedation

Bladder agents

Bethanechol / oxybutynin
  • Bethanechol (muscarinic agonist): stimulates bladder emptying for urinary retention — watch for cholinergic effects (bradycardia, salivation)
  • Oxybutynin (muscarinic antagonist): relaxes the bladder for overactive/neurogenic bladder — anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention)
  • Teach the expected effects and what to report

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse manager in a surgical center is reviewing nursing responsibilities regarding administration of succinylcholine. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify two common indications for use.
  • MEDICATION ADMINISTRATION: Identify two nursing responsibilities regarding the use of succinylcholine.

Therapeutic Uses

  • Endotracheal intubation
  • Electroconvulsive therapy
  • Endoscopy
  • Adjunct to mechanical ventilation
  • Muscle relaxation during surgery

Medication Administration

  • Clients must receive continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring during therapy.
  • Monitor clients following administration of a neuromuscular blocker for respiratory depression and have life support equipment available.
  • Continue to carefully monitor for return of respiratory function.
  • Succinylcholine is contraindicated for clients at risk for hyperkalemia (trauma, severe burns).

Exercise 15.1

A nurse in the operating room is caring for a client who received a dose of succinylcholine. During the operation, the client suddenly develops rigidity and a rise in body temperature. The nurse should expect a prescription for which of the following medications?

  1. Neostigmine
  2. Naloxone
  3. Dantrolene
  4. Vecuronium
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Neostigmine reverses nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers.
  • B. Naloxone reverses opioids.
  • C. Correct — Muscle rigidity and a sudden temperature rise indicate malignant hyperthermia; dantrolene is the treatment.
  • D. Vecuronium is itself a neuromuscular blocking agent.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 15.2

A nurse in the post-anesthesia care unit is caring for a client who is experiencing malignant hyperthermia. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Place a cooling blanket on the client.
  2. Administer oxygen at 100%.
  3. Administer iced 0.9% sodium chloride.
  4. Administer potassium chloride IV.
  5. Monitor core body temperature.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, E

  • A. Correct — A cooling blanket helps reduce the dangerously high body temperature.
  • B. Correct — Administer 100% oxygen to meet increased metabolic demand.
  • C. Correct — Iced 0.9% sodium chloride IV helps cool the client.
  • D. Incorrect — Malignant hyperthermia causes hyperkalemia; potassium chloride would worsen it.
  • E. Correct — Monitor core body temperature continuously.

NCLEX® Connection: Physiological Adaptation — Medical Emergencies

Exercise 15.3

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for baclofen to treat muscle spasms. Which of the following statements by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "I will stop taking this medication right away if I develop dizziness."
  2. "I know the doctor will gradually increase my dose of this medication for a while."
  3. "I should increase fiber to prevent constipation from this medication."
  4. "I won't be able to drink alcohol while I'm taking this medication."
  5. "I should take this medication on an empty stomach each morning."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C, D

  • A. Incorrect — Do not abruptly stop baclofen; abrupt withdrawal can cause serious effects. Taper under provider guidance.
  • B. Correct — The provider starts a low dose and gradually titrates up.
  • C. Correct — Increase fluids and fiber to prevent constipation.
  • D. Correct — Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants while taking baclofen.
  • E. Incorrect — Take baclofen with food to reduce GI upset, not on an empty stomach.

Exercise 15.4

A nurse is reviewing the medical record of a client who reports urinary incontinence and asks about a prescription for oxybutynin. The nurse should recognize that oxybutynin is contraindicated in the presence of which of the following conditions?

  1. Bursitis
  2. Sinusitis
  3. Depression
  4. Glaucoma
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Bursitis, sinusitis, and depression are not contraindications to oxybutynin.
  • D. Correct — Oxybutynin is an anticholinergic; it is contraindicated in glaucoma (especially angle-closure) because it can raise intraocular pressure.

Exercise 15.5

A nurse is assessing a client who has a prescription for bethanechol to treat urinary retention. The nurse should identify that which of the following findings is a manifestation of muscarinic stimulation?

  1. Dry mouth
  2. Hypertension
  3. Excessive perspiration
  4. Fecal impaction
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Increased salivation (not dry mouth) is a muscarinic effect.
  • B. Hypotension (not hypertension) is a manifestation of muscarinic stimulation.
  • C. Correct — Bethanechol is a muscarinic agonist; excessive perspiration is an expected cholinergic effect.
  • D. Diarrhea (not fecal impaction) is an adverse effect of bethanechol.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 2 · Nervous System · Chapter 16

Sedative-Hypnotics

Sedative-hypnotics treat insomnia and induce sedation. Three classes dominate: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, temazepam), non-benzodiazepine "Z-drugs" (zolpidem, eszopiclone), and newer agents (ramelteon, suvorexant). All risk dependence; benzos reversed with flumazenil.

Sedative-Hypnotics — Overview

CNS depressants that calm anxiety and induce sleep — benzodiazepines lead because barbiturates are so dangerous.

Sedative-hypnotics — overview

CNS depressants
  • Sedatives calm and reduce anxiety; hypnotics induce sleep
  • Three types: benzodiazepines, barbiturates, and benzodiazepine-like agents
  • Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are preferred — barbiturates cause tolerance, dependence, and severe respiratory depression

Barbiturates & Newer Hypnotics

Older barbiturates versus the safer Z-drugs and melatonin agonist.

Barbiturates

Phenobarbital
  • CNS depressants (phenobarbital, secobarbital) used for seizures and, historically, sedation
  • High risk of tolerance, dependence, and respiratory depression; many drug interactions (enzyme induction)
  • Largely replaced by benzodiazepines; taper to discontinue

Benzodiazepine-like agents (Z-drugs)

Zolpidem
  • Zolpidem, zaleplon, eszopiclone treat insomnia with less dependence risk than benzodiazepines
  • Take immediately before bed with time for 7–8 hr of sleep
  • Watch for complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleep-eating) — report them

Melatonin agonist — ramelteon

Chronic insomnia
  • Ramelteon activates melatonin receptors to help with falling asleep (not staying asleep)
  • Take ~30 min before bed on an empty stomach; avoid high-fat meals (delay absorption)
  • Generally well tolerated; can cause hormonal effects (amenorrhea, decreased libido)

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse manager is preparing an educational session to review client use of benzodiazepines for the nurses on their unit. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify five therapeutic uses for benzodiazepines.
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS/PRECAUTIONS: Identify four contraindications for taking benzodiazepines.

Therapeutic Uses

  • Anxiety disorders
  • Seizure disorders
  • Insomnia
  • Muscle spasms
  • Alcohol withdrawal
  • Panic disorder
  • Induction of anesthesia

Contraindications / Precautions

  • Pregnancy: Benzodiazepines are Pregnancy Risk Category D (a high risk to the fetus)
  • Sleep apnea
  • Respiratory depression
  • Organic brain disease
  • Lactation
  • Cautious use in clients who have a history of substance use disorders, liver dysfunction, and kidney failure

Exercise 16.5

A nurse is providing instructions to a client who has a new prescription for zolpidem. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. "Notify the provider if you plan to become pregnant."
  2. "Take the medication 1 hr before you plan to go to sleep."
  3. "Allow at least 6 hr for sleep when taking zolpidem."
  4. "To increase the effectiveness of zolpidem, take it with a bedtime snack."

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Zolpidem is Pregnancy Risk Category C; the client should notify the provider if planning pregnancy.
  • B. Take zolpidem at bedtime (immediately before sleep), not 1 hr before.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 3 · Respiratory · Chapter 17

Airflow Disorders

Airflow disorders (asthma, COPD) are managed with bronchodilators (short- and long-acting beta-2 agonists, anticholinergics, methylxanthines), anti-inflammatory medications (inhaled glucocorticoids, leukotriene modifiers, mast cell stabilizers), and biologics (omalizumab). Quick-relief vs. long-term controller distinction guides therapy.

Airflow Disorders — Overview

Asthma and COPD therapy works on two fronts: open the airway (bronchodilators) and calm it (anti-inflammatories).

Airflow disorders — overview

Open + calm the airway
  • Asthma is reversible airflow obstruction from inflammation and bronchoconstriction; the same drugs treat COPD
  • Two strategies: bronchodilators (beta₂ agonists, methylxanthines, inhaled anticholinergics) and anti-inflammatories (glucocorticoids, leukotriene modifiers, mast cell stabilizers)

Anti-Inflammatory Agents

These prevent attacks rather than relieve them — rinse the mouth after inhaled steroids.

Glucocorticoids

Fluticasone / prednisone
  • Inhaled glucocorticoids (fluticasone, beclomethasone) are first-line controllers; oral (prednisone) for exacerbations
  • Rinse the mouth after inhalation to prevent oral candidiasis (thrush); use a spacer
  • Not for acute attacks; taper oral steroids; monitor for systemic effects with long-term use

Leukotriene modifiers

Montelukast
  • Montelukast suppresses inflammation and bronchoconstriction for long-term asthma control
  • Taken orally (often once daily in the evening) — not for an acute attack
  • Monitor for mood/behavior changes

Mast cell stabilizers & inhaler use

Cromolyn
  • Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells to prevent inflammation — prophylaxis only (including exercise-induced asthma)
  • Teach correct MDI/DPI/nebulizer technique and the dosing schedule (fixed vs as-needed)
  • Keep a log of exacerbation frequency/intensity and report increases

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is instructing a client who has a new prescription for albuterol PO. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects.

Therapeutic Uses

Beta2-adrenergic agonists act by selectively activating the beta2-receptors in the bronchial smooth muscle, resulting in bronchodilation. They also suppress histamine release and promote ciliary motility.

Complications

  • Oral agents can cause tachycardia and angina due to activation of alpha1 receptors in the heart.
  • Activation of beta2 receptors in skeletal muscle causes tremors.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 17.1

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for beclomethasone. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. "Rinse your mouth after each use of this medication."
  2. "Limit fluid intake while taking this medication."
  3. "Increase your intake of vitamin B12 while taking this medication."
  4. "You can take the medication as needed."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Rinse the mouth after each use of inhaled beclomethasone (a glucocorticoid) to prevent oral candidiasis.
  • B. Clients with asthma should increase fluids to liquefy secretions.
  • C. Glucocorticoids increase bone-loss risk (calcium/vitamin D matter), not vitamin B12.
  • D. Beclomethasone is taken on a fixed schedule for control, not as needed.

Exercise 17.2

A nurse is providing instructions to a client who has a new prescription for albuterol and beclomethasone inhalers for the control of asthma. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Take the albuterol at the same time each day.
  2. Administer the albuterol inhaler prior to using the beclomethasone inhaler.
  3. Use beclomethasone if experiencing an acute episode.
  4. Avoid shaking the beclomethasone before use.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Albuterol (short-acting beta2-agonist) is used as needed for symptoms, not on a fixed daily schedule.
  • B. Correct — Use the albuterol (bronchodilator) first to open airways, then the beclomethasone, improving steroid delivery.
  • C. Beclomethasone is taken on a fixed schedule, not for acute episodes.
  • D. The client should shake the metered-dose inhaler before use.

Exercise 17.3

A nurse is providing instructions to a client who has a new prescription for albuterol, PO. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. "You can take this medication to abort an acute asthma attack."
  2. "Tremors are an adverse effect of this medication."
  3. "Prolonged use of this medication can cause hyperglycemia."
  4. "This medication can slow skeletal growth rate."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Inhaled albuterol aborts acute attacks; oral albuterol has a slower onset and is not for acute relief.
  • B. Correct — Tremors occur due to excessive beta2-adrenergic stimulation.
  • C, D. Hyperglycemia and slowed skeletal growth are effects of glucocorticoids, not albuterol.

Exercise 17.4

A nurse is teaching a client who has a prescription for long-term use of oral prednisone for treatment of chronic asthma. The nurse should instruct the client to monitor for which of the following manifestations as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Weight gain
  2. Nervousness
  3. Bradycardia
  4. Constipation
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Weight gain and fluid retention are adverse effects of long-term oral prednisone (a glucocorticoid).
  • B. Nervousness and insomnia are adverse effects of beta2-agonists (e.g., albuterol).
  • C. Tachycardia (not bradycardia) is associated with beta2-agonists.
  • D. Diarrhea (not constipation) is an adverse effect of prednisone.

Unit 3 · Respiratory · Chapter 18

Upper Respiratory Disorders

Upper respiratory medications target cough (antitussives — codeine, dextromethorphan), mucus production (expectorants — guaifenesin), thick secretions (mucolytics — acetylcysteine), nasal congestion (decongestants — phenylephrine, pseudoephedrine), and allergy symptoms (antihistamines — diphenhydramine, loratadine, cetirizine).

Upper Respiratory Disorders — Overview

Cough, congestion, and allergy — often treated with combination products.

Upper respiratory medications — overview

Cough & congestion
  • Treat allergic/nonallergic rhinitis and cough from colds and other disorders
  • Classes: antitussives, expectorants, mucolytics, decongestants, and antihistamines — frequently combined for effect

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a provider's office is providing teaching for a client who has a new prescription for guaifenesin. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects of this medication.
  • EVALUATION OF MEDICATION EFFECTIVENESS: Identify two findings that indicate that the medication is effective.

Complications

  • GI upset
  • Drowsiness
  • Dizziness
  • Rash

Evaluation Of Medication Effectiveness

  • Cough is more productive, mucous is easier to expectorate.
  • Chest congestion is decreased.

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 18.1

A nurse is caring for a client who has been taking phenylephrine nasal drops for the past 10 days for sinusitis. The nurse should assess the client for which of the following manifestations as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Sedation
  2. Nasal congestion
  3. Productive cough
  4. Constipation
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Insomnia, rather than sedation, is an adverse effect of phenylephrine.
  • B. Correct — When a topical decongestant is used for more than 3-5 days, rebound nasal congestion occurs.
  • C. Phenylephrine can cause a headache, but not a productive cough.
  • D. Constipation is an adverse effect of first-generation antihistamines, not phenylephrine.

  2. Anxiety

  4. Palpitations

Answer: C

  • A. Dextromethorphan can cause nausea, not diarrhea.
  • B. Phenylephrine can cause anxiety and irritability, not dextromethorphan.
  • C. Correct — Dextromethorphan can cause sedation; advise the client to avoid hazardous activities until effects are known.
  • D. Phenylephrine can cause tachycardia and palpitations, not dextromethorphan.

Exercise 18.3

A nurse is teaching the family of a child who has cystic fibrosis and a new prescription for acetylcysteine. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the instructions?

  1. "Expect this medication to suppress your child's cough."
  2. "Expect this medication to smell like rotten eggs."
  3. "Expect this medication to cause euphoria."
  4. "Expect this medication to turn your child's urine orange."

Answer: B

  • A. Acetylcysteine (a mucolytic) can stimulate a cough to clear secretions, not suppress it.
  • B. Correct — Acetylcysteine has a sulfur content that gives it a "rotten egg" odor.
  • C. Dextromethorphan can cause euphoria at high doses, not acetylcysteine.
