Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Dry mouth is an anticholinergic manifestation of diphenhydramine (a first-generation antihistamine).
  • B. Incorrect — Cough is not an adverse reaction to diphenhydramine.
  • C. Incorrect — Skin rash is not an adverse reaction to this medication.

Exercise 18.5

A nurse is teaching a client about the use of fluticasone to treat perennial rhinitis. Which of the following statements by the client indicates an understanding of the teaching?

  1. "I should use the spray every 4 hours while I am awake."
  2. "It can take as long as 3 weeks before the medication takes a maximum effect."
  3. "This medication can also be used to treat motion sickness."
  4. "I can use this medication when my nasal passages are blocked."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Intranasal fluticasone is used once daily, not every 4 hours.
  • B. Correct — Maximum benefit of intranasal glucocorticoids can take 1-3 weeks to develop.
  • C. Diphenhydramine, not fluticasone, is used for motion sickness.
  • D. The client should blow their nose to clear passages before use; it is not a rescue decongestant for blocked passages.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 19

Medications Affecting Urinary Output

Diuretics remove excess fluid by inhibiting sodium and water reabsorption in different parts of the nephron. Four classes: loop diuretics (furosemide), thiazide (hydrochlorothiazide), potassium-sparing (spironolactone), and osmotic (mannitol). Used for HTN, heart failure, edema, and cerebral edema.

Medications Affecting Urinary Output — Overview

Diuretics pull off fluid for blood pressure, edema, and heart failure — the class predicts the electrolyte risk.

Diuretics — overview

Four classes
  • Used for blood pressure control, edema (heart, liver, kidney disease), and prevention of kidney failure
  • Classes: high-ceiling loop, thiazide, potassium-sparing, and osmotic diuretics

Loop Diuretics

The most powerful diuretic — potassium loss and ototoxicity define its risks.

Loop diuretics — action & uses

Furosemide
  • Prototype furosemide (also bumetanide, torsemide); block sodium/chloride reabsorption in the loop of Henle — extensive diuresis even in renal impairment
  • Uses: pulmonary edema/heart failure and edema unresponsive to other diuretics; rapid fluid mobilization
  • Routes: oral, IV, IM

Loop diuretics — complications & interactions

Hypokalemia
  • Dehydration, hyponatremia, hypokalemia, hypotension, ototoxicity, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia — monitor electrolytes, daily weight, I&O; report urine output <30 mL/hr
  • Hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk — monitor K⁺ and digoxin; may add a potassium-sparing diuretic or supplement
  • Lithium toxicity (monitor levels); NSAIDs reduce the diuretic effect; give in the morning to prevent nocturia

Other Diuretics

Thiazides for everyday hypertension, potassium-sparing to protect K⁺, and osmotics for pressure emergencies.

Thiazide diuretics

Hydrochlorothiazide
  • Hydrochlorothiazide: a moderate diuretic for hypertension and mild edema
  • Similar electrolyte effects to loop diuretics (hypokalemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia, hyperlipidemia) but no ototoxicity
  • Ineffective in significant renal impairment; encourage potassium-rich foods

Potassium-sparing diuretics

Spironolactone
  • Spironolactone (aldosterone antagonist): mild diuresis that retains potassium
  • Hyperkalemia is the key risk — avoid potassium supplements and salt substitutes; report K⁺ >5.0
  • Can cause gynecomastia and menstrual irregularities

Osmotic diuretics

Mannitol
  • Mannitol pulls fluid into the vasculature by osmosis — reduces intracranial and intraocular pressure
  • Given IV through a filter; watch for heart failure/pulmonary edema from fluid shift
  • Monitor neurologic status, I&O, and electrolytes

Diuretic nursing care

Monitoring
  • Obtain baseline weight, orthostatic blood pressure, electrolytes, and edema location/extent
  • Weigh daily at the same time with the same clothing; monitor BP and I&O
  • Teach fall precautions (orthostatic hypotension) and the manifestations of electrolyte imbalance to report

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A charge nurse is reviewing the use of loop diuretics with a group of nurses. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify two.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe three adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two interventions for each of the three adverse effects.

Therapeutic Uses

  • Used when there is an emergent need for rapid mobilization of fluid
  • Pulmonary edema caused by heart failure
  • Liver, cardiac, or kidney disease
  • Hypertension
  • Unlabeled use: hypercalcemia

Complications

  • Dehydration
  • Hypotension
  • Ototoxicity
  • Hypokalemia

Nursing Interventions

  • Dehydration: Assess for dry mouth, increased thirst, low urine output, weight loss.
  • Hypotension: monitor orthostatic blood pressure and pulse; monitor for manifestations of postural hypotension.
  • Ototoxicity: Assess for tinnitus; avoid administering ototoxic medications.
  • Hypokalemia: monitor laboratory values; offer potassium-rich foods; assess for general weakness, nausea, and vomiting.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 19.1

A nurse is planning care for a client who is receiving furosemide IV for peripheral edema. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Assess for tinnitus.
  2. Report urine output 50 mL/hr.
  3. Monitor blood potassium levels.
  4. Elevate the head of bed slowly before ambulation.
  5. Recommend eating a banana daily.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, C, D, E

  • A. Correct — Ototoxicity (tinnitus) is an adverse effect of furosemide.
  • B. Incorrect — A urine output of 50 mL/hr is within the expected range; no need to report.
  • C. Correct — Hypokalemia is an adverse effect; monitor potassium.
  • D. Correct — Furosemide can cause orthostatic hypotension; rise slowly.
  • E. Correct — A banana is high in potassium to help offset hypokalemia.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 20

Medications Affecting Blood Pressure

Antihypertensive medications work through multiple mechanisms: ACE inhibitors (captopril) and ARBs (losartan), aldosterone antagonists, direct renin inhibitors, alpha blockers, central alpha-2 agonists (clonidine), beta blockers, calcium channel blockers (covered in Ch 22-23), vasodilators (hydralazine), and emergency IV agents (nitroprusside).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

ACE inhibitors (captopril, lisinopril, enalapril) — "-pril"; dry cough, angioedema, hyperkalemia; Category D — teratogenic. ARBs (losartan, valsartan) — "-sartan"; switch from ACEi for cough; same risks otherwise. Clonidine — central α2; rebound HTN if abruptly stopped. Hydralazine, nitroprusside — direct vasodilators (IV for emergency).

ACE inhibitors & ARBs

  • ACE inhibitors — Captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril ("-pril")
  • Mechanism: Block conversion of angiotensin I → II; ↓ aldosterone; vasodilation
  • Uses: HTN, HF, post-MI, diabetic nephropathy (renoprotective)
  • Key AE: Persistent dry cough (10–20%), angioedema (life-threatening), hyperkalemia, hypotension (especially first dose)
  • ARBs — Losartan, valsartan, irbesartan ("-sartan") — no cough, less angioedema
  • BOTH contraindicated in pregnancy (Category D — fetal renal damage)
  • Monitor BUN/Cr (renal function) and K+
  • AVOID combining ACE + ARB (no benefit, more harm)

Aldosterone antagonists & DRI

  • Eplerenone, spironolactone: Block aldosterone; hyperkalemia risk
  • Aliskiren (direct renin inhibitor): Less commonly used; same Category D pregnancy restriction

Alpha blockers, central agonists, vasodilators

  • Alpha-1 blockers — Prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin: First-dose orthostatic hypotension — take at bedtime; rise slowly
  • Central alpha-2 — Clonidine, methyldopa: NEVER abruptly stop — rebound HTN crisis; sedation, dry mouth
  • Methyldopa = safe in pregnancy
  • Hydralazine (PO/IV): Direct vasodilator; reflex tachycardia; lupus-like syndrome at high dose
  • Nitroprusside (IV only): Hypertensive emergency; cyanide toxicity (max 72 hr); protect from light
A client started on lisinopril 4 weeks ago calls reporting a persistent dry cough that won't resolve. What is the cause, and what is the nursing action?
ACE-inhibitor cough — a class effect from bradykinin accumulation (ACE normally inactivates bradykinin). Occurs in 10–20% of clients, often after weeks. Not dose-dependent, doesn't resolve over time. Action: notify provider — switch to an ARB ("-sartan") which preserves the BP/renal benefits without the bradykinin effect. Worse than cough: angioedema (swelling of lips/tongue/airway) — life-threatening, requires immediate discontinuation and emergency care. Both ACE and ARB are Category D — teratogenic.
Why is clonidine particularly dangerous to abruptly discontinue, and what is the safe approach?
Rebound hypertension crisis — abruptly stopping clonidine (central α2 agonist) causes sympathetic surge with severe HTN, tachycardia, tremor, anxiety, headache — can precipitate stroke or MI. Safe approach: taper over 2–4 days. Critical patient teaching: never miss doses, fill prescriptions on time, keep a backup supply when traveling, NEVER stop on your own. Same precaution applies to methyldopa (the safer-in-pregnancy alternative).
A client is starting prazosin for HTN. What is the "first-dose phenomenon," and what teaching prevents injury?
First-dose orthostatic hypotension — alpha-1 blockers (prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin) cause profound BP drop on initial dose, with risk of syncope and falls. Teaching: take first dose at bedtime, while in bed, and don't plan activities afterward. Going forward: rise slowly (sit on edge of bed before standing), avoid hot showers/alcohol/dehydration, take consistently with food. Prazosin also has off-label use for PTSD-related nightmares.
A client is on IV nitroprusside for hypertensive emergency. What is the major toxicity risk, the time limit, and the storage requirement?
Cyanide / thiocyanate toxicity — nitroprusside breaks down to release cyanide ions; the body detoxifies them to thiocyanate (renally cleared). Time limit: max 72 hours; shorter in renal impairment. Signs: metabolic acidosis, tachycardia, altered mental status, almond-scented breath (cyanide). Storage: protect from light — wrap bag in foil; solution turns from clear to brown/blue/green if degraded → discard. Always have an arterial line for tight BP monitoring; titrate continuously.

Blood Pressure — Overview

Antihypertensives lower blood pressure through several complementary mechanisms; combination therapy is common, alongside lifestyle change.

Approach to hypertension

By mechanism
  • Drug classes act on different targets: the RAAS (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, aldosterone antagonists, renin inhibitors), vessels/heart (calcium channel blockers, vasodilators), and sympathetic tone (alpha blockers, central agonists, beta blockers)
  • Diuretics (Ch 19) are frequently combined with these agents
  • Monitor blood pressure and for orthostatic hypotension; emphasize adherence and lifestyle measures

RAAS Inhibitors

Medications that interrupt the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system at different points. ACE inhibitors block formation of angiotensin II; ARBs block its action at the receptor.

ACE inhibitors — Captopril, lisinopril, enalapril, ramipril

"-pril" · prototype captopril

Block conversion of angiotensin I → II and increase bradykinin, producing arteriolar vasodilation, sodium/water excretion with potassium retention, and reduced cardiac/vascular remodeling.

Therapeutic uses

  • Hypertension, heart failure
  • Post-MI (decreases mortality)
  • Diabetic & nondiabetic nephropathy (renoprotective)

Key complications

  • First-dose orthostatic hypotension
  • Persistent dry cough (bradykinin) — reason to switch to an ARB
  • Angioedema (treat severe with SQ epinephrine; discontinue)
  • Hyperkalemia; rash/dysgeusia (captopril); rare neutropenia (captopril — monitor WBC)

Contraindications & interactions

  • Pregnancy Risk Category D (2nd/3rd trimester)
  • Bilateral renal artery stenosis, single kidney
  • Diuretics → first-dose hypotension; K⁺ supplements/K-sparing diuretics → hyperkalemia; ↑ lithium levels; NSAIDs ↓ effect

Nursing/administration

  • Oral (enalaprilat is the only IV form); monitor BP ≥ 2 hr after first dose
  • Take captopril/moexipril ≥ 1 hr before meals; report cough, rash, altered taste, or signs of infection

Angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs) — Losartan, valsartan

"-sartan" · prototype losartan

Block angiotensin II at the receptor → vasodilation and sodium/water excretion. The major advantage over ACE inhibitors is no cough and less angioedema.

Therapeutic uses

  • Hypertension; heart failure (valsartan, candesartan)
  • Stroke prevention & diabetic nephropathy (losartan)
  • Alternative when ACE inhibitor cough is intolerable

Complications & cautions

  • Angioedema (less common than ACEi), fetal injury, hypotension, dizziness
  • Pregnancy Risk Category D; bilateral renal stenosis/single kidney
  • Additive hypotension with antihypertensives; ↑ lithium toxicity

Aldosterone Antagonists & Direct Renin Inhibitor

Two further points of RAAS blockade — at the aldosterone receptor and at renin itself. Both carry hyperkalemia risk.

Aldosterone antagonists — Eplerenone, spironolactone

Potassium-sparing

Block aldosterone receptors in the kidney → sodium/water excretion with potassium retention.

Uses

  • Hypertension, heart failure
  • PMS, PCOS, acne in young females (spironolactone)

Complications

  • Hyperkalemia, hyponatremia
  • Endocrine effects (gynecomastia, menstrual irregularities, hirsutism) — chiefly spironolactone
  • Avoid grapefruit juice with eplerenone (CYP3A4 → hyperkalemia)

Cautions

  • Eplerenone Pregnancy B, spironolactone C
  • Contraindicated with high K⁺, renal impairment, hepatic disease
  • Many drugs raise hyperkalemia risk (ACEi, ARBs, K-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs)

Direct renin inhibitor — Aliskiren

Prototype

Binds renin to inhibit production of angiotensin I, lowering both angiotensin II and aldosterone. Used for hypertension alone or in combination.

  • Complications: angioedema, rash, cough; hyperkalemia; dose-related diarrhea (more in females/older adults); hypotension
  • Pregnancy Risk Category D; contraindicated with hyperkalemia
  • High-fat meals reduce absorption — take consistently and avoid high-fat foods at dosing

Calcium Channel Blockers

Block calcium entry to relax vascular smooth muscle. Dihydropyridines act mainly on vessels; verapamil and diltiazem also act on the heart's conduction system.

Dihydropyridines — Nifedipine, amlodipine

Vascular-selective

Act primarily on arterioles (veins not significantly affected); little direct cardiac effect at therapeutic doses.

  • Uses: angina, hypertension
  • Complications: reflex tachycardia (a beta blocker like metoprolol counteracts it), orthostatic hypotension, peripheral edema, acute toxicity
  • Pregnancy C; nifedipine contraindicated in cardiogenic shock
  • Grapefruit juice, cimetidine → toxicity

Non-dihydropyridines — Verapamil, diltiazem

Cardiac + vascular

Act on vessels and the myocardium/SA/AV node → decreased contractility, heart rate, and AV conduction.

  • Uses: angina, hypertension, dysrhythmias (atrial fibrillation/flutter, SVT)
  • Complications: bradycardia/heart failure (cardiac suppression), AV block, constipation (verapamil), orthostatic hypotension, peripheral edema, acute toxicity
  • Verapamil ↑ digoxin levels (toxicity); beta blockers add risk of HF/AV block/bradycardia; grapefruit juice
  • Hold for pulse < 50/min or systolic BP < 90 mm Hg; do not chew/crush sustained-release tablets

Sympatholytics

Agents that lower blood pressure by reducing sympathetic tone — at peripheral alpha-1 receptors, centrally, or at cardiac beta receptors.

Alpha-adrenergic blockers — Prazosin, doxazosin, terazosin

Alpha-1 blockade
  • Selective alpha-1 blockade → venous/arterial dilation and relaxation of the prostatic capsule/bladder neck
  • Uses: primary hypertension; BPH symptoms (doxazosin, terazosin)
  • First-dose orthostatic hypotension — give the first dose at bedtime; start low
  • Pregnancy C; contraindicated with hypotension

Centrally-acting alpha-2 agonists — Clonidine, guanfacine, methyldopa

Central sympatholytic
  • Act in the CNS to decrease sympathetic outflow → bradycardia, decreased CO, vasodilation
  • Uses: primary hypertension; severe cancer pain (epidural); ADHD; (investigational: withdrawal from alcohol/tobacco/opioids)
  • Complications: drowsiness/sedation, dry mouth, and rebound hypertension if abruptly stopped — taper over 2-4 days
  • Oral/transdermal (clonidine patch every 7 days); larger dose at bedtime

Beta-adrenergic blockers — Metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol

Detailed in Ch 22-23
  • Beta-1 blockade → decreased heart rate, contractility, cardiac output, and AV conduction; carvedilol/labetalol add alpha blockade (vasodilation)
  • Uses: hypertension, angina, tachydysrhythmias, heart failure, MI; suppress reflex tachycardia from vasodilators
  • Complications: bradycardia (hold if < 50/min), masks signs of hypoglycemia (caution in diabetes), bronchospasm (nonselective agents contraindicated in asthma), rebound excitation if abruptly stopped
  • Contraindicated in AV block and sinus bradycardia

Direct Vasodilators (Emergency)

Direct-acting vasodilators relax vascular smooth muscle; the IV agents are reserved for hypertensive crisis.

Hydralazine & nitroprusside

Hypertensive crisis
  • Hydralazine — direct arteriolar vasodilation; oral for primary hypertension/heart failure; causes reflex tachycardia (often paired with a beta blocker) and can cause a lupus-like syndrome
  • Nitroprusside — rapid arterial/venous dilation by IV infusion for hypertensive crisis
  • Cyanide/thiocyanate toxicity is the major nitroprusside risk — limit infusion duration, monitor, and discontinue if toxicity occurs

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in an outpatient facility is teaching a client who has a new prescription for aliskiren to treat hypertension. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for aliskiren.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one test to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify two teaching points.

Therapeutic Uses

Aliskiren binds with renin to inhibit production of angiotensin I, thus decreasing production of both angiotensin II and aldosterone. Aliskiren is used solely for treating hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensives.

Complications

  • Diarrhea: dose-related, occurs most frequently in females and older adult clients
  • Risk for angioedema and rash caused by allergy to the medication
  • Hyperkalemia
  • Hypotension

Nursing Interventions

Monitor blood electrolytes, paying close attention to potassium levels, because the client is at risk for hyperkalemia. This is especially important when the client takes ACE inhibitors concurrently, because these medications also raise potassium levels.

Client Education

  • Do not take aliskiren with foods high in fat, which decreases absorption of the medication.
  • Do not take potassium supplements or salt substitutes containing potassium.
  • Clients should not take aliskiren during pregnancy.
  • If a rash or angioedema occurs, discontinue aliskiren and notify the provider.
  • Call 911 if severe manifestations of allergy are present.

Exercise 20.1

  1. Asthma

  3. Hypertension
  4. Tachycardia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Propranolol is a nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker; it can cause bronchoconstriction and is contraindicated in asthma.
  • B. Propranolol is not contraindicated in glaucoma (beta-blockers may even lower IOP).
  • C. Propranolol is used to treat hypertension.
  • D. Propranolol is used to treat tachydysrhythmias.

Answer: C

  • A. ACE inhibitors cause hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.

Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Intestinal ileus is not a typical nitroprusside effect.
  • B. Neutropenia is associated with captopril, not nitroprusside.
  • C. Correct — Delirium and other mental status changes can result from thiocyanate accumulation with prolonged nitroprusside use.

  4. Clonidine
  5. Aliskiren

Answer: B, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Simvastatin (an antilipemic) does not intensify first-dose hypotension.
  • B. Correct — Hydrochlorothiazide (a diuretic) can intensify first-dose hypotension.
  • C. Incorrect — Phenytoin does not interact to intensify hypotension here.
  • D. Correct — Clonidine (a centrally acting alpha2 agonist) can intensify hypotension.
  • E. Correct — Aliskiren (a direct renin inhibitor) can intensify hypotension.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 21

Cardiac Glycosides and Heart Failure

Heart failure management uses cardiac glycosides (digoxin) for inotropic support and rate control in atrial fibrillation. Other key agents: catecholamines (dopamine, dobutamine), human B-type natriuretic peptide (nesiritide), and combination ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan).

TL;DR · One-glance summary

Digoxin: positive inotrope (↑ contractility), negative chronotrope (↓ HR). Therapeutic 0.5–2.0 ng/mL. Apical pulse 1 min before dose — hold if <60 (adult) or <90–110 (infants/kids). Toxicity: N/V, anorexia, visual halos (yellow-green), dysrhythmias. Hypokalemia ↑ toxicity. Antidote: digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).

Digoxin

  • Mechanism: Inhibits Na/K ATPase → ↑ intracellular Ca → ↑ contractility (positive inotrope); slows AV conduction (negative chronotrope/dromotrope)
  • Uses: HF with reduced EF, atrial fibrillation (rate control)
  • Therapeutic level: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL
  • Before each dose: Check apical pulse for 1 full minute
  • HOLD and call provider: Adult HR <60; child <90; infant <110

Digoxin toxicity

  • Early signs: Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
  • Cardiac: Bradycardia, AV blocks, ventricular dysrhythmias
  • Visual: Yellow-green halos around lights, blurred vision
  • Neurological: Fatigue, weakness, confusion
  • Risk factors: Hypokalemia (most common), hypomagnesemia, hypercalcemia, renal impairment, advanced age
  • Antidote: Digoxin immune Fab (Digibind) for life-threatening toxicity

Other inotropic & HF agents

  • Catecholamines — Dopamine, dobutamine: IV infusion; short-term inotropic support (cardiogenic shock)
  • Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto): ARNI for HF; replaces ACE/ARB (don't combine — angioedema)
  • Nesiritide: Recombinant BNP for acute decompensated HF
  • Ivabradine: Slows HR; for HF with elevated HR despite beta blockade
A client on digoxin reports yellow-green halos around lights and lost appetite. What is the therapeutic range, what does this presentation suggest, and what are the next steps?
Therapeutic range: 0.5–2.0 ng/mL. Yellow-green halos and anorexia are classic digoxin toxicity. Other early signs: N/V, fatigue, confusion. Cardiac: bradycardia, AV blocks, ventricular dysrhythmias. Steps: hold the next dose, obtain stat digoxin level + serum K, Mg, Ca, BUN/Cr, ECG. Severe toxicity → digoxin immune Fab (Digibind).
What is the pre-administration assessment for every digoxin dose, and the hold parameters by age?
Check apical pulse for a full minute before every dose. HOLD and call provider: Adult HR < 60, child < 90, infant < 110. Document rhythm regularity. Also assess for digoxin toxicity signs (vision changes, anorexia, N/V). Digoxin acts as a positive inotrope (↑ contractility) and negative chronotrope (↓ HR, slows AV conduction) — that's why bradycardia is the hold trigger.
A client on digoxin and furosemide has a serum K of 3.0 mEq/L. Why is this particularly dangerous?
Hypokalemia dramatically increases digoxin toxicity risk, even at therapeutic digoxin levels. Mechanism: digoxin competes with K⁺ for Na/K-ATPase binding; when K⁺ is low, more digoxin binds → toxicity. Furosemide commonly causes hypokalemia → classic dangerous combo. Actions: replace K⁺ before next digoxin dose, monitor ECG, consider adding K-sparing diuretic or K supplement. Hypomagnesemia and hypercalcemia also potentiate toxicity.
Why must sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) never be combined with an ACE inhibitor — and what is the washout requirement?
Severe angioedema risk — sacubitril inhibits neprilysin (which degrades bradykinin and ANP); ACE inhibitors also raise bradykinin. Combination → markedly elevated bradykinin → potentially fatal angioedema. Washout: at least 36 hours after stopping ACE inhibitor before starting Entresto (and vice versa). Entresto replaces ACE/ARB in HFrEF (it contains valsartan, an ARB). Same Category D pregnancy restriction.

Heart Failure — Overview

Heart failure is the heart’s inability to pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs. Understanding the failing pump explains every medication in this chapter.

Heart failure — pathophysiology & types

Pump failure
  • Inadequate pumping of the heart muscle leaves the heart unable to meet the body’s circulatory needs; decreased tissue perfusion causes fatigue, shortness of breath, weakness, and activity intolerance
  • Reduces cardiac output (CO) and affects heart rate, stroke volume, preload, and afterload
  • Left-sided HF: pulmonary manifestations — dyspnea, cough, oliguria
  • Right-sided HF: systemic congestion — peripheral edema, jugular vein distention, weight gain

Heart failure — pharmacotherapy overview

Treatment ladder
  • First-line (medications of choice): diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARBs), and beta-adrenergic blockers
  • Cardiac glycosides (digoxin): added when first-line medications cannot control manifestations (second-line)
  • IV inotropic sympathomimetics (dopamine, dobutamine): short-term support for acute decompensated HF or cardiogenic shock
  • Goals: improve contractility and CO, reduce preload/afterload, and control symptoms

Inotropic Sympathomimetics

When the failing heart needs urgent support, IV catecholamines boost contractility and perfusion. For dopamine, the dose determines the effect.

Dopamine — dose-dependent effects

Dose matters
  • Low dose (dopamine receptors): dilates renal blood vessels → increased renal perfusion and urine output (protects kidneys)
  • Moderate dose (beta₁): increases heart rate, contractility, and AV conduction → increased cardiac output
  • High dose (alpha₁): vasoconstriction (viscera/skin) and can constrict renal vessels
  • Uses: shock, heart failure, and acute kidney injury

Dobutamine & epinephrine

Catecholamines
  • Dobutamine (beta₁): increases heart rate, contractility, cardiac output, and AV conduction — short-term inotropic support in HF
  • Epinephrine (alpha₁/beta₁/beta₂): vasoconstriction, increased HR/contractility/CO, and bronchodilation — used for anaphylactic shock, cardiac arrest, AV block, and shock
  • Both are given by IV infusion with continuous monitoring

Inotrope nursing care & complications

Continuous monitoring
  • Cardiac complications: beta₁ activation can cause dysrhythmias and increase myocardial oxygen demand (angina) — provide continuous cardiac monitoring and watch HR, rhythm, chest pain, and urine output
  • Extravasation of high-dose dopamine can cause tissue necrosis — infuse through a central line, monitor the IV site, stop at first sign of irritation; antidote is phentolamine (alpha blocker)
  • Interactions: MAOIs (prolong/intensify effects, cardiotoxicity — avoid), tricyclic antidepressants (intensify effects), general anesthetics (cardiac hypersensitivity → dysrhythmias)
  • Contraindications: dopamine in tachydysrhythmias/VF; caution with hypovolemia, angina, recent MI, hypertension, diabetes, and in older adults

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is caring for a client who has heart failure and a new prescription for digoxin 0.125 mg PO daily. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include three teaching points.

Therapeutic Uses

Digoxin improves the heart's pumping effectiveness and increases cardiac output and stroke volume. It decreases heart rate by slowing depolarization through the SA node, thus allowing more time for the ventricles to fill with blood. Due to these effects, digoxin is used to treat heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and some other tachydysrhythmias.

Complications

The client should monitor for manifestations of digoxin toxicity, which include GI effects (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), CNS effects (fatigue, weakness), visual effects (yellow-tinged vision, halos around lights, diplopia), heart rate less than 60/ min in adults, or skipped beats when checking the pulse.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor digoxin blood levels periodically during treatment. The expected reference range is 0.5 to 0.8 ng/mL.
  • Monitor blood potassium levels because hypokalemia can cause cardiac dysrhythmias, especially in older adult clients. monitoring ECG is also important to check for dysrhythmias.

Client Education

  • Take oral digoxin at the same time each day. Do not skip a dose or take more than the prescribed dose each day.
  • Monitor for manifestations of toxicity.
  • Report any new prescriptions and to contact provider before taking OTC medications, because digoxin interacts with many other substances.

Exercise 21.1

  4. Potassium 4.8 mEq/L

Answer: C

  • C. Correct — Potassium 3.4 mEq/L is below the expected range; hypokalemia increases the risk of digoxin toxicity.
  • D. Potassium 4.8 mEq/L is within the expected range.

  2. Increased urine output

Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Dopamine increases heart rate and contractility at higher doses (beta1), not lowers it.
  • B. Correct — At low doses, dopamine dilates renal blood vessels, increasing renal perfusion and urine output.
  • C. Decreased AV conduction is an effect of digoxin, not low-dose dopamine.
  • D. Renal vasoconstriction occurs only at high doses (alpha1 stimulation).

Answer: A, C, E

  • A. Correct — Fatigue and weakness are early CNS manifestations of digoxin toxicity.
  • B. Incorrect — Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (not constipation) are GI manifestations.
  • C. Correct — Anorexia is an early GI manifestation of toxicity.
  • D. Incorrect — Rash is not a manifestation of digoxin toxicity.
  • E. Correct — Visual changes such as blurred and yellow-tinged vision indicate toxicity.

  2. Check pulse rate for 30 seconds and multiply result by 2.
  3. Increase intake of sodium.
  4. Take with food if nausea occurs.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Teach the client to check the pulse and contact the provider (and hold the dose) if the heart rate is less than 60/min.
  • B. Check the pulse for a full minute, not 30 seconds × 2.
  • C. The client should reduce sodium intake for heart failure, not increase it.
  • D. Nausea can be an early sign of digoxin toxicity and should be reported, not self-managed with food.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 22

Angina

Angina (chest pain from coronary ischemia) is treated with organic nitrates (nitroglycerin — prototype), beta blockers, calcium channel blockers, and ranolazine. Goal: decrease myocardial oxygen demand and increase supply. Nitroglycerin remains the cornerstone for acute attacks.

Angina — Overview

Anginal pain comes from too little oxygen reaching a working myocardium. Every drug here either cuts demand or boosts supply.

Angina — pathophysiology & management

O₂ supply vs demand
  • Sudden pain beneath the sternum radiating to the left shoulder, arm, and jaw, from an inadequate oxygen supply to meet myocardial demand
  • Goal of therapy: prevent myocardial ischemia, pain, myocardial infarction, and death
  • Managed with organic nitrates, beta-adrenergic blockers, calcium channel blockers, and ranolazine
  • Chronic stable angina also includes an antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel), a cholesterol-lowering agent, and an ACE inhibitor to prevent MI and death

Other Antianginals

Beyond nitrates, ranolazine and the rate-lowering drugs round out angina therapy.

Ranolazine

Antianginal
  • Lowers cardiac oxygen demand → improves exercise tolerance and decreases pain by making myocardial energy use more efficient (less Na/Ca accumulation)
  • Use: chronic stable angina, combined with amlodipine, a beta blocker, or an organic nitrate
  • QT prolongation → risk of torsades de pointes: monitor ECG; avoid with prolonged QT or other QT-prolonging drugs; report palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea
  • Elevated blood pressure (can rise ~15 mm Hg in severe kidney impairment): monitor BP
  • Contraindicated: QT prolongation, hepatic impairment, ventricular tachycardia/dysrhythmias, hypokalemia

Beta blockers, CCBs & adjunct therapy

Combination
  • Beta-adrenergic blockers and calcium channel blockers reduce myocardial oxygen demand for long-term angina control
  • Chronic stable angina regimen also includes an antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel), a cholesterol-lowering agent, and an ACE inhibitor to prevent MI and death
  • Reinforce modifiable risk-factor reduction (activity, diet, smoking cessation)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is caring for a client who has angina pectoris and a new prescription for oral nitroglycerin capsules. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify similarities and differences for the forms of nitroglycerin: oral, sublingual, and transdermal.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects of the medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three nursing actions for clients taking nitroglycerin oral capsules.

Therapeutic Uses

Sublingual tablets or spray are used to treat an angina attack after it begins, while the oral tablets, transdermal patch, and transdermal ointment are used for prevention of angina. The capsules and transdermal forms have a slower onset and longer duration of action than the sublingual forms. Sublingual nitroglycerin begins working within 2 min, but the duration of action is only 30 min. Oral forms are taken several times daily, but duration of action is several hours.

Complications

Major adverse effects include headache, dizziness caused by hypotension, and rebound tachycardia.

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach the client that the oral sustained-release form of nitroglycerin should not be used to abort an angina attack. In addition, it should be taken on an empty stomach with at least 8 oz of water and must be swallowed whole.
  • Teach the client not to perform activities that require alertness if dizziness is experienced while taking oral nitroglycerin.
  • The client should inform the provider if headaches are persistent because the dose of nitroglycerin might need to be decreased.
  • The client should inform the provider if tachycardia occurs, because a beta-adrenergic blocker or other medication can be prescribed to slow the pulse rate.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 22.1

A nurse is teaching a client who has angina pectoris and is learning how to treat acute anginal attacks. The client asks, "What is my next step if I take one tablet, wait 5 minutes, but still have anginal pain?" Which of the following responses should the nurse make?

  1. "Take two more sublingual tablets at the same time."
  2. "Call the emergency response team."
  3. "Take a sustained-release nitroglycerin capsule."
  4. "Wait another 5 minutes then take a second sublingual tablet."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. The client should not take two sublingual doses at once.
  • B. Correct — If pain is unrelieved after the first tablet, call 911 (emergency response), then a second tablet may be taken while waiting.
  • C. An oral sustained-release capsule is not used to treat an acute attack.
  • D. The client should not wait an additional 5 minutes before calling for help.

Exercise 22.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for nitroglycerin transdermal patch for angina pectoris. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. Remove the patch each evening.
  2. Cut each patch in half if angina attacks are under control.
  3. Take off the nitroglycerin patch for 30 min if a headache occurs.
  4. Apply a new patch every 48 hr.

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Remove the patch each evening to provide a nitrate-free interval and prevent tolerance.
  • B. Always apply a whole patch; do not cut it.
  • C. Do not remove the patch for 30 min for a headache (headache is an expected effect; treat with analgesics).
  • D. Apply a new patch every 24 hr, not every 48 hr.

  1. Digoxin
  2. Simvastatin
  3. Verapamil
  4. Amlodipine

Answer: A, B, C

  • B. Correct — Concurrent use increases simvastatin levels.
  • C. Correct — Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4, raising ranolazine levels.
  • D. Incorrect — Amlodipine (a calcium channel blocker) is used for angina without this interaction concern.
  • E. Incorrect — Nitroglycerin transdermal patches are used for angina and do not pose this interaction.

  1. Furosemide
  2. Captopril
  3. Ranolazine
  4. Metoprolol

Answer: D

  • A. Furosemide (a loop diuretic) treats fluid overload/hypertension.
  • B. Captopril (an ACE inhibitor) treats hypertension/heart failure.
  • C. Ranolazine treats chronic stable angina but does not counter reflex tachycardia.
  • D. Correct — Metoprolol (a beta-blocker) slows the heart rate to counter nitrate-induced reflex tachycardia.

A nurse is teaching a client who has angina how to use nitroglycerin transdermal ointment. The nurse should include which of the following instructions?

  1. "Remove the prior dose before applying a new dose."
  2. "Rub the ointment directly into your skin until it is no longer visible."
  3. "Cover the applied ointment with a clean gauze pad."
  4. "Apply the ointment to the same skin area each time."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Remove the prior dose (wipe off old ointment) before applying a new dose.
  • B. Do not rub it in; spread a thin layer over the measured paper without massaging.
  • C. Cover with plastic wrap (not gauze) to protect clothing and aid absorption.
  • D. Rotate application sites to prevent skin irritation.

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 23

Medications Affecting Cardiac Rhythm

Antidysrhythmics are organized by Vaughan Williams classification: Class I (sodium channel blockers — procainamide, lidocaine, propafenone), Class II (beta blockers — propranolol), Class III (potassium channel blockers — amiodarone), Class IV (calcium channel blockers — verapamil). Plus adenosine and digoxin.

Antidysrhythmics — Overview

These drugs reshape the heart’s electrical signal. The catch: the same power that fixes a rhythm can cause one.

Antidysrhythmics — mechanism & classes

Electrophysiology
  • Alter cardiac electrophysiology to treat or prevent dysrhythmias (prolong the AV node, change conduction speed, reduce excitability, lengthen the refractory period)
  • Four main classes: Class I sodium channel blockers, Class II beta-adrenergic blockers, Class III potassium channel blockers, Class IV calcium channel blockers
  • Toxicity is the major concern — antidysrhythmics are proarrhythmic (toxicity can increase dysrhythmias)

The Four Classes

Each class blocks a different channel or receptor — know the prototype and what it treats.

Class I — sodium channel blockers

Class I
  • Slow cardiac conduction velocity; divided into IA, IB, IC
  • IA — procainamide (also quinidine, disopyramide)
  • IB — lidocaine IV (also mexiletine, phenytoin); used for ventricular dysrhythmias
  • IC — propafenone (also flecainide); decrease conduction in atria/ventricles/His-Purkinje; used for SVT

Class II — beta blockers

Class II
  • Prototype propranolol (oral, IV); also esmolol, acebutolol; block sympathetic stimulation of the heart
  • Decrease heart rate, SA automaticity, AV conduction velocity, and myocardial contractility
  • Uses: atrial fibrillation/flutter, paroxysmal SVT, hypertension, angina, PVCs, ventricular tachycardia
  • Check apical pulse before dosing; hold for pulse <50/min and notify provider; watch for bronchospasm in asthma

Class III — potassium channel blockers

Amiodarone
  • Prototype amiodarone (oral, IV); also sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide, dronedarone; prolong the action potential and refractory period
  • Decrease SA automaticity and AV/ventricular conduction; dilate coronary vessels
  • Uses: conversion of atrial fibrillation, recurrent ventricular fibrillation/tachycardia, atrial flutter

Class IV & adenosine

Class IV
  • Class IV calcium channel blockers verapamil, diltiazem: decrease force of contraction and heart rate, slow SA/AV conduction (effects similar to beta blockers)
  • Uses: rate control in atrial fibrillation/flutter, SVT, hypertension, angina
  • Adenosine: decreases AV conduction and SA automaticity; used for paroxysmal SVT and Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
  • Digoxin may also be used for ventricular rate control

Toxicity & Monitoring

Amiodarone’s organ toxicity and the proarrhythmic risk of the whole class drive nursing care.

Amiodarone — toxicity profile

High-alert
  • Pulmonary toxicity: obtain baseline chest x-ray and pulmonary function tests, monitor throughout therapy; report dyspnea, cough, chest pain
  • Sinus bradycardia and AV block (can lead to heart failure): monitor BP/ECG; if AV block occurs, discontinue and consider a pacemaker
  • Visual disturbances (photophobia, blurred vision), corneal deposits
  • Very long half-life — effects persist after discontinuation; numerous drug interactions

Other antidysrhythmic complications

Monitoring
  • Lidocaine: CNS toxicity (drowsiness, altered mental status, paresthesias, seizures) and respiratory arrest — monitor, give phenytoin for seizures, keep resuscitation equipment ready
  • Propafenone (IC): bradycardia, heart failure, dizziness, hypotension, bronchospasm; can worsen or cause new dysrhythmias
  • Propranolol (II): hypotension, bradycardia, heart failure, AV block, bronchospasm in asthma — check apical pulse, hold <50/min

Proarrhythmic safety principles

Safety
  • All antidysrhythmics can worsen or cause dysrhythmias — provide continuous ECG monitoring during IV administration
  • Monitor for heart failure (dyspnea, cough, neck vein distention, crackles) and report promptly
  • Correct electrolyte imbalances; many agents need dose adjustment in renal or hepatic impairment

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is preparing to provide teaching to a client who has a new prescription for verapamil for recurrent supraventricular tachycardia. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Identify three adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three, including diagnostic tests the nurse should monitor.

Therapeutic Uses

Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker and a class IV antidysrhythmic medication that decreases heart rate, slows conduction through both the SA and AV nodes, and decreases force of contraction of the heart. It is used to treat supraventricular tachycardia (SVT).

Complications

  • Bradycardia
  • Hypotension
  • Heart failure
  • Constipation

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor both kidney and liver function because the medication dosage might need to be lowered if either kidney or liver impairment are present.
  • Monitor blood pressure and pulse.
  • Monitor periodic ECG testing for dysrhythmias and for improvement of SVT.
  • Assess for manifestations of heart failure, such as dyspnea and crackles in the lungs.
  • Question the client about dizziness, which can occur due to hypotension.
  • Teach the client to move slowly from lying to sitting or standing and to avoid driving or operating heavy machinery until effects of verapamil are known.

Exercise 23.1

A nurse is assessing a client who is taking amiodarone to treat atrial fibrillation. Which of the following findings is a manifestation of amiodarone toxicity?

  1. Light yellow urine
  2. Report of tinnitus
  3. Productive cough
  4. Blue-gray skin discoloration
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Light yellow urine is an expected finding.
  • B. Tinnitus (ototoxicity) is associated with aminoglycoside antibiotics.
  • C. Correct — A productive cough can indicate pulmonary toxicity, a serious adverse effect of amiodarone requiring prompt evaluation.
  • D. Blue-gray skin discoloration can occur with long-term use but is not the acute toxicity finding of concern here.

  1. Calcium gluconate
  2. Sodium bicarbonate
  3. Potassium chloride
  4. Magnesium sulfate
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — IV calcium gluconate reverses the severe hypotension caused by verapamil (a calcium channel blocker).
  • B. IV sodium bicarbonate treats metabolic acidosis.
  • C. IV potassium chloride treats hypokalemia.
  • D. IV magnesium sulfate treats certain ventricular dysrhythmias.

  1. Bruising
  2. Report of metallic taste
  3. Muscle pain
  4. Report of anorexia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Bruising is an adverse effect of anticoagulants.
  • B. Metallic taste is not a hallmark of digoxin toxicity.
  • C. Weakness (rather than focal muscle pain) is a digoxin toxicity finding.
  • D. Correct — Anorexia, along with blurred vision and stomach pain, is a classic manifestation of digoxin toxicity.

A nurse is assessing a client who has taken procainamide to treat dysrhythmias for the last 12 months. The nurse should assess the client for which of the following manifestations as an adverse effect of this medication? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Hypertension
  2. Widened QRS complex
  3. Narrowed QT interval
  4. Easy bruising
  5. Swollen joints
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Hypotension, rather than hypertension, is an adverse effect.
  • B. Correct — Procainamide can cause a widened QRS complex on the ECG.
  • C. Incorrect — Procainamide prolongs (not narrows) the QT interval.
  • D. Correct — Easy bruising can result from bone marrow suppression.
  • E. Correct — A systemic lupus erythematosus-like syndrome (swollen joints) can occur with long-term use.

Exercise 23.5

A nurse is preparing to administer propranolol to a client who has a dysrhythmia. Which of the following actions should the nurse plan to take?

  1. Hold propranolol for an apical pulse greater than 100/min.
  2. Administer propranolol to increase the client's blood pressure.
  3. Assist the client when sitting up or standing after taking this medication.
  4. Check for hypokalemia frequently due to the risk for propranolol toxicity.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Hold propranolol for an apical pulse less than 60/min, not greater than 100.
  • B. Propranolol lowers (not increases) blood pressure.
  • C. Correct — Propranolol can cause orthostatic hypotension; assist the client when changing positions.
  • D. Propranolol can raise potassium levels; hypokalemia is not the concern.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 4 · Cardiovascular · Chapter 24

Antilipemic Agents

Antilipemic medications lower LDL and triglycerides, raise HDL. Statins (atorvastatin — prototype) reduce LDL production and are first-line. Other agents: cholesterol absorption inhibitors (ezetimibe), bile acid sequestrants (colesevelam), fibrates (gemfibrozil), niacin, and PCSK9 inhibitors (alirocumab).

Antilipemics — Overview

Lipid-lowering drugs back up lifestyle change, not replace it. Statins lead; the rest fill specific gaps.

Antilipemics — overview & monitoring

Lipid management
  • Lower LDL cholesterol, raise HDL, and may decrease VLDL — used with lifestyle modifications (activity, diet, weight control)
  • Not first-line for coronary artery disease — used when lifestyle change doesn’t lower LDL adequately
  • Baseline and periodic labs: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, and liver/kidney function
  • Classes: statins (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors), cholesterol absorption inhibitors, bile-acid sequestrants, fibrates, and monoclonal antibodies (PCSK9 inhibitors)

Other Lipid-Lowering Agents

When statins aren’t enough or aren’t tolerated, these add or substitute.

Ezetimibe — cholesterol absorption inhibitor

Absorption
  • Decreases cholesterol absorption in the small intestine → lowers LDL; often combined with a statin (e.g., simvastatin)
  • Take 2 hr before or 4 hr after bile-acid sequestrants (which interfere with absorption)
  • With statins → increased liver dysfunction/myopathy risk; with fibrates → increased cholelithiasis/myopathy (not recommended together)
  • Monitor liver function; report muscle aches and signs of liver damage

Bile-acid sequestrants

Colesevelam
  • Prototype colesevelam; also colestipol; decrease LDL cholesterol
  • Used alone or as an adjunct with a statin plus dietary measures
  • Constipation: increase high-fiber foods and fluids if not restricted
  • Can interfere with absorption of other medications — separate dosing times

Fibrates & PCSK9 inhibitors

Adjuncts
  • Fibrates (gemfibrozil, fenofibrate): primarily lower triglycerides; increase myopathy risk when combined with statins
  • PCSK9 inhibitors (monoclonal antibodies): markedly lower LDL by injection — for clients not controlled on statins or with familial hypercholesterolemia
  • Reinforce a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet and regular exercise; monitor the lipid panel and liver/kidney function

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is providing care for a client who has elevated total cholesterol, LDL, and triglycerides, and has a new prescription for atorvastatin once daily. The client has type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension. What should the nurse teach the client about atorvastatin? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for atorvastatin.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three two tests to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include two teaching points.

Therapeutic Uses

Atorvastatin decreases LDL and triglycerides, and elevates hDL. It reduces the risk for cardiovascular events (myocardial infarction) and also provides secondary prevention in clients who have had a cardiovascular event. In clients who have diabetes mellitus and hypertension, atorvastatin can reduce mortality by controlling cholesterol levels.

Complications

  • Muscle pain/tenderness (myopathy)
  • Liver toxicity with findings (jaundice, upper abdominal pain, anorexia, and nausea)

Nursing Interventions

Monitor baseline and periodic cholesterol levels (including LDL, hDL, and triglycerides), creatine kinase levels for myopathy, and liver function tests for liver toxicity.

Client Education

  • Perform additional ways to help decrease cholesterol and improve health (exercise, low-fat diet, weight control, and smoking cessation).
  • Take atorvastatin in the evening without regard to meals. (Antilipemic agents are given in the evening because cholesterol is mostly synthesized during the night.)

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 24.1

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is starting simvastatin. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Take this medication in the evening.
  2. Change position slowly when rising from a chair.
  3. Maintain a steady intake of green leafy vegetables.
  4. Consume no more than 1 L/day of fluid.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Take simvastatin in the evening; cholesterol synthesis is highest at night, maximizing effectiveness.
  • B. Orthostatic precautions are not specific to statins.
  • C. Steady green leafy vegetable (vitamin K) intake applies to warfarin, not statins.
  • D. There is no fluid restriction with simvastatin.

  2. Tremor

  4. Pneumonia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Mental status changes, tremor, and pneumonia are not adverse effects of gemfibrozil.
  • C. Correct — Jaundice (along with anorexia and upper abdominal pain) can indicate hepatotoxicity, an adverse effect of gemfibrozil.

Exercise 24.3

A nurse is teaching a client who is taking digoxin and has a new prescription for colesevelam. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include in the teaching?

  3. "Watch for bleeding or bruising while taking colesevelam."

Answer: D

  • A. Many medications (including digoxin) should be taken 1 hr before or 4 hr after colesevelam, which binds drugs in the gut.
  • B. Blood electrolytes are not routinely monitored with colesevelam.
  • C. Bleeding/bruising is not an expected effect.
  • D. Correct — Take colesevelam with food and at least one glass of water to aid administration.

  2. History of hypertension
  3. Active hepatitis C
  4. Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Unlike bile-acid sequestrants, ezetimibe does not cause significant constipation; it is not a contraindication.
  • B, D. Hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus are not contraindications.
  • C. Correct — Ezetimibe combined with a statin is contraindicated in active liver disease (e.g., active hepatitis C) due to hepatotoxicity risk.

  1. Muscle aches
  2. Vasculitis
  3. Hearing loss
  4. Urticaria
  5. Jaundice
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Myopathy (muscle aches) is associated with statins, not alirocumab.
  • B. Correct — Vasculitis can occur as part of a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
  • C. Incorrect — Hearing loss is not an adverse effect (it is associated with niacin).
  • D. Correct — Urticaria can occur as a severe hypersensitivity reaction.
  • E. Correct — Monitor for jaundice/liver disorder; report hepatic signs.

Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 25

Medications Affecting Coagulation

Coagulation medications prevent and treat thromboembolic events. Three classes: anticoagulants (heparin, warfarin, DOACs), antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, abciximab), and thrombolytics (alteplase). All carry significant bleeding risk requiring careful monitoring.

Coagulation — Overview

These drugs prevent clots, stop platelets from clumping, or dissolve a clot — and every one of them raises bleeding risk.

Anticoagulation — overview

Bleeding risk
  • Used to prevent clot formation or break apart an existing clot by altering the clotting cascade, preventing platelet aggregation, or dissolving a clot
  • Goals: increase circulation/perfusion, decrease pain, and prevent further tissue damage
  • All carry a significant bleeding risk
  • Groups: anticoagulants (heparins, vitamin K antagonists, direct thrombin inhibitors, factor Xa inhibitors), antiplatelets, and thrombolytics

Warfarin (Vitamin K Antagonist)

Oral, slow-onset anticoagulant with a long list of interactions — INR is everything.

Warfarin — action, monitoring & antidote

INR 2–3
  • Antagonizes vitamin K → decreases synthesis of clotting factors; slow onset, so heparin often bridges initial therapy
  • Monitor PT and INR (typical therapeutic INR 2–3); antidote is vitamin K (phytonadione)
  • Client education: consistent vitamin K intake, regular INR checks, bleeding precautions, report bleeding

Warfarin — contraindications & interactions

High interaction
  • Pregnancy Risk Category X (D with mechanical heart valves) — fetal hemorrhage/death, CNS defects; avoid in lactation; use heparin/LMWH if anticoagulation needed in pregnancy
  • Contraindicated: thrombocytopenia, uncontrolled bleeding, recent eye/brain/spinal surgery, vitamin K deficiency, liver disorders, alcohol use disorder
  • Increase bleeding (heparin, aspirin, acetaminophen, glucocorticoids, sulfonamides); decrease effect (phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, oral contraceptives, vitamin K)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for clopidogrel following a myocardial infarction. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the intended effect.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects for this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three, including one test the nurse should monitor periodically.

Therapeutic Uses

Clopidogrel inhibits platelet aggregation and prolongs bleeding time. It is used to prevent myocardial infarction (mI) or stroke in clients who have already had an mI or stroke.

Complications

Like other platelet inhibitors, clopidogrel can cause bleeding due to thrombocytopenia. It can also cause GI effects (abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea).

Nursing Interventions

  • The nurse should plan to monitor the platelet count periodically while the client takes clopidogrel.
  • Teach the client to monitor for bleeding. The client should watch for black stools, coffee-ground emesis, blood in the urine, nose bleeds, unusual bruising, or petechiae. The client should inform the provider if these occur and about GI effects.
  • The nurse should be aware of all medications the client is taking, because risk for bleeding increases if the medication is taken with anticoagulants or antiplatelet medications. Clopidogrel is sometimes administered concurrently with aspirin, and that increases the risk for bleeding. The medication should be discontinued 7 days before any elective surgery.

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 25.1

A nurse is planning to administer subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg using a prefilled syringe of enoxaparin 40 mg/0.4 mL to an adult client following hip arthroplasty. Which of the following actions should the nurse plan to take?

  1. Expel the air bubble from the prefilled syringe before injecting.
  2. Insert the needle completely into the client's tissue.
  3. Administer the injection in the client's thigh.
  4. Aspirate carefully after inserting the needle into the client's skin.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Do not expel the air bubble in the prefilled syringe; it ensures the full dose is delivered.
  • B. Correct — Insert the needle of the prefilled syringe completely into a skin fold of the abdomen.
  • C. Administer in the abdomen ("love handles"), not the thigh.
  • D. Do not aspirate when administering enoxaparin.

  4. Calcium gluconate

Answer: C

  • A. Vitamin K1 reverses warfarin, not heparin.
  • B. Atropine reverses bradycardia.

Exercise 25.3

A nurse is planning to administer IV alteplase to a client. Which of the following interventions should the nurse plan to take?

  1. Administer IM enoxaparin along with the alteplase dose.
  2. Obtain the client's weight.
  3. Administer aminocaproic acid IV prior to alteplase infusion.
  4. Prepare to administer alteplase within 8 hr of manifestation onset.

Answer: B

  • A. Avoid IM injections with thrombolytics (bleeding risk); enoxaparin is only subcutaneous regardless.
  • B. Correct — An accurate weight is required to calculate the weight-based alteplase dose.
  • C. Aminocaproic acid is the antidote to alteplase; it is not given beforehand.
  • D. Administer alteplase as soon as possible after onset, within the narrow approved window (not 8 hr).

  1. Hypertension

  • C. Correct — Tinnitus and hearing loss can occur (salicylism).
  • D. Incorrect — Paresthesias of the extremities are not an aspirin effect.

  1. Vitamin K1

  3. Omeprazole
  4. Probenecid

Answer: C

  • A. Vitamin K1 treats warfarin-related hemorrhage.
  • B. Protamine treats heparin-related hemorrhage.

Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 26

Growth Factors

Hematopoietic growth factors stimulate production of specific blood cells: erythropoietin (epoetin alfa) for RBCs, granulocyte colony-stimulating factors (filgrastim, sargramostim) for WBCs, and thrombopoietin agonists (oprelvekin, romiplostim) for platelets. Used in anemia of chronic disease, chemo-induced cytopenias.

Growth Factors — Overview

Engineered versions of the body’s own hematopoietic hormones, used to rebuild blood cells after chemo or in kidney disease.

Hematopoietic growth factors — overview

Hematopoiesis
  • Genetically engineered hematopoietic growth factors stimulate the bone marrow to produce blood cells
  • Uses: replace neutrophils/platelets after chemotherapy, hasten marrow recovery after bone marrow transplant, and increase RBC production in chronic kidney disease
  • Three groups: erythropoietic (ESAs), and two leukopoietic (G-CSF and GM-CSF)

Leukopoietic Growth Factors

Filgrastim and sargramostim rebuild white cells to fight infection after marrow suppression.

Filgrastim & sargramostim — action & uses

↑ WBC
  • Filgrastim (G-CSF; pegfilgrastim long-acting) and sargramostim (GM-CSF) act on bone marrow to increase WBC/neutrophil production
  • Uses: neutropenia, hastening marrow recovery after bone marrow transplant, accelerating neutrophil recovery after chemotherapy to reduce life-threatening infection
  • Effectiveness: absence of infection; WBC and differential within expected range

Leukopoietic agents — complications & administration

Bone pain
  • Bone pain, diarrhea, weakness, rash, malaise — treat bone pain with acetaminophen
  • Leukocytosis/thrombocytosis: monitor CBC twice weekly; reduce or interrupt for ANC ≥20,000, WBC ≥50,000, or platelets ≥500,000/mm³
  • Sargramostim is contraindicated with yeast allergy; do not shake the vial; use each vial for one dose and discard

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has chronic kidney disease and a new prescription for subcutaneous epoetin alfa three times weekly. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify why epoetin alfa would benefit this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe four, including two tests the nurse should monitor periodically.

Therapeutic Uses

Erythropoietin, a substance that stimulates bone marrow to produce red blood cells, is produced by the kidney. In clients who have chronic kidney disease, erythropoietin is no longer present and anemia results. Epoetin alfa stimulates production of red blood cells in these clients.

Complications

  • Headaches and myalgia (body aches)
  • Thrombotic events, such as myocardial infarction and stroke
  • Hypertension (common, sometimes serious)
  • A too-rapid increase (hgb greater than 1 g/dL over 2 weeks, or hgb greater than 10 g/dL) can worsen hypertension, increase risk of thrombosis, and cause seizures.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor baseline iron levels, CBC with differential, and platelet count.
  • Monitor hgb and hct twice weekly until blood counts stabilize.
  • Calculate dosages carefully. Both subcutaneous and IV epoetin alfa have dosages based on the client's weight. Do not shake the epoetin alfa vial, and discard vial after one dose is removed.
  • Monitor blood pressure carefully, and report increases to the provider. Question the client about frequency and severity of headaches, which could be an indication of increasing blood pressure or a simple adverse effect.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 26.1

A nurse is reviewing the medical record of a client who has a new prescription for sargramostim. Which of the following findings should the nurse identify as a contraindication to administering the medication?

  1. Allergy to yeast
  2. Hypermagnesemia
  3. Hypotension
  4. Allergy to eggs
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Sargramostim is produced using yeast; a documented yeast allergy is a contraindication.
  • B. Hypomagnesemia (not hypermagnesemia) can be an adverse effect.
  • C. Sargramostim can cause hypertension and tachycardia, not hypotension as a contraindication.
  • D. An egg allergy is not a contraindication to sargramostim.

  2. Ensure that the medication is refrigerated until just prior to administration.
  3. Shake vial gently to mix well before withdrawing dose.
  4. Discard vial after removing one dose of the medication.

Answer: D

  • A. Filgrastim is not given IM (it is given subcutaneously or IV).
  • B. Allow the medication to reach room temperature before administration.

Unit 5 · Hematologic · Chapter 27

Blood and Blood Products

Blood and blood products replace deficient components: packed RBCs (anemia, blood loss), platelets (thrombocytopenia, bleeding), fresh frozen plasma (clotting factor deficiency), cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen, factor VIII). Strict transfusion protocols prevent acute and delayed reactions.

Blood Products — Overview

Transfusion replaces whole blood or specific components; the nurse's verification and monitoring are central to safety.

Principles of transfusion therapy

Safety-driven
  • Requires type and crossmatch, informed consent, and a dedicated IV line with 0.9% normal saline
  • Replace the specific deficit — red cells for oxygen capacity, platelets/plasma for clotting, albumin for volume
  • The greatest risks are transfusion reactions, so identity verification and close early monitoring are essential

Blood Products & Compatibility

Each product replaces something specific — and the right type-and-crossmatch is what keeps a transfusion safe.

Blood products & therapeutic uses

Components
  • Used to increase intravascular volume, replace clotting factors/components, replace blood loss, and improve oxygen-carrying capacity
  • PRBCs: severe anemia (Hgb 6–10 g/dL); platelets: thrombocytopenia (count <20,000/mm³) or active bleeding
  • Albumin: expands volume by oncotic pressure (hypovolemia, burns); plasma: replaces clotting factors; whole blood: acute large-volume loss

Blood typing & crossmatching

ABO / Rh
  • ABO typing detects A and B antibodies (clients with neither have type O); plasma products require ABO typing only
  • Rh testing: Rh antigens present = Rh+, absent = Rh−
  • Crossmatching is required for any RBC-containing product (after ABO/Rh) to detect incompatibility before transfusion

Transfusion Reactions

Recognize the reaction by its pattern — the acute hemolytic reaction is the one that kills.

Acute hemolytic reaction

Emergency
  • Caused by ABO incompatibility — chills, fever, low back pain, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension
  • Prevent: verify client identity with two nurses and confirm ABO/Rh compatibility
  • Assess vital signs at baseline and during the first 15–30 min, staying with the client; this is a medical emergency

Other transfusion reactions

Recognize the pattern
  • Febrile nonhemolytic: fever/chills (most common); mild allergic: urticaria/itching; anaphylactic: respiratory distress, shock
  • Circulatory overload: dyspnea, crackles, distended neck veins — transfuse slowly, especially in older adults
  • Hyperkalemia (cell lysis, K ≥5.0): bradycardia, paresthesias — more likely in older/previously frozen units; sepsis: rapid chills/fever, hypotension; TA-GVHD: prevented with irradiated products

Administration & Reaction Response

Tight timing, two-nurse checks, and a clear stop-the-line protocol define safe transfusion.

Transfusion administration & safety

Timing
  • Establish IV access and prepare equipment before removing the product from refrigeration; inspect for gas bubbles, discoloration, or cloudiness
  • Transfuse a unit within 4 hr of removal from refrigeration; older adults: transfuse slowly over 2–4 hr, vital signs every 15 min, watch for overload
  • Massive transfusion (≈10 units/24 hr): monitor platelets, PT, aPTT every 5 units and potassium/calcium levels

If a transfusion reaction occurs

Stop the line
  • Stop the transfusion immediately and notify the provider
  • Do not run the IV fluids connected to the Y-tubing (would infuse more blood) — hang 0.9% sodium chloride through new tubing
  • Stay with the client, monitor vital signs and urine output, send the blood bag/tubing and a urine specimen to the lab, recheck identification, and document thoroughly

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Therapeutic Procedure.

Active Learning Scenario

Therapeutic Procedure

A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to a client who has who has a GI bleed and hgb 6.0 g/dL. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Therapeutic Procedure to complete this item.

  • INDICATIONS: What assessment data would indicate to the nurse that transfusion of PRBCs is indicated in this client?

Indications

A client who lost blood from a GI bleed can need a unit of PRBCs for a hgb level below 10 g/dL especially if demonstrating manifestations of hypovolemia (increase in pulse and respiration rate; decrease in blood pressure; low oxygen saturation; cool and pale or cyanotic; increased capillary refill time; increased urinary output). If hypoxic, the client will exhibit decreased level of consciousness and confusion. PRBCs restore red blood cells and improve oxygenation. If the client has lost a large amount of fluid volume, whole blood, rather than PRBCs, can be indicated.

Exercise 27.1

A nurse is preparing to administer a transfusion of 300 mL of pooled platelets to a client who has severe thrombocytopenia. The nurse should plan to administer the transfusion over which of the following time frames?

  1. Within 30 min/unit
  2. Within 60 min/unit
  3. Within 2 hr/unit
  4. Within 4 hr/unit
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Platelets are fragile and should be administered rapidly, within about 30 min/unit.
  • B. Fresh frozen plasma is given within 30 to 60 min/unit.
  • C, D. Whole blood or PRBCs are administered over 2 to 4 hr/unit.

Exercise 27.2

A nurse is transfusing a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to a client who has anemia due to chemotherapy. The client reports a sudden headache and chills. The client's temperature is 2°F higher than the baseline reading. In addition to notifying the provider, which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Stop the transfusion.
  2. Place the client in an upright position with feet down.
  3. Remove the blood bag and tubing from the IV catheter.
  4. Obtain a urine specimen.
  5. Infuse dextrose 5% in water through the IV.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, C, D

  • A. Correct — Stop the transfusion immediately for a temperature rise (possible febrile or hemolytic reaction).
  • B. Incorrect — Upright with feet down is for circulatory overload, not this reaction.
  • C. Correct — Remove the blood bag and tubing to avoid infusing more incompatible blood.
  • D. Correct — Obtain a urine specimen to check for hemolysis (hemoglobinuria).
  • E. Incorrect — Only 0.9% sodium chloride is infused with blood; never dextrose (it causes hemolysis).

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Blood and Blood Products

Exercise 27.3

A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells (PRBCs) to a client who has severe anemia. Which of the following interventions can prevent an acute hemolytic reaction?

  1. Ensure that the client has a patent IV line before obtaining blood product from the refrigerator.
  2. Obtain help from another nurse to confirm the correct client and blood product.
  3. Take a complete set of vital signs before beginning transfusion and periodically during the transfusion.
  4. Stay with the client for the first 15 to 30 min of the transfusion.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. A patent IV line is necessary but does not prevent a hemolytic (mismatch) reaction.
  • B. Correct — Acute hemolytic reactions result from ABO incompatibility; a two-person verification of client identity and blood product prevents mismatch.
  • C. Vital signs help detect a reaction but do not prevent the mismatch.
  • D. Staying with the client helps early detection, not prevention of the mismatch.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Blood and Blood Products

Exercise 27.4

A nurse is caring for a client who has an activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) greater than 1.5 times the expected reference range. Which of the following blood products should the nurse prepare to transfuse?

  1. Whole blood
  2. Platelets
  3. Fresh frozen plasma
  4. Packed red blood cells
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Whole blood is used for significant volume loss with RBC need.
  • B. Platelets are transfused for thrombocytopenia/platelet dysfunction.
  • C. Correct — Fresh frozen plasma replaces clotting factors and is indicated for a prolonged aPTT (coagulopathy).
  • D. PRBCs are transfused for severe anemia.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Blood and Blood Products

Exercise 27.5

A nurse is assessing a client during transfusion of a unit of whole blood. The client develops a cough, shortness of breath, elevated blood pressure, and distended neck veins. The nurse should expect a prescription for which of the following medications?

  1. Epinephrine
  2. Lorazepam
  3. Furosemide
  4. Diphenhydramine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Epinephrine is for anaphylactic reactions.
  • B. Lorazepam is a benzodiazepine, not indicated here.
  • C. Correct — Cough, dyspnea, elevated BP, and distended neck veins indicate transfusion-associated circulatory overload; furosemide (a loop diuretic) is prescribed.
  • D. Diphenhydramine is for mild allergic reactions.

Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 28

Peptic Ulcer Disease

Peptic ulcer disease (PUD) and GERD are treated by reducing gastric acid and protecting the mucosa. Categories: H2 receptor antagonists (cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine), proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole — most effective), mucosal protectants (sucralfate, misoprostol), and antacids.

Peptic Ulcer Disease — Overview

PUD is an imbalance between mucosal defenses and aggressors. Therapy eradicates the cause and lets the mucosa heal.

Peptic ulcer disease — overview

Defense vs aggression
  • Reflects an imbalance between gastric mucosal defenses (mucus, bicarbonate) and aggressive factors (H. pylori, gastric acid, pepsin, smoking, NSAIDs)
  • H. pylori infection is treated with antibiotics; other agents promote GI healing
  • Therapeutic goals: reduce manifestations, promote healing, and prevent complications and recurrence

H. pylori Eradication

When H. pylori is the cause, antibiotics in combination are the cure.

Antibiotics for H. pylori

Combination therapy
  • Agents: amoxicillin, clarithromycin, metronidazole, tetracycline, bismuth, tinidazole
  • Use a combination of two or three antibiotics for 14 days to increase effectiveness and minimize resistance
  • Administer metronidazole with food to decrease gastric upset; nausea and diarrhea are common — complete the full course

Acid-Suppressing Agents

H₂ blockers and proton pump inhibitors cut acid output — PPIs more powerfully, with long-term cautions.

H₂-receptor antagonists

Cimetidine/famotidine
  • Prototype cimetidine (also famotidine, nizatidine); block H₂ receptors → suppress gastric acid secretion
  • Use: prevent or treat gastric and duodenal ulcers; usually twice daily until healed, then a bedtime maintenance dose
  • Cimetidine inhibits drug-metabolizing enzymes → increases warfarin, phenytoin, theophylline, and lidocaine levels (monitor); separate antacids by 1 hr; smoking reduces effectiveness

Proton pump inhibitors — action & uses

Omeprazole
  • Prototype omeprazole (also pantoprazole, esomeprazole); irreversibly inhibit the gastric proton pump → profound acid suppression
  • Uses: PUD, GERD, erosive esophagitis, stress-ulcer prophylaxis, and part of H. pylori regimens
  • Do not crush, chew, or break sustained-release capsules

PPIs — complications & interactions

Long-term cautions
  • Hypomagnesemia (long-term): baseline and ongoing Mg; report tremors, muscle cramps, seizures
  • C. difficile diarrhea and increased pneumonia risk; report fever, diarrhea, abdominal cramping, or bloody stools
  • Interactions: increases digoxin/methotrexate/phenytoin levels; decreases ketoconazole/atazanavir absorption and the effect of clopidogrel

Antacids & Mucosal Protectants

Neutralize acid or shield the ulcer crater directly — watch the bowel effects.

Antacids

Neutralize acid
  • Prototype aluminum hydroxide (also magnesium hydroxide, calcium carbonate); neutralize gastric acid and reduce pepsin activity
  • Aluminum/calcium → constipation; magnesium → diarrhea — alternate or combine to normalize bowel function
  • Avoid sodium-containing antacids in hypertension/HF (fluid retention); avoid magnesium antacids in renal impairment (hypermagnesemia); separate from other drugs by ~1 hr

Mucosal protectants

Sucralfate
  • Sucralfate forms a protective barrier over the ulcer crater; give on an empty stomach and separate from other medications and antacids
  • Misoprostol (prostaglandin analog) prevents NSAID-induced ulcers — contraindicated in pregnancy (causes uterine contractions/miscarriage)
  • Take protectants as scheduled and report ongoing pain or GI bleeding
