Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is caring for a client who has a prescription for calcium carbonate. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use of calcium carbonate.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Identify three instructions the nurse should include regarding taking this medication. on Exercises

Therapeutic Uses

Calcium carbonate is an antacid that raises the ph of gastric contents, which reduces irritation of stomach mucosa, resulting in relief of pain.

Client Education

  • Shake liquid suspensions prior to taking each dose in order to disperse the medication.
  • Take other medications at least 1 hr before or after taking aluminum hydroxide.
  • Calcium carbonate can cause constipation. Notify the provider if it persists. You might need to alternate this antacid with one that is a magnesium compound and has diarrhea as an adverse effect.
  • Report manifestations of hypercalcemia (constipation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, confusion) to the provider.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 28.1

A nurse is teaching a client who will begin taking aluminum hydroxide. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. "If constipation develops, switch to a calcium-based antacid."
  2. "Take this medication two hours before or after other medications."
  3. "This medication increases the risk for pneumonia."
  4. "Have your magnesium level monitored while taking this medication."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Aluminum antacids cause constipation; alternate with a magnesium-based antacid (not calcium) to normalize bowel pattern.
  • B. Correct — Antacids alter the absorption of many medications; take other medications 1-2 hr before or after.
  • C. Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole), not aluminum hydroxide, increase pneumonia risk.
  • D. Hypomagnesemia monitoring applies to PPIs (omeprazole), not aluminum hydroxide.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 28.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for omeprazole. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Take this medication at bedtime.
  2. This medication decreases the production of gastric acid.
  3. Take this medication 2 hr after eating.
  4. This medication can cause hyperkalemia.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Omeprazole is taken in the morning, not at bedtime.
  • B. Correct — Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor; it decreases gastric acid production by inhibiting the acid-producing enzyme.
  • C. Take it before meals with a glass of water, not 2 hr after eating.
  • D. Omeprazole can cause hypomagnesemia, not hyperkalemia.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 28.3

A nurse is teaching a client who takes phenytoin and has a new prescription for sucralfate tablets. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include?

  1. Take an antacid with the sucralfate.
  2. Take sucralfate with a glass of milk.
  3. Allow a 2-hr interval between these medications.
  4. Chew the sucralfate thoroughly before swallowing.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Antacids interfere with sucralfate; allow a 30-min interval between them.
  • B. Take sucralfate on an empty stomach, 1 hr before meals.
  • C. Correct — Sucralfate interferes with phenytoin absorption; allow a 2-hr interval between the two.
  • D. Swallow sucralfate whole.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 28.4

A nurse is caring for four clients who have peptic ulcer disease. The nurse should identify misoprostol is contraindicated for which of the following clients?

  1. A client who is pregnant
  2. A client who has osteoarthritis
  3. A client who has a kidney stone
  4. A client who has a urinary tract infection
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Misoprostol can induce labor/uterine contractions and is contraindicated in pregnancy (Pregnancy Risk Category X).
  • B, C, D. Osteoarthritis, kidney stones, and urinary tract infections are not contraindications to misoprostol.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 28.5

A nurse is teaching a client about cimetidine. Which of the following are adverse effects of cimetidine? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Increased libido
  2. Insomnia
  3. Enlargement of breast tissue
  4. Confusion
  5. Decreased sperm count
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Cimetidine causes decreased libido, not increased.
  • B. Incorrect — Cimetidine causes lethargy/CNS depression rather than insomnia.
  • C. Correct — Gynecomastia (breast tissue enlargement) is an antiandrogenic effect.
  • D. Correct — Confusion is an adverse CNS effect, especially in older adults.
  • E. Correct — Decreased sperm count is an antiandrogenic effect.

Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 29

Gastrointestinal Disorders

GI medications include antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine), antidiarrheals (diphenoxylate, loperamide), laxatives (psyllium, docusate, bisacodyl, lactulose, polyethylene glycol), prokinetic agents, IBS therapies (alosetron, lubiprostone), and IBD medications (sulfasalazine, glucocorticoids, biologics).

GI Disorders — Overview

This chapter spans nausea, motion, diarrhea, and constipation — matched drug class to symptom.

GI medications — overview

Symptom-targeted
  • Treat or prevent nausea/vomiting, motion sickness, diarrhea, and constipation, and manage GERD
  • Classes: antiemetics, laxatives, antidiarrheals, prokinetic agents, IBS medications, 5-aminosalicylates, and probiotics

Prokinetics, IBS & Bowel Disease

Drugs that speed the gut, calm IBS, or quiet inflammatory bowel disease round out GI therapy.

Prokinetics, IBS & 5-aminosalicylates

Motility & inflammation
  • Metoclopramide (prokinetic): increases gastric motility for GERD/gastroparesis — risk of EPS and tardive dyskinesia with long use
  • IBS agents target diarrhea- or constipation-predominant patterns; probiotics support normal flora
  • 5-aminosalicylates (sulfasalazine, mesalamine): reduce inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease — monitor CBC and renal function, ensure adequate fluids

GERD & reflux management

Lifestyle + drugs
  • Combine acid suppression (PPI or H₂ blocker) with lifestyle measures: elevate the head of the bed, avoid late meals, limit caffeine/alcohol/fatty foods
  • Prokinetics may help by increasing lower-esophageal tone and gastric emptying
  • Report persistent symptoms, difficulty swallowing, or weight loss for further evaluation

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is caring for a client who has a prescription for sulfasalazine. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item to include the following sections.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify two therapeutic uses for sulfasalazine.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two blood disorders that occur as a complication with the use of sulfasalazine.
  • MEDICATION ADMINISTRATION: Identify how frequently the client should take the medication.

Therapeutic Uses

Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis

Complications

Complications that occur with the use of sulfasalazine include agranulocytosis, and hemolytic and macrocytic anemia.

Medication Administration

The client should take sulfasalazine four times per day in divided doses.

Exercise 29.1

A nurse is caring for a client who received prochlorperazine 4 hr ago. The client reports spasms of the face. The nurse should expect a prescription for which of the following medications?

  1. Fomepizole
  2. Naloxone
  3. Phytonadione
  4. Diphenhydramine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Fomepizole treats methanol/ethylene glycol poisoning.
  • B. Naloxone treats opioid toxicity.
  • C. Phytonadione (vitamin K1) treats warfarin toxicity.
  • D. Correct — Facial spasms indicate an acute dystonic reaction (EPS) from prochlorperazine; diphenhydramine is given to treat it.

A nurse is planning to administer ondansetron to a client. For which of the following adverse effects of ondansetron should the nurse monitor? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Headache
  2. Diarrhea

  4. Hyperglycemia
  5. Prolonged QT interval

Answer: A, B, E

Exercise 29.3

A nurse is providing instructions about the use of laxatives to a client who has heart failure. The nurse should tell the client to avoid which of the following laxatives?

  1. Sodium phosphate
  2. Psyllium
  3. Bisacodyl
  4. Polyethylene glycol
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Sodium is absorbed from sodium phosphate, causing fluid retention that can worsen heart failure; avoid it.
  • B. Psyllium (a bulk-forming laxative) is not absorbed and is acceptable.
  • C. Bisacodyl has minimal systemic effects.
  • D. Polyethylene glycol is not the laxative to avoid specifically for heart failure here.

Answer: B

  • A. Lubiprostone is used for irritable bowel syndrome with constipation.

  • C. Bisacodyl is a stimulant laxative for constipation.

Exercise 29.5

A nurse is teaching a client about probiotic supplements. Which of the following information should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "Probiotics are micro-organisms that are normally found in the GI tract."
  2. "Probiotics are used to treat Clostridium difficile."
  3. "Probiotics are used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia."
  4. "You can experience bloating while taking probiotic supplements."
  5. "If you are prescribed an antibiotic, you should take it at the same time you take your probiotic supplement."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, D

  • A. Correct — Probiotics consist of micro-organisms (e.g., lactobacilli) normally found in the GI tract.
  • B. Correct — Probiotics are used to treat a number of GI conditions, including Clostridium difficile.
  • C. Incorrect — Saw palmetto, not probiotics, is used for benign prostatic hyperplasia.
  • D. Correct — Flatulence and bloating are adverse effects of probiotics.
  • E. Incorrect — Take the probiotic at least 2 hr apart from an antibiotic, not at the same time.

Unit 6 · GI & Nutrition · Chapter 30

Vitamins and Minerals

Vitamins and minerals correct deficiencies: iron (ferrous sulfate) for iron-deficiency anemia, B12 (cyanocobalamin) for pernicious anemia, folic acid for megaloblastic anemia and pregnancy, potassium chloride for hypokalemia. Each has specific administration considerations and monitoring needs.

Vitamins & Minerals — Overview

Supplements correct deficiencies that drive anemia, bone disease, and more — absorption is the recurring theme.

Vitamins & minerals — overview

Deficiency correction
  • Vitamins and minerals support RBC production, bone formation, hormone synthesis, fluid balance, and nerve function
  • Deficiencies increase the risk of anemia, heart disease, and osteoporosis; supplements help prevent and treat these conditions

Vitamin B₁₂ & Folic Acid

The two anemia vitamins — and why B₁₂ must be checked before folic acid.

Vitamin B₁₂ & folic acid

Megaloblastic anemia
  • Cyanocobalamin (B₁₂): for pernicious anemia (lack of intrinsic factor) and malabsorption — given oral, intranasal, IM, or subcutaneous; parenteral/lifelong for total malabsorption
  • Monitor B₁₂, Hgb, Hct, reticulocytes; watch for deficiency signs (beefy red tongue, pallor, neuropathy)
  • Folic acid treats folate-deficiency anemia and prevents neural tube defects; folic acid can mask B₁₂ deficiency — ensure adequate B₁₂ when giving folate

Mineral Supplements

Potassium is the high-alert mineral — never IV push, and watch both ends of the range.

Potassium supplements

High-alert: never IV push
  • Prototype potassium chloride — essential for nerve conduction, muscle excitability, and acid/base balance; treats hypokalemia (<3.5 mEq/L), especially with loop diuretics or GI losses
  • Oral: take with meals or 8 oz water to prevent GI ulceration; do not let tablets dissolve in the mouth
  • IV potassium is NEVER given by IV push — always dilute and infuse on a pump; monitor for hyperkalemia (bradycardia, ECG changes, weakness); contraindicated in severe kidney disease

Calcium, magnesium & other minerals

Electrolyte support
  • Calcium (with vitamin D): bone health and hypocalcemia; can cause constipation and (in excess) hypercalcemia/renal stones
  • Magnesium: corrects hypomagnesemia; monitor for toxicity (hyporeflexia, respiratory depression) in renal impairment
  • Take fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) with food; teach that megadoses can be toxic

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is educating a client about a new prescription for cyanocobalamin. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe four teaching points for the client.
  • EVALUATION OF MEDICATION EFFECTIVENESS: Describe two nursing interventions.

Expected Pharmacological Action

Cyanocobalamin converts folic acid from an inactive form to an active form. It corrects megaloblastic anemia related to a deficiency of vitamin B12.

Client Education

  • Review manifestations of hypokalemia.
  • Discuss the use of potassium supplements, if prescribed.
  • Discuss dietary sources of potassium.
  • Consume foods high in vitamin B12.
  • Administer intranasal cyanocobalamin 1 hr before or after eating hot foods when nasal secretions are decreased.
  • Periodic laboratory testing of hgb, hct, RBC, reticulocyte count, and folate levels is advised.

Evaluation Of Medication Effectiveness

  • Review laboratory values for increased reticulocyte count and macrocytes and hgb and hct levels within the expected reference range.
  • Assess for improvement of neurologic manifestations (numbness, tingling of hands and feet).

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 30.1

A nurse is teaching a client who has anemia and a new prescription for a liquid iron supplement. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "Add foods that are high in fiber to your diet."
  2. "Rinse your mouth after taking the medication."
  3. "Expect stools to be green or black in color."
  4. "Take the medication with a glass of milk."
  5. "Add red meat to your diet."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, E

  • A. Correct — High-fiber foods help prevent the constipation iron supplements can cause.
  • B. Correct — Liquid iron can stain teeth; rinse the mouth (or use a straw) after taking it.
  • C. Correct — Dark green or black stools are an expected effect of iron.
  • D. Incorrect — Dairy products (and caffeine) decrease iron absorption; avoid taking with milk.
  • E. Correct — Red meats are high in dietary iron.

Exercise 30.3

A nurse is evaluating a group of clients at a health fair to identify the need for folic acid therapy. Which of the following clients require folic acid therapy? (Select all that apply.)

  1. 12-year-old child who has iron deficiency anemia
  2. 24-year-old female who has no health problems
  3. 44-year-old male who has hypertension
  4. 55-year-old female who has alcohol use disorder
  5. 35-year-old male who has type 2 diabetes mellitus
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, D

  • A. Incorrect — Iron deficiency anemia requires iron, not folic acid.
  • B. Correct — A person of childbearing age should take folic acid to reduce neural tube defect risk.
  • C. Incorrect — Hypertension requires antihypertensive therapy, not folic acid.
  • D. Correct — Alcohol use disorder commonly causes folic acid deficiency.
  • E. Incorrect — Type 2 diabetes mellitus requires glucose management, not folic acid.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 30.4

A nurse is preparing to administer potassium chloride IV to a client who has hypokalemia. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Infuse medication through a large-bore needle.
  2. Monitor urine output to ensure at least 20 mL/hr.
  3. Administer medication via direct IV bolus.
  4. Implement cardiac monitoring.
  5. Administer the infusion using an IV pump.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Infuse IV potassium through a large-bore needle to reduce vein irritation.
  • B. Incorrect — Ensure urine output of at least 30 mL/hr (not 20) before/during administration.
  • C. Incorrect — Never give IV potassium by direct bolus; this can be fatal. Infuse slowly (no faster than 10 mEq/hr).
  • D. Correct — Implement cardiac monitoring to detect dysrhythmias.
  • E. Correct — Always use an infusion pump to control the rate.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 30.5

A nurse is caring for a client who is receiving IV potassium. The nurse should monitor the client for which of the following manifestations as an indication of hyperkalemia?

  1. Tachycardia
  2. Dyspnea
  3. Lethargy
  4. Increased thirst
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Bradycardia (not tachycardia) is a manifestation of hyperkalemia.
  • B. Correct — Dyspnea can occur with hyperkalemia (muscle weakness affecting respiration).
  • C. Anxiety (not lethargy) can occur with hyperkalemia.
  • D. Vomiting (not increased thirst) can occur with hyperkalemia.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 7 · Reproductive · Chapter 31

Medications Affecting the Reproductive Tract

Reproductive medications include: estrogens and progestins (combined oral contraceptives, HRT), androgens (testosterone), drugs for BPH (finasteride, tamsulosin), erectile dysfunction (sildenafil, tadalafil), and infertility agents (clomiphene, gonadotropins).

Reproductive Tract — Overview

Hormones drive puberty, replace deficiencies, and prevent pregnancy — plus the drugs for BPH and erectile dysfunction.

Reproductive medications — overview

Hormones & more
  • Hormones stimulate puberty (estrogen/progesterone in females, testosterone in males), replace deficiencies, or prevent pregnancy (oral contraceptives, patch, ring, injection)
  • BPH is treated with 5-alpha reductase inhibitors and alpha₁-adrenergic antagonists
  • PDE5 inhibitors treat erectile dysfunction

Men’s Health Agents

BPH, erectile dysfunction, and androgen therapy — the nitrate interaction is the can’t-miss point.

BPH medications

Finasteride / tamsulosin
  • 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride): shrink the prostate over months; pregnant partners should not handle crushed tablets (fetal harm)
  • Alpha₁ blockers (tamsulosin): relax bladder-neck/prostate smooth muscle for faster relief — watch for orthostatic hypotension (first-dose effect)
  • Monitor urinary symptoms; rise slowly to prevent dizziness

Erectile dysfunction — PDE5 inhibitors

Avoid with nitrates
  • PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil): enhance erection by promoting vasodilation
  • Contraindicated with nitrates and alpha blockers — combined vasodilation causes life-threatening hypotension
  • Seek care for an erection lasting >4 hr (priapism) or sudden vision/hearing changes

Androgens

Testosterone
  • Testosterone replaces deficiency and supports male secondary sex characteristics; routes include transdermal, IM, and buccal
  • Monitor for fluid retention, polycythemia, and liver effects; avoid skin transfer to women/children from gels
  • Pregnancy Risk Category X; monitor growth in adolescents

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a provider's office is instructing a client who has a new prescription for finasteride to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.

Expected Pharmacological Action

Finasteride slows the production of testosterone, which reduces the size of the prostate and subsequently promotes urinary elimination.

Complications

  • Decreased libido
  • Decreased ejaculate volume
  • Gynecomastia
  • Orthostatic hypotension

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 31.1

A nurse is reviewing the health care record of a client who is asking about conjugated equine estrogens. The nurse should inform the client this medication is contraindicated in which of the following conditions?

  1. Atrophic vaginitis
  2. Dysfunctional uterine bleeding
  3. Osteoporosis
  4. Thrombophlebitis
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Atrophic vaginitis, dysfunctional uterine bleeding, and osteoporosis are conditions estrogen may treat or relate to estrogen deficiency.
  • D. Correct — Estrogen increases the risk of thromboembolism; it is contraindicated in thrombophlebitis.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 31.2

A nurse is providing teaching to a female client who is taking testosterone to treat advanced breast cancer. The nurse should tell the client that which of the following are adverse effects of this medication? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Deepening voice
  2. Weight gain
  3. Low blood pressure
  4. Dry mouth
  5. Facial hair
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, E

  • A. Correct — A deepening voice is part of virilization (development of male characteristics).
  • B. Correct — Edema and weight gain are adverse effects.
  • C. Incorrect — High blood pressure (not low) is an adverse effect.
  • D. Incorrect — Nasal congestion (not dry mouth) is an adverse effect.
  • E. Correct — Facial hair is part of virilization.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 31.3

A nurse is explaining the mechanism of action of combination oral contraceptives to a group of clients. The nurse should tell the clients that which of the following actions occur with the use of combination oral contraceptives? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Thickening the cervical mucus
  2. Inducing maturation of ovarian follicle
  3. Increasing development of the corpus luteum
  4. Altering the endometrial lining
  5. Inhibiting ovulation
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Combination oral contraceptives thicken cervical mucus, impeding sperm.
  • B. Incorrect — They suppress (not induce) follicle maturation.
  • C. Incorrect — They do not increase corpus luteum development.
  • D. Correct — They alter the endometrial lining, making implantation less likely.
  • E. Correct — They prevent (inhibit) ovulation, the primary mechanism.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 31.4

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who will start alfuzosin for treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia. The nurse should instruct the client that which of the following is an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Bradycardia
  2. Edema
  3. Hypotension
  4. Tremor
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Alfuzosin can cause tachycardia, not bradycardia.
  • B. Alfuzosin can cause GI effects (diarrhea/constipation); edema is not characteristic.
  • C. Correct — Alfuzosin (an alpha-blocker) relaxes vascular smooth muscle, causing hypotension/dizziness.
  • D. Alfuzosin can cause dizziness; tremor is not an effect.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 31.5

A nurse is caring for a client who has angina and asks about obtaining a prescription for sildenafil to treat erectile dysfunction. Which of the following medications is contraindicated with sildenafil?

  1. Aspirin
  2. Isosorbide
  3. Clopidogrel
  4. Atorvastatin
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Aspirin, clopidogrel, and atorvastatin are not contraindicated with sildenafil for this reason.
  • B. Correct — Isosorbide is an organic nitrate; combining nitrates with sildenafil causes life-threatening hypotension and is contraindicated.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 7 · Reproductive · Chapter 32

Medications Affecting Labor and Delivery

Labor and delivery medications: oxytocin (induction, augmentation, postpartum hemorrhage), tocolytics (terbutaline, magnesium sulfate, nifedipine), prostaglandins for cervical ripening (misoprostol, dinoprostone), and analgesics (fentanyl epidural, opioid IV).

Labor & Delivery — Overview

Two opposing goals: stimulate contractions to deliver, or suppress them to buy time in preterm labor.

Labor & delivery medications — overview

Stimulate vs suppress
  • Uterine stimulants (oxytocics) induce/augment labor and control postpartum hemorrhage
  • Tocolytics suppress preterm labor to delay delivery
  • Continuous maternal and fetal monitoring is essential with all of these agents

Uterine Stimulants

Oxytocin drives labor and stops postpartum bleeding — but uterine tachysystole and rupture are the dangers.

Oxytocin — action & uses

Pitocin
  • Increases the strength, frequency, and length of uterine contractions
  • Uses: induction/augmentation of labor, delivery of the placenta, and management of postpartum hemorrhage
  • Titrate by IV infusion pump with continuous fetal monitoring

Oxytocin — complications & safety

Tachysystole
  • Uterine tachysystole, uterine rupture, placental abruption, and water intoxication
  • Monitor contraction length/strength/frequency and fetal status; stop the infusion for tachysystole or fetal distress
  • Contraindicated with cephalopelvic disproportion, fetal malpresentation, prolapsed cord, or fetal distress

Other uterine stimulants

Ripening & hemorrhage
  • Dinoprostone (prostaglandin) and off-label misoprostol: cervical ripening
  • Methylergonovine: contracts the uterus for serious postpartum hemorrhage — used only after delivery, never during labor; contraindicated in hypertension/preeclampsia
  • Monitor blood pressure (methylergonovine) and fetal/uterine status (ripening agents)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is reviewing a new prescription for methylergonovine for a client who is postpartum. What information should the nurse include in this review? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Describe one adverse effect.
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS/PRECAUTIONS: Describe one contraindication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe at least three.

Therapeutic Uses

Prevent postpartum hemorrhage

Complications

Hypertensive crisis

Contraindications / Precautions

Hypertension, preeclampsia, cardiac disease: Use with caution with maternal history of severe renal or hepatic disease, and sepsis.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor vital signs for increase in blood pressure.
  • Monitor for manifestations of hypertensive crisis (headache, nausea, vomiting, and increased blood pressure).
  • Monitor for uterine tone and vaginal bleeding.
  • Provide emergency interventions.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 32.1

A nurse is teaching a client about terbutaline. Which of the following statements by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

  1. "This medication will stop my contractions."
  2. "This medication will prevent vaginal bleeding."
  3. "This medication will promote blood flow to my baby."
  4. "This medication will increase my prostaglandin production."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Terbutaline (a beta2-adrenergic agonist tocolytic) relaxes uterine smooth muscle to suppress/stop preterm contractions.
  • B. Terbutaline suppresses preterm labor; it does not prevent vaginal bleeding.
  • C. Its purpose is uterine relaxation, not specifically promoting fetal blood flow.
  • D. Terbutaline suppresses contractions; it does not increase prostaglandin production.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 32.2

A nurse is caring for a client who has preeclampsia and is receiving magnesium sulfate IV continuous infusion. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider?

  1. 2+ deep tendon reflexes
  2. 2+ pedal edema
  3. 24 mL/hr urinary output
  4. Respirations 12/min
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. 2+ deep tendon reflexes are an expected (normal) finding.
  • B. 2+ pedal edema is an expected finding in preeclampsia.
  • C. Correct — Urine output less than 25-30 mL/hr indicates risk of magnesium accumulation/toxicity; report it.
  • D. A respiratory rate of 12/min is at the lower edge of expected and does not require reporting on its own.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 32.3

A nurse is caring for a client who has a new prescription for oxytocin to stimulate uterine contractions. Which of the following actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Use an infusion pump for medication administration.
  2. Obtain vital signs frequently and with every dosage change.
  3. Stop infusion if uterine contractions occur every 4 min and last 45 seconds.
  4. Increase medication infusion rate rapidly.
  5. Monitor fetal heart rate continuously.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, E

  • A. Correct — Oxytocin must be administered via an infusion pump.
  • B. Correct — Obtain vital signs frequently and with each dosage change.
  • C. Incorrect — Contractions every 4 min lasting 45 seconds are adequate, not excessive; do not stop for this.
  • D. Incorrect — Increase the rate gradually to prevent uterine tachysystole.
  • E. Correct — Continuous fetal heart rate monitoring is required.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 32.4

A nurse is caring for a client who is in labor and is receiving oxytocin. The nurse should monitor the client for which of the following as complications of oxytocin? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Uterine rupture
  2. Uterine tachysystole
  3. Placental abruption
  4. Hyponatremia
  5. Placenta previa
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, D

  • A. Correct — Uterine rupture is a potential complication of excessive stimulation.
  • B. Correct — Uterine tachysystole (excessive contractions) is a complication.
  • C. Correct — Placental abruption can result from overstimulation.
  • D. Correct — Hyponatremia (water intoxication) can occur from oxytocin's antidiuretic effect.
  • E. Incorrect — Placenta previa is a pre-existing condition, not a complication of oxytocin.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 32.5

A nurse is reviewing a new prescription for terbutaline with a client who has a history of preterm labor. Which of the following client statements indicates understanding of the teaching?

  1. "I can increase my activity now that I've started on this medication."
  2. "I will increase my daily fluid intake to 3 quarts."
  3. "I will report increasing intensity of contractions to my doctor."
  4. "I am glad this will prevent preterm labor."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. The client should not increase activity; rest helps reduce contractions.
  • B. Fluid intake is typically limited (around 2,400 mL/day), not increased to 3 quarts.
  • C. Correct — Report increasing contraction intensity/frequency, which may signal progressing labor.
  • D. Terbutaline delays preterm labor; it does not prevent it.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 8 · Joint & Bone · Chapter 33

Connective Tissue Disorders

Connective tissue disorders are treated with: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen — Ch 35), DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine), biologic DMARDs (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab), glucocorticoids (prednisone), and gout-specific agents (colchicine, allopurinol, probenecid).

Connective Tissue Disorders — Overview

RA, gout, and lupus are autoimmune/inflammatory — therapy ranges from rapid relief to disease modification.

Rheumatoid arthritis, gout & lupus — overview

Autoimmune/inflammatory
  • Rheumatoid arthritis: chronic autoimmune inflammation — DMARDs slow progression, glucocorticoids relieve inflammation, NSAIDs give rapid relief without slowing disease
  • Gout: elevated uric acid → urate crystals in joints — treated by reducing inflammation or lowering uric acid
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus: autoimmune damage to joints/skin/organs — NSAIDs, corticosteroids, antimalarials, immunomodulators

Gout & Lupus Therapy

Lower the uric acid or calm the crystal-driven inflammation; antimalarials anchor lupus.

Antigout medications

Acute vs chronic
  • Acute attack: colchicine (anti-inflammatory), NSAIDs, or glucocorticoids
  • Chronic (lower uric acid): allopurinol and febuxostat (reduce production); probenecid (increases excretion)
  • Encourage fluids to prevent urate stones; report rash with allopurinol (severe hypersensitivity)

Lupus & immunosuppressants

Antimalarials
  • Hydroxychloroquine (antimalarial) is a mainstay for SLE — requires periodic eye exams (retinal toxicity)
  • Corticosteroids and NSAIDs control inflammation; topical cortisone reduces the skin rash
  • Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, azathioprine) and monoclonal antibodies for severe disease — monitor for infection and organ toxicity

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has rheumatoid arthritis (RA) about a new prescription for etanercept. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for etanercept in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe at least three adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one for each of the adverse effects above.
  • MEDICATION ADMINISTRATION: Describe at least three important factors.

Therapeutic Uses

Etanercept is a biologic DMARD classified as a tumor necrosis factor antagonist. It suppresses manifestations of moderate to severe RA and slows the progression of the disorder.

Complications

  • Severe infections, including tuberculosis or reactivation of hepatitis B
  • Heart failure
  • Severe skin reactions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome
  • Hematologic disorders

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct clients to monitor for infection, and to report sore throat and other manifestations.
  • Discuss reasons for TB testing and possible hepatitis B testing.
  • Clients should notify the provider for edema, shortness of breath, and other manifestations of heart failure.
  • Report skin rash to provider.
  • Report easy bruising, bleeding, or unusual fatigue to provider.

Medication Administration

  • Teach clients to administer by subcutaneous injection twice weekly.
  • Discard solutions that are discolored or that contain particulate matter.
  • Monitor for injection-site reactions, and report them to provider.
  • Rotate injection sites.
  • Avoid skin areas that are bruised or reddened when injecting.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 33.1

A nurse is providing teaching for a client who has gout and a new prescription for allopurinol. For which of the following adverse effects should the client be taught to monitor? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Stomatitis
  2. Insomnia
  3. Nausea
  4. Rash
  5. Increased gout pain
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Stomatitis occurs with medications that affect cell turnover (e.g., methotrexate), not allopurinol.
  • B. Incorrect — Insomnia is not an adverse effect of allopurinol.
  • C. Correct — Nausea and vomiting are adverse effects.
  • D. Correct — Rash and other hypersensitivity reactions can occur (can be serious).
  • E. Correct — An increase in gout attacks can occur when therapy is first started.

Exercise 33.2

A nurse is caring for a client who has a new prescription for adalimumab for rheumatoid arthritis. Based on the route of administration of adalimumab, which of the following should the nurse plan to monitor?

  1. The vein for thrombophlebitis during IV administration
  2. The subcutaneous site for redness following injection
  3. The oral mucosa for ulceration after oral administration
  4. The skin for irritation following removal of transdermal patch
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Adalimumab is not administered IV, orally, or transdermally.
  • B. Correct — Adalimumab is given subcutaneously; monitor the injection site for redness/reactions.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 33.3

A nurse is preparing to administer belimumab for a client who has systemic lupus erythematosus. Which of the following actions should the nurse plan to take?

  1. Warm the medication to room temperature over 1 hr before administering.
  2. Administer the medication by IV bolus over 5 min.
  3. Dilute the medication in 5% dextrose and water solution.
  4. Monitor the client for hypersensitivity reactions.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. The solution should be carefully refrigerated/handled, not warmed over 1 hr.
  • B. Belimumab is given by intermittent IV infusion, not a 5-min bolus.
  • C. Dilute belimumab only in 0.9% sodium chloride, not dextrose.
  • D. Correct — Belimumab can cause severe infusion/hypersensitivity reactions; monitor the client closely.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 33.4

A nurse is caring for a client who has a new diagnosis of fibromyalgia. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect to administer to this client?

  1. Colchicine
  2. Hydroxychloroquine
  3. Auranofin
  4. Duloxetine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Colchicine is an anti-inflammatory used for gout.
  • B. Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial used in RA/SLE.
  • C. Auranofin is a gold salt used for joint pain in RA.
  • D. Correct — Duloxetine (an SNRI) is used to treat fibromyalgia.

Exercise 33.5

A nurse is evaluating teaching for a client who has rheumatoid arthritis and a new prescription for methotrexate. Which of the following statements by the client indicates understanding of the teaching?

  1. "I will be sure to return to the clinic at least once a year to have my blood drawn while I'm taking methotrexate."
  2. "I can receive live-virus vaccines while taking this medication."
  3. "I'll let the doctor know if I develop sores in my mouth while taking this medication."
  4. "I should stop taking oral contraceptives while I'm taking methotrexate."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Methotrexate requires frequent monitoring (CBC, liver, kidney) — more often than once a year.
  • B. Avoid live-virus vaccines; methotrexate is immunosuppressive.
  • C. Correct — Mouth ulcers/sores can signal bone marrow suppression or toxicity; report them.
  • D. Methotrexate is Pregnancy Category X; continue effective contraception rather than stopping it.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 8 · Joint & Bone · Chapter 34

Bone Disorders

Bone disorders are treated with: calcium and vitamin D supplements (foundation), bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate), selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene), calcitonin-salmon, monoclonal antibodies (denosumab), and parathyroid hormone analogs (teriparatide).

Bone Disorders — Overview

Calcium and vitamin D are the foundation; SERMs, bisphosphonates, and calcitonin protect bone density.

Bone medications — overview

Build & protect bone
  • Calcium and vitamin D support heart, bone, nerve, muscle, and coagulation function and are given when intake is insufficient
  • Osteoporosis/fracture prevention agents: calcium supplements, selective estrogen receptor modulators (SERMs), bisphosphonates, and calcitonin

Calcium & Vitamin D

The base of every bone regimen — timing around other drugs matters.

Calcium & vitamin D supplements

Foundation
  • Prototype calcium citrate (also carbonate; IV calcium gluconate/chloride for critically low levels) — for hypocalcemia and bone health
  • Vitamin D aids calcium absorption; with a bisphosphonate or calcitonin they reduce osteoporosis risk; target calcium 9–10.5 mg/dL
  • Take with 8 oz water; separate from glucocorticoids/tetracyclines by 1 hr and thyroid hormone by 4 hr; warm and infuse IV calcium slowly; watch for hypercalcemia

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a provider's office is teaching a client who is postmenopausal and at high risk for osteoporosis about a new prescription for alendronate. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for alendronate.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects of this medication. NURSING INTERVENTIONS ● Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor. ● Describe two nursing actions.

Therapeutic Uses

In this client who is at high risk for osteoporosis, the purpose of alendronate is to prevent osteoporosis from occurring by decreasing resorption of bone. The medication also is used to treat existing osteoporosis and Paget's disease.

Complications

Alendronate can cause esophagitis and esophageal ulceration; other GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, and constipation); muscle pain; and visual disturbances. Rarely, it can cause atraumatic femoral fracture.

Nursing Interventions

Diagnostic tests: Blood calcium, bone density scans Nursing interventions

  • Assess the client's ability to follow administration directions (must be able to sit upright or stand for at least 30 min after taking alendronate).
  • Teach the client to take this medication first thing in the morning with at least 240 mL (8 oz) water and wait 30 min before eating or drinking anything else or taking any other medications or supplements.
  • Teach the client other ways to help prevent osteoporosis, such as performing weight-bearing exercises daily and obtaining adequate amounts of calcium and vitamin D.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 34.1

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is taking raloxifene to prevent postmenopausal osteoporosis. The nurse should advise the client that which of the following are adverse effects of this medication? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Hot flashes
  2. Lump in breast
  3. Swelling or redness in calf
  4. Shortness of breath
  5. Difficulty swallowing
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, C, D

  • A. Correct — Raloxifene can cause hot flashes.
  • B. Incorrect — Raloxifene does not cause breast lumps (it reduces breast cancer risk).
  • C. Correct — Calf swelling/redness can indicate DVT; raloxifene increases thromboembolism risk.
  • D. Correct — Shortness of breath can indicate pulmonary embolism, a thromboembolic risk.
  • E. Incorrect — Difficulty swallowing (esophagitis) is associated with bisphosphonates, not raloxifene.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 34.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has osteoporosis and a new prescription for alendronate. Which of the following instructions should the nurse provide? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Take medication in the morning before eating.
  2. Chew tablets to increase bioavailability.
  3. Drink an 8 oz glass of water with each tablet.
  4. Take medication with an antacid if heartburn occurs.
  5. Avoid lying down after taking this medication.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, C, E

  • A. Correct — Take alendronate first thing in the morning on an empty stomach.
  • B. Incorrect — Do not chew tablets; this can cause esophageal irritation.
  • C. Correct — Take with at least 240 mL (8 oz) of water.
  • D. Incorrect — Do not take alendronate within 2 hr of an antacid.
  • E. Correct — Sit upright or stand for at least 30 min after taking it to prevent esophagitis.

Exercise 34.3

A nurse is caring for a client who has a new prescription for calcitonin-salmon for osteoporosis. Which of the following tests should the nurse tell the client to expect before beginning this medication?

  1. Skin test for allergy to the medication
  2. ECG to rule out cardiac dysrhythmias
  3. Mantoux test to rule out exposure to tuberculosis
  4. Liver function tests to assess risk for medication toxicity
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Calcitonin-salmon is a protein; anaphylaxis can occur, so a skin test for allergy is done first.
  • B, C, D. An ECG, Mantoux test, and liver function tests are not required before starting calcitonin-salmon.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 34.4

A nurse is caring for a client whose blood calcium is 8.8 mg/dL. Which of the following medications should the nurse anticipate administering to this client?

  1. Calcitonin-salmon
  2. Calcium carbonate
  3. Zoledronic acid
  4. Ibandronate
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Calcitonin-salmon lowers calcium (wrong direction for a low level).
  • B. Correct — A calcium of 8.8 mg/dL is below the expected range; administer calcium carbonate to raise it.
  • C, D. Zoledronic acid and ibandronate are bisphosphonates for osteoporosis, not for treating hypocalcemia.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 34.5

A nurse is providing instruction to a client who has a new prescription for calcitonin-salmon for postmenopausal osteoporosis. Which of the following instructions should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Swallow tablets on an empty stomach with plenty of water.
  2. Watch for skin rash and redness when applying calcitonin-salmon topically.
  3. Mix the liquid medication with juice and take it after meals.
  4. Alternate nostrils each time calcitonin-salmon is inhaled.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Calcitonin-salmon is not given as oral tablets, a topical product, or an oral liquid in this context.
  • D. Correct — The intranasal form is administered by alternating nostrils with each dose to reduce mucosal irritation.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 35

Non-Opioid Analgesics

Non-opioid analgesics include acetaminophen (no anti-inflammatory effect, hepatotoxic in overdose) and NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, celecoxib). NSAIDs reduce pain, inflammation, and fever via COX inhibition. Aspirin also has antiplatelet effects.

Non-Opioid Analgesics — Overview

NSAIDs and acetaminophen relieve pain and fever — but one fights inflammation and one spares the stomach.

Non-opioid analgesics — overview

NSAIDs vs acetaminophen
  • Non-opioid analgesics provide analgesic, antipyretic, and (NSAIDs only) anti-inflammatory effects
  • NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase; acetaminophen acts centrally with no anti-inflammatory or antiplatelet effect

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse at a provider's office is providing teaching to a client who has osteoarthritis and is starting long-term therapy with NSAIDs. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe three nursing actions, including two laboratory values the nurse should monitor.

Therapeutic Uses

NSAIDs will treat mild to moderate joint pain and stiffness, and decrease inflammation in the client who has osteoarthritis.

Complications

  • Gastrointestinal effects can occur, including anorexia, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and heartburn.
  • GI bleeding can occur because NSAIDs affect platelet function.
  • Nephrotoxicity can occur.
  • NSAIDs can cause CNS effects (dizziness, headache, blurred vision, and tinnitus).
  • Allergy can occur, including cross allergy with other NSAIDs (aspirin).

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor hgb/hct and kidney function tests.
  • Assess the client for previous allergy to NSAIDs.
  • Assess the GI system, and ask about any history of GI bleed or peptic ulcer disease.
  • Advise the client to take the medication with food, milk, or an 8 oz glass of water to prevent GI distress.
  • Advise the client to tell provider about any over-the-counter medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements before taking them.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 35.1

A nurse is assessing a client who has salicylism. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Dizziness
  2. Diarrhea
  3. Jaundice
  4. Tinnitus
  5. Headache
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Dizziness occurs with salicylism (salicylate toxicity).
  • B. Incorrect — Diarrhea is not an expected finding.
  • C. Incorrect — Jaundice is not expected with salicylism.
  • D. Correct — Tinnitus is a hallmark of salicylism.
  • E. Correct — Headache is an expected finding.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 35.2

A nurse is admitting a client to the hospital following acetaminophen toxicity. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect to administer to this client?

  1. Acetylcysteine
  2. Pegfilgrastim
  3. Misoprostol
  4. Naltrexone
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen toxicity.
  • B. Pegfilgrastim increases neutrophil production.
  • C. Misoprostol prevents NSAID-induced gastric ulcers.
  • D. Naltrexone reduces alcohol/opioid craving.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 35.3

A nurse is teaching a client about a new prescription for celecoxib. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching?

  1. Increases the risk for a myocardial infarction
  2. Decreases the risk of stroke
  3. Inhibits COX-1
  4. Increases platelet aggregation
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Celecoxib (a COX-2 inhibitor) increases the risk of myocardial infarction and other cardiovascular events.
  • B. It increases (not decreases) stroke risk.
  • C. Celecoxib selectively inhibits COX-2, not COX-1.
  • D. Celecoxib does not affect platelet aggregation.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 35.4

A nurse is taking a history for a client who reports taking aspirin about four times daily for a sprained wrist. Which of the following prescribed medications taken by the client is contraindicated with aspirin?

  1. Digoxin
  2. Metformin
  3. Warfarin
  4. Nitroglycerin
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Digoxin, metformin, and nitroglycerin do not have a contraindicating interaction with aspirin.
  • C. Correct — Aspirin enhances the effect of warfarin and other anticoagulants, greatly increasing bleeding risk.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 35.5

A nurse in an emergency department is performing an admission assessment for a client who has severe aspirin toxicity. Which of the following findings should the nurse expect?

  1. Body temperature 35° C (95° F)
  2. Lung crackles
  3. Cool, dry skin
  4. Respiratory depression
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Expect an elevated body temperature (hyperthermia), not hypothermia.
  • B. Dehydration, not lung crackles, is expected.
  • C. Diaphoresis (not cool, dry skin) is expected.
  • D. Correct — Respiratory depression occurs in severe (late) aspirin toxicity after initial hyperventilation.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 36

Opioid Agonists and Antagonists

Opioid analgesics activate mu receptors for severe pain. Three categories: pure agonists (morphine — prototype, oxycodone, fentanyl, codeine), agonist-antagonists (butorphanol, nalbuphine), and antagonists (naloxone — overdose reversal, naltrexone — addiction therapy).

Opioids — Overview

Opioids relieve moderate-to-severe pain at the mu receptor — and respiratory depression is the price of that power.

Opioids — classes & receptors

Agonist/antagonist
  • Treat moderate-to-severe pain by acting on CNS receptors to alter pain perception
  • Mu receptor activation produces analgesia, respiratory depression, euphoria, and sedation
  • Classified as agonists, agonist-antagonists, and antagonists; pure agonists are Schedule II controlled substances

Agonist-Antagonists & Antagonists

Mixed agents and pure reversal agents round out opioid pharmacology.

Agonist-antagonist opioids

Butorphanol
  • Prototype butorphanol (also nalbuphine, buprenorphine, pentazocine): antagonist at mu, agonist at kappa
  • Lower abuse potential and less respiratory depression than pure agonists, but a ceiling on analgesia; used for moderate-severe pain, labor pain, and opioid dependence (buprenorphine)
  • Abstinence (withdrawal) syndrome can be triggered if given to an opioid-dependent client — screen for current opioid use first

Opioid antagonists

Naloxone / naltrexone
  • Naloxone reverses opioid effects (respiratory depression, sedation) in overdose — given IV/IM/intranasal
  • Naltrexone is used for maintenance treatment of opioid and alcohol use disorders
  • Monitor for abrupt withdrawal after reversal; titrate naloxone to restore breathing without precipitating severe withdrawal

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is providing discharge teaching for a client who is postoperative and has a new prescription for an opioid medication for incisional pain. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe for oxycodone.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List three adverse effects for oxycodone.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: List three.

Therapeutic Uses

Opioid medication is indicated for relief of moderate to severe pain.

Complications

  • Sedation
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Constipation
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Urinary retention

Nursing Interventions

  • Instruct the client not to drive or perform other hazardous activities while using this medication.
  • Notify the provider for severe nausea or vomiting.
  • Prevent constipation by increasing intake of liquids and foods with fiber. Consider use of a stool softener or laxatives if necessary.
  • Move the client slowly from lying or sitting to standing to minimize effects of orthostatic hypotension.
  • Instruct the client to void every 4 hr. Contact the provider for manifestations of dysuria.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 36.1

A nurse is preparing to administer an opioid agonist to a client who has acute pain. For which of the following manifestations should the nurse monitor as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Urinary retention
  2. Tachypnea
  3. Hypertension
  4. Irritating cough
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Opioid agonists (e.g., morphine) commonly cause urinary retention.
  • B. Monitor for respiratory depression (bradypnea), not tachypnea.
  • C. Opioids can cause hypotension, not hypertension.
  • D. Opioids suppress cough; they do not cause an irritating cough.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 36.2

A nurse is caring for a client who has end-stage cancer and is receiving morphine. The client's family member asks why the provider prescribed methylnaltrexone. Which of the following responses should the nurse make?

  1. "The medication will increase respirations."
  2. "The medication will prevent dependence on the morphine."
  3. "The medication will relieve constipation."
  4. "The medication works with the morphine to increase pain relief."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Methylnaltrexone does not increase respirations, prevent dependence, or add to analgesia.
  • C. Correct — Methylnaltrexone is a peripheral opioid antagonist that relieves opioid-induced constipation without reducing pain relief.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 36.3

A nurse is preparing to administer butorphanol to a client who has a history of substance use disorder. The nurse should identify which of the following information as true regarding butorphanol?

  1. Butorphanol has a greater risk for abuse than morphine.
  2. Butorphanol causes a higher incidence of respiratory depression than morphine.
  3. Butorphanol cannot be reversed with an opioid antagonist.
  4. Butorphanol can cause abstinence syndrome in opioid-dependent clients.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Butorphanol has a lower risk for misuse than morphine.
  • B. Butorphanol is less likely to cause respiratory depression.
  • C. Its toxicity can be reversed with an opioid antagonist.
  • D. Correct — As an opioid agonist-antagonist, butorphanol can precipitate withdrawal (abstinence syndrome) in opioid-dependent clients.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 36.4

A nurse is planning to administer morphine IV to a client who is postoperative. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?

  1. Monitor for seizures and confusion with repeated doses.
  2. Protect the client's skin from the severe diarrhea that occurs with morphine.
  3. Withhold this medication if respiratory rate is less than 12/min.
  4. Give morphine intermittent via IV bolus over 30 seconds or less.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Seizures/confusion with repeated doses are associated with meperidine, not morphine.
  • B. Morphine causes constipation, not diarrhea.
  • C. Correct — Withhold opioids if the respiratory rate is below 12/min to prevent respiratory depression.
  • D. Administer IV morphine slowly over 3 to 5 min, not 30 seconds.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 36.5

A nurse is reviewing the medication administration record for a client who is receiving transdermal fentanyl for severe pain. The nurse should identify that which of the following medications can cause an adverse effect when administered concurrently with fentanyl?

  1. Ampicillin
  2. Diazepam
  3. Furosemide
  4. Prednisone
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Ampicillin, furosemide, and prednisone do not have a significant CNS-depressant interaction with fentanyl.
  • B. Correct — Diazepam (a benzodiazepine) is a CNS depressant; combined with fentanyl it increases the risk of respiratory depression and sedation.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 37

Adjuvant Medications for Pain

Adjuvant pain medications enhance pain relief in specific conditions: anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain (gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine), tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), SNRIs (duloxetine), and topical agents (lidocaine patches, capsaicin).

Adjuvant Pain Medications — Overview

Drugs that aren’t primarily analgesics but boost opioid relief and let the opioid dose come down.

Adjuvant analgesics — overview

Opioid-sparing
  • Used with a primary opioid to increase pain relief while reducing the opioid dose — which reduces respiratory depression, sedation, and constipation
  • Categories: tricyclic antidepressants, anticonvulsants, CNS stimulants, antihistamines, glucocorticoids, bisphosphonates, and NSAIDs (often off-label)

Adjuvant Agents

Antidepressants and anticonvulsants target neuropathic pain; other classes add specific benefits.

Antidepressants & anticonvulsants

Neuropathic pain
  • TCAs (amitriptyline): relieve neuropathic pain — contraindicated after recent MI and within 14 days of an MAOI; caution with glaucoma, urinary retention, BPH
  • Anticonvulsants (gabapentin, carbamazepine): for neuropathic pain — carbamazepine carries bone marrow suppression (monitor CBC) and reduces oral contraceptive effectiveness
  • Report easy bruising, bleeding, fever, or sore throat (myelosuppression); take with food; avoid hazardous activity (drowsiness)

Other adjuvant classes

Targeted add-ons
  • CNS stimulants (methylphenidate): counter opioid sedation — weight loss and insomnia (last dose by 4 p.m.)
  • Antihistamines (hydroxyzine): add sedation/antiemetic effect — dry mouth, sedation (reduce dose in older adults)
  • Glucocorticoids (dexamethasone) for inflammatory/bone pain; bisphosphonates for bone-metastasis pain; NSAIDs for inflammatory components

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in an acute care facility is teaching a client who has metastatic cancer and is receiving morphine and carbamazepine for pain. What information should the nurse provide about the use of these medications? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for carbamazepine in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • INTERACTIONS: Describe two interactions with carbamazepine.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two. on Exercises

Therapeutic Uses

Carbamazepine relieves neuropathic (nerve) pain, which can be described as sharp, burning, or aching.

Complications

Adverse effects of carbamazepine include GI manifestations (abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting). It also can cause bone marrow suppression, affecting all blood cell types.

Interactions

  • The medication can cause hypertensive crisis if taken within 14 days of an mAOI antidepressant.
  • Toxicity can result if the client drinks grapefruit juice while taking carbamazepine.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor CBC, including platelet counts.
  • Assess for abnormal bleeding, bruising, or infection.
  • Monitor for GI manifestations, and advise the client to take the medication with food.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 37.1

A nurse is caring for a client who has cancer and is taking morphine and carbamazepine for pain. Which of the following effects should the nurse monitor for when giving the medications together? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Need for reduced dosage of the opioid
  2. Reduced adverse effects of the opioid
  3. Increased analgesic effects
  4. Enhanced CNS stimulation
  5. Increased opioid tolerance
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C

  • A. Correct — The opioid dose can be reduced when an adjuvant is added.
  • B. Correct — Adverse effects of the opioid can be reduced (lower opioid dose needed).
  • C. Correct — Analgesic effects are increased when the adjuvant is combined with the opioid.
  • D. Incorrect — CNS stimulation is not enhanced (these agents cause CNS depression).
  • E. Incorrect — Opioid tolerance can be decreased, not increased, with an adjuvant.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 37.2

A nurse is planning care for a client who has brain cancer and is experiencing headaches. Which of the following adjuvant medications are indicated for this client?

  1. Dexamethasone
  2. Methylphenidate
  3. Hydroxyzine
  4. Amitriptyline
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Dexamethasone (a glucocorticoid) decreases cerebral edema and the associated headaches in brain cancer.
  • B. Methylphenidate is used as an adjuvant to counteract opioid-induced sedation.
  • C. Hydroxyzine is used as an adjuvant for anxiety/nausea.
  • D. Amitriptyline is used as an adjuvant for neuropathic pain.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 37.3

A nurse is preparing to administer pamidronate to a client who has bone pain related to cancer. Which of the following precautions should the nurse take when administering pamidronate?

  1. Inspect the skin for redness and irritation when changing the intradermal patch.
  2. Assess the IV site for thrombophlebitis frequently during administration.
  3. Instruct the client to sit upright or stand for 30 min following oral administration.
  4. Watch for manifestations of anaphylaxis for 20 min after IM administration.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Pamidronate is not given by intradermal patch, orally, or IM.
  • B. Correct — Pamidronate is administered by IV infusion; assess the IV site for thrombophlebitis frequently.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 37.4

A nurse is planning care for a client who has cancer and is taking a glucocorticoid as an adjuvant medication for pain control. Which of the following interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Monitor for urinary retention.
  2. Monitor blood glucose.
  3. Monitor blood potassium level.
  4. Monitor for gastric bleeding.
  5. Monitor for respiratory depression.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C, D

  • A. Incorrect — Urinary retention is not a glucocorticoid concern.
  • B. Correct — Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose; monitor it.
  • C. Correct — Glucocorticoids can cause hypokalemia; monitor potassium.
  • D. Correct — Glucocorticoids increase the risk of gastric (GI) bleeding; monitor for it.
  • E. Incorrect — Respiratory depression is an opioid concern, not a glucocorticoid one.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 37.5

A nurse is administering amitriptyline to a client who is experiencing cancer pain. For which of the following adverse effects should the nurse monitor?

  1. Decreased appetite
  2. Explosive diarrhea
  3. Decreased pulse rate
  4. Orthostatic hypotension
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Amitriptyline can increase appetite.
  • B. Amitriptyline causes constipation (anticholinergic), not diarrhea.
  • C. Amitriptyline can increase pulse rate (tachycardia).
  • D. Correct — Amitriptyline (a tricyclic antidepressant) commonly causes orthostatic hypotension.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 9 · Pain & Inflammation · Chapter 38

Miscellaneous Pain Medications

Miscellaneous pain medications include migraine-specific agents (triptans, ergot alkaloids), antiemetics for migraine, prophylactic agents (propranolol, topiramate), and newer CGRP inhibitors (erenumab, fremanezumab) for migraine prevention.

Miscellaneous Pain Medications — Overview

Migraine therapy (abort vs prevent) and local anesthetics complete the pain unit.

Migraine therapy & local anesthetics — overview

Abort vs prevent
  • Migraine medications either stop an attack (abortive) or prevent attacks (prophylactic)
  • Local anesthetics block motor and sensory neurons in a specific area — topical, injected, regional, epidural, or spinal

Local Anesthetics

Numb a defined area — watch for systemic absorption and allergy.

Local anesthetics

Lidocaine
  • Block nerve conduction in a targeted area (topical, infiltration, regional, epidural, spinal); examples include lidocaine and bupivacaine
  • Epinephrine is often added to prolong the effect and limit systemic absorption (avoid in fingers, toes, nose, ears, penis)
  • Monitor for systemic toxicity (CNS excitation then depression, dysrhythmias) and, with spinal/epidural, hypotension and respiratory effects

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has frequent migraine headaches about a new prescription for sumatriptan. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for sumatriptan in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Describe two adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • INTERACTIONS: Describe two interactions the nurse should teach the client about.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two for this client.

Therapeutic Uses

Sumatriptan is used to abort a migraine headache and associated manifestations (nausea and vomiting) after it begins by causing cranial artery vasoconstriction.

Complications

The nurse should monitor for chest and arm heaviness/pressure, angina caused by coronary vasospasm, dizziness, and vertigo.

Interactions

Toxicity can result if sumatriptan is given concurrently or within 2 weeks of an mAOI antidepressant. Sumatriptan should not be given concurrently with other triptan medications or within 24 hr of ergotamine or dihydroergotamine.

Nursing Interventions

  • Teach clients to take sumatriptan at the first finding of migraine manifestations.
  • Teach client how to administer sumatriptan if it is prescribed intranasally or by subcutaneous injection.
  • Monitor cardiovascular risk factors and vital signs while taking this medication.
  • Advise clients to notify the provider immediately for onset of angina pain. Teach clients to distinguish transient chest or arm heaviness caused by sumatriptan from angina pain.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 38.1

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who is experiencing migraine headaches. Which of the following instructions should the nurse provide? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Take ergotamine as a prophylaxis to prevent a migraine headache.
  2. Identify and avoid trigger factors.
  3. Lie down in a dark quiet room at the onset of a migraine.
  4. Avoid foods that contain tyramine.
  5. Avoid exercise that can increase heart rate.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C, D

  • A. Incorrect — Ergotamine is used at the onset to abort a migraine, not as prophylaxis.
  • B. Correct — Identifying and avoiding trigger factors helps prevent migraines.
  • C. Correct — Lying down in a dark, quiet room at onset reduces stimulation.
  • D. Correct — Tyramine-containing foods can trigger migraines; avoid them.
  • E. Incorrect — Regular exercise between migraines is encouraged.

Exercise 38.2

A nurse is planning care for a client who is to receive tetracaine prior to a bronchoscopy. Which of the following actions should the nurse include in the plan of care?

  1. Keep the client NPO until pharyngeal response returns.
  2. Monitor the insertion site for a hematoma.
  3. Palpate the bladder to detect urinary retention.
  4. Maintain the client on bed rest for 12 hr following the procedure.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Topical tetracaine suppresses the gag reflex; keep the client NPO until the pharyngeal (gag) response returns to prevent aspiration.
  • B, C, D. Hematoma monitoring, bladder palpation, and 12 hr bed rest are not indicated for topical airway anesthesia.

  2. Tachycardia
  3. Hypertension
  4. Fever

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Seizure activity is a CNS adverse effect of local anesthetic systemic absorption.
  • B. Bradycardia (not tachycardia) can occur.
  • C. Hypotension (not hypertension) can occur.

Exercise 38.4

A nurse is reviewing the health history of a client who has migraine headaches and is to begin prophylaxis therapy with propranolol. Which of the following findings in the client history should the nurse report to the provider?

  1. The client had a prior myocardial infarction.
  2. The client takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation.
  3. The client takes an SSRI for depression.
  4. An ECG indicates a first-degree heart block.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. A prior MI is not a contraindication (beta-blockers are often used post-MI).
  • B, C. Concurrent warfarin or an SSRI is not a contraindication to propranolol.
