Exercise 38.5

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who has migraine headaches and a new prescription for ergotamine. For which of the following manifestations indicating a possible adverse reaction should the nurse instruct the client to stop taking the medication and notify the provider? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Nausea
  2. Visual disturbances
  3. Positive home pregnancy test
  4. Numbness and tingling in fingers
  5. Muscle pain
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Nausea is a common migraine symptom, not a reason to stop ergotamine.
  • B. Incorrect — Visual disturbances (flashing lights) are common migraine aura findings.
  • C. Correct — Ergotamine is contraindicated in pregnancy; a positive pregnancy test requires stopping it.
  • D. Correct — Numbness/tingling in fingers or toes indicates ergotism (excessive vasoconstriction).
  • E. Correct — Unexplained muscle pain can indicate ergotism; stop and notify the provider.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Unit 10 · Endocrine · Chapter 39

Diabetes Mellitus

Diabetes mellitus is managed with insulin (Type 1, advanced Type 2) and oral antidiabetic agents (Type 2). Insulin categories: rapid-acting, short-acting, intermediate, long-acting. Oral agents include biguanides (metformin — first-line), sulfonylureas, GLP-1 agonists, SGLT2 inhibitors.

Diabetes Mellitus — Overview

Diabetes is insulin deficiency and/or resistance. Therapy replaces insulin or makes the body use its own better.

Diabetes pharmacology — overview

Insulin & oral agents
  • Diabetes results from an absolute or relative insulin deficiency, often with cellular insulin resistance
  • Insulins differ by onset, peak, and duration; oral and injectable agents increase available insulin or modify carbohydrate metabolism
  • Goal: maintain glucose control while preventing hypoglycemia and long-term complications

Insulin

Onset-peak-duration is everything — it dictates timing, meal coordination, and when hypoglycemia is most likely.

Insulin types — onset, peak, duration

Time-action
  • Rapid-acting (lispro, aspart, glulisine): onset 15–30 min, peak 0.5–3 hr — give with meals
  • Short-acting (regular): onset 0.5–1 hr, peak 1–5 hr — the only insulin given IV
  • Intermediate (NPH): onset 1–2 hr, peak 4–14 hr (cloudy); long-acting (glargine, detemir): onset 1–4 hr, no pronounced peak, ~24 hr
  • Premixed (e.g., 70/30) combine intermediate and short/rapid insulin

Insulin — complications & interactions

Hypoglycemia
  • Hypoglycemia (<70 mg/dL): the major risk — sweating, tremor, tachycardia, confusion; sulfonylureas, alcohol, and beta blockers add to it
  • Beta blockers mask the warning signs (tachycardia, tremor) — teach reliance on glucose monitoring; thiazides/glucocorticoids raise glucose
  • Hypokalemia with large doses; lipohypertrophy — rotate injection sites, ~1 inch apart

Insulin — administration

Mixing & IV
  • Mixing: draw up the clear (regular) before the cloudy (NPH) — “clear before cloudy”; do not mix glargine/detemir with other insulins
  • Subcutaneous injection at 90° (45° if thin); rotate sites systematically
  • IV insulin (regular, or rapid-acting): flush ~50 mL through the tubing first because insulin binds to IV tubing

Oral Antidiabetics

Several classes, several mechanisms — metformin is first-line, and lactic acidosis is its red flag.

Sulfonylureas & meglitinides

Insulin secretagogues
  • Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, glimepiride): stimulate pancreatic insulin release — hypoglycemia and weight gain
  • Meglitinides (repaglinide, nateglinide): rapid, short-acting insulin release — taken with meals
  • Teach hypoglycemia recognition/treatment; avoid alcohol (disulfiram-like reaction with some sulfonylureas)

Metformin (biguanide)

First-line
  • Decreases hepatic glucose production and increases insulin sensitivity — does not cause hypoglycemia alone; first-line for type 2 diabetes
  • GI effects (anorexia, nausea, diarrhea, mild weight loss) and possible B₁₂/folate deficiency
  • Lactic acidosis (rare, high mortality): avoid in renal impairment; hold before iodinated contrast and resume after renal function confirmed

Other oral agents

TZDs, gliptins, gliflozins
  • Thiazolidinediones (pioglitazone): increase insulin sensitivity — fluid retention/HF, hepatotoxicity (monitor LFTs)
  • Alpha-glucosidase inhibitors (acarbose): slow carbohydrate absorption; DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin): prolong incretins
  • SGLT-2 inhibitors (canagliflozin): increase urinary glucose excretion — genital infections, volume depletion

Injectable Non-Insulin & Rescue

Incretin-based injectables and the glucagon rescue for severe hypoglycemia.

GLP-1 agonists & amylin analogs

Incretin-based
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists (exenatide, liraglutide): enhance glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slow gastric emptying, promote satiety/weight loss
  • Amylin analog (pramlintide): slows gastric emptying and suppresses glucagon — used with insulin
  • Both are subcutaneous; monitor for nausea and hypoglycemia (especially with concurrent insulin/sulfonylureas)

Hypoglycemia management & glucagon

Rescue
  • Conscious client: 15 g fast-acting carbohydrate (juice, glucose tablets), recheck in 15 min (“rule of 15”)
  • Unconscious client: IV dextrose (D50) in facility, or glucagon IM/subcutaneous at home; turn on side (glucagon may cause vomiting)
  • Follow recovery with a complex carbohydrate + protein snack to prevent recurrence

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has type 2 diabetes mellitus and is taking exenatide along with an oral antidiabetic agent. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI active learning template: Medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify the therapeutic use for exenatide in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two laboratory tests the nurse should monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe teaching points to give a client taking exenatide.

Therapeutic Uses

Exenatide is prescribed along with an oral antidiabetic medication (metformin or a sulfonylurea medication) for clients who have type 2 diabetes mellitus to improve diabetes control. exenatide improves insulin secretion by the pancreas, decreases secretion of glucagon, and slows gastric emptying.

Complications

  • Gi effects (nausea and vomiting)
  • Pancreatitis manifested by acute abdominal pain and possibly severe vomiting
  • Hypoglycemia, especially when taken concurrently with a sulfonylurea medication (glipizide)

Nursing Interventions

Monitor daily blood glucose testing by the client, periodic Hba1c tests, and periodic kidney function testing. exenatide should be used cautiously in clients who have any renal impairment.

Client Education

  • Inject exenatide subcutaneously.
  • Take exenatide within 60 min before the morning and evening meal but not following the meal.
  • Withhold exenatide and notify the provider for severe abdominal pain.
  • Recognize and treat hypoglycemia.
  • Exenatide should not be given within 1 hr of oral medications, particularly antibiotics, acetaminophen, or contraceptives due to its ability to slow gastric emptying.

  3. Regular insulin
  4. Insulin lispro
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Insulin glargine (long-acting) has no pronounced peak.
  • B. NPH insulin peaks later (around 4-14 hr).
  • C. Correct — Regular (short-acting) insulin peaks about 1 to 5 hr after administration.
  • D. Insulin lispro (rapid-acting) peaks around 30-90 min.

  2. Amylase
  3. Platelet count
  4. Liver function tests
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Infection/WBC change is not an adverse effect of acarbose.
  • B. Pancreatitis (amylase) is associated with sitagliptin/exenatide.
  • C. Acarbose does not affect platelet levels.

Exercise 39.3

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who has type 2 diabetes mellitus and is starting repaglinide. Which of the following statements by the client indicates understanding of the administration of this medication?

  1. "I'll take this medication after I eat."
  2. "I'll take this medicine 30 minutes before I eat."
  3. "I'll take this medicine just before I go to bed."
  4. "I'll take this medication at least 1 hour before I eat."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Taking it after eating misses its rapid, short-lived action timed to the meal.
  • B. Correct — Repaglinide has a rapid, short-lived effect; take it shortly before a meal (within about 30 min), and skip the dose if skipping the meal.
  • C. Taking it at bedtime does not match meal-related glucose rise.
  • D. Taking it a full hour before eating risks hypoglycemia before the meal.

  1. Somnolence
  2. Constipation
  3. Fluid retention
  4. Weight gain
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Somnolence can indicate lactic acidosis, a rare but serious adverse effect of metformin; report it.
  • B. Diarrhea (not constipation) is a common metformin effect.
  • C. Fluid retention is an effect of pioglitazone.
  • D. Metformin tends to cause anorexia and weight loss, not weight gain.

Exercise 39.5

A nurse is providing teaching to a client who has a prescription for pramlintide for type 1 diabetes mellitus. Which of the following should the nurse include in the teaching? (Select all that apply.)

  1. "Take oral medications 30 min before injection."
  2. "Use upper arms as preferred injection sites."
  3. "Mix pramlintide with the breakfast dose of insulin."
  4. "Inject pramlintide just before a meal."
  5. "Discard open vials after 28 days."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Pramlintide delays gastric emptying/oral drug absorption; take oral medications 1 hr before or 2 hr after, not 30 min before.
  • B. Incorrect — Use the thigh or abdomen, not the upper arms.
  • C. Incorrect — Do not mix pramlintide with insulin in the same syringe.
  • D. Correct — Inject pramlintide just before a meal.
  • E. Correct — Discard open (unused) vials after 28 days.

Unit 10 · Endocrine · Chapter 40

Endocrine Disorders

Endocrine disorders covered: thyroid (hypothyroid — levothyroxine; hyperthyroid — methimazole, PTU, RAI), pituitary (somatropin, vasopressin), and adrenal (glucocorticoids — prednisone, hydrocortisone). Each has specific monitoring and lifelong implications.

Endocrine Disorders — Overview

Replace a missing hormone or block an excess one — thyroid, pituitary, and adrenal.

Endocrine medications — overview

Replace or suppress
  • Endocrine disorders involve over- or under-secretion of hormones, or altered target response
  • This chapter covers medications for the thyroid, anterior/posterior pituitary, and adrenal glands

Pituitary & Adrenal Agents

Growth hormone, ADH replacement, and the corticosteroids that replace or suppress adrenal output.

Pituitary hormones

GH & ADH
  • Growth hormone (somatropin): for growth failure in children — monitor growth and glucose
  • Antidiuretic hormone (desmopressin, vasopressin): for diabetes insipidus — promotes water reabsorption
  • Monitor I&O, daily weight, and sodium; watch for water intoxication (headache, confusion, hyponatremia)

Adrenal hormones — glucocorticoids

Cortisol replacement
  • Glucocorticoids (hydrocortisone, prednisone): replace cortisol in adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s) and suppress inflammation
  • Long-term effects: hyperglycemia, infection risk, osteoporosis, fluid retention, Cushingoid features, adrenal suppression
  • Never stop abruptly — taper to avoid adrenal crisis; increase dose during physical stress/illness

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a provider's office is providing instructions to a client who has a new prescription for levothyroxine to treat hypothyroidism. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use of levothyroxine in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects of this medication.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two laboratory tests the nurse should monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe teaching points for a client taking levothyroxine.

Therapeutic Uses

Levothyroxine replaces T4 and is used as thyroid hormone replacement therapy. Replacement of T4 also raises T3 levels, because some T4 is converted into T3.

Complications

Adverse effects are essentially the same as manifestations of hyperthyroidism: cardiac manifestations (hypertension and angina pectoris); insomnia; anxiety; weight loss; heat intolerance; increased body temperature; tremors; and menstrual irregularities.

Nursing Interventions

Monitor thyroid function tests: T3, T4, and TSh.

Client Education

  • Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, usually 1 hr before breakfast.
  • Thyroid replacement therapy is usually required for life
  • Monitor for adverse effects that indicate that the dosage needs to be adjusted.

  1. Bradycardia
  2. Insomnia

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Propylthiouracil treats hyperthyroidism and can produce hypothyroid effects such as bradycardia.
  • B. Drowsiness, not insomnia, can occur.
  • C. Cold intolerance, not heat intolerance, can occur.
  • D. Weight gain, not weight loss, can occur.

Exercise 40.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has Grave's disease and a new prescription for propranolol. Which of the following client statements indicates effective teaching?

  1. "Propranolol helps increase blood flow to my thyroid gland."
  2. "Propranolol is used to prevent excess glucose in my blood."
  3. "Propranolol will decrease my tremors and fast heart beat."
  4. "Propranolol promotes a decrease of thyroid hormone in my body."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Propranolol does not increase thyroid blood flow, prevent hyperglycemia, or lower thyroid hormone levels.
  • C. Correct — Propranolol (a beta-adrenergic antagonist) relieves the sympathetic symptoms of hyperthyroidism, such as tremors and tachycardia.

Exercise 40.3

A nurse is caring for an older adult client who has hypothyroidism and a new prescription for levothyroxine. Which of the following dosage schedules should the nurse expect for this client?

  1. The client will start at a high dosage, and the amount will be tapered as needed.
  2. The client will remain on the initial dosage during the course of treatment.
  3. The client's dosage will be adjusted daily based on blood levels.
  4. The client will start on a low dosage, which can be gradually increased.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B. Levothyroxine is not started high then tapered, nor kept static throughout.
  • C. Dosage is based on periodic blood levels, not adjusted daily.
  • D. Correct — In older adults, start levothyroxine at a low dose and increase gradually to avoid cardiac strain.

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Bilirubin and protein may appear with other conditions; potassium is not expected in the urine.

Exercise 40.5

A nurse is reviewing the medical record of a client who takes desmopressin for diabetes insipidus. Which of the following findings is an adverse effect of desmopressin?

  1. Hypovolemia
  2. Hypercalcemia
  3. Agitation
  4. Headache
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Edema/hypervolemia (water retention), not hypovolemia, occurs.
  • B. Calcium imbalance is not an adverse effect of desmopressin.
  • C. Sleepiness, not agitation, is an adverse effect.
  • D. Correct — Headache is an adverse effect (related to water retention/hyponatremia).

Exercise 40.6

A nurse is admitting a client for a total hip arthroplasty. The client takes hydrocortisone for Addison's disease. Which of the following actions is the nurse's priority?

  1. Administering a supplemental dose of hydrocortisone
  2. Instructing the client about coughing and deep breathing
  3. Collecting additional information about the client's history of Addison's disease
  4. Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Surgery is a major stressor; a client with Addison's disease needs a supplemental ("stress") dose of hydrocortisone to prevent acute adrenal insufficiency (adrenal crisis). This is the priority.
  • B, C, D. Coughing/deep breathing teaching, history-gathering, and catheter insertion are important but not the immediate priority over preventing adrenal crisis.

NCLEX® Connection: Physiological Adaptation — Medical Emergencies

Unit 11 · Immune · Chapter 41

Immunizations

Immunizations confer active immunity through live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella, rotavirus, intranasal flu) or inactivated/subunit vaccines. Schedule based on CDC recommendations. Live vaccines contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise.

Immunizations — Types of Immunity

Vaccines train the immune system. The active/passive distinction explains why some protection lasts and some doesn’t.

Active immunity

Long-lasting
  • Develops when the immune system produces its own antibodies in response to an antigen — takes weeks to months but is long-lasting
  • Active-artificial: a vaccine (killed or attenuated organism) prompts antibody production
  • Active-natural: a natural infection prompts antibody production

Passive immunity

Temporary
  • Develops when antibodies made by another person or animal are transferred to the client — immediate but temporary
  • Passive-natural: antibodies cross the placenta or pass through breast milk
  • Passive-artificial: immune globulins given for immediate protection after exposure (e.g., rabies, snakebite)

Vaccines — Administration & Safety

Live vaccines carry the key contraindications; reactions are usually minor but reportable.

Vaccine types & schedule

Killed vs live
  • Vaccines are made from killed (inactivated) organisms or live, attenuated (weakened) organisms
  • Follow the CDC recommended immunization schedule for childhood and adult vaccines
  • Document lot number, site, and date; provide the Vaccine Information Statement

Contraindications & precautions

Live-vaccine cautions
  • Live attenuated vaccines (MMR, varicella) are generally contraindicated in pregnancy and immunocompromise
  • Defer for moderate-to-severe acute illness; screen for prior severe allergic reaction to a vaccine component (e.g., egg, gelatin)
  • Use clinical judgment with mild illness — a low-grade cold is not a reason to defer

Adverse effects & reporting

VAERS
  • Common, minor reactions: soreness/redness at the site and low-grade fever — treat with a non-aspirin analgesic
  • Watch for rare anaphylaxis — keep emergency equipment available and observe after administration
  • Report significant adverse events to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse at a community health clinic is planning to administer the human papilloma virus (9vHPV) vaccine to an 11-year-old client. Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • CONTRAINDICATIONS/PRECAUTIONS: Identify contraindications to receiving the HPV vaccine.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe two teaching points for a client who receives a first dose of the HPV vaccine.

Complications

  • The 9vHPV vaccine can cause redness, tenderness, and swelling at the injection site.
  • It has caused fainting in some clients shortly after the vaccine is administered.
  • Headache and mild to moderate fever are also possible adverse effects the client should monitor for.

Contraindications / Precautions

Contraindications to receiving the 9vHPV vaccine include pregnancy and a severe allergy to yeast.

Client Education

  • Monitor for adverse effects; the common adverse effects are mild and temporary.
  • The adolescent will require a second dose in 6 to 12 months since this one occurred before age 16. Initial administration after 16 years of age requires a three dose series.

Exercise 41.1

A nurse is caring for several clients who came to the clinic for a seasonal influenza immunization. The nurse should identify that which of the following clients is a candidate to receive the vaccine via nasal spray rather than an injection?

  3. 25-year-old who is pregnant

  • D. Adults older than 50 are not eligible for the LAIV.

Unit 11 · Immune · Chapter 42

Chemotherapy Agents

Chemotherapy agents target rapidly-dividing cells. Categories include alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide), antimetabolites (methotrexate, 5-FU), antitumor antibiotics (doxorubicin — cardiotoxic), mitotic inhibitors (vincristine), hormonal agents, and targeted therapies. Severe toxicity requires careful monitoring.

Chemotherapy — Principles & Safety

Cytotoxic drugs kill fast-dividing cells — cancer and healthy alike — which is why handling and toxicity dominate care.

Chemotherapy principles

Combination therapy
  • Used to cure, control, or palliate cancer; combination chemotherapy uses agents acting in different cell-cycle phases to improve effectiveness and reduce resistance
  • Cytotoxic agents kill fast-growing cells — including skin, hair, GI mucosa, and bone marrow — which explains most adverse effects
  • Routes: oral, IV, intracavitary, intrathecal; some require special certification

Safe handling & spills

Hazardous drugs
  • Personnel must follow safe-handling procedures to prevent skin absorption (gowns, gloves, eye protection)
  • Manage small spills with a chemotherapy spill kit (goggles, mask, protective clothing, absorbent pads, waste bags)
  • Dispose of chemotherapy waste per institutional policy; contact occupational safety for large spills

Cytotoxic Agent Classes

Each class attacks DNA differently; the prototype and its signature toxicity are the high-yield facts.

Antimetabolites

Methotrexate, 5-FU
  • Disrupt DNA/RNA synthesis (S-phase specific): folic acid analog methotrexate, pyrimidine analogs (cytarabine, fluorouracil), purine analogs (mercaptopurine)
  • Methotrexate: mucositis, renal damage from hyperuricemia (hydration + allopurinol), reproductive toxicity — leucovorin (folinic acid) rescue limits toxicity
  • Monitor CBC, liver, and kidney function

Alkylating agents

Cyclophosphamide, cisplatin
  • Damage DNA in all cell-cycle phases: cyclophosphamide, cisplatin, carmustine
  • Cyclophosphamide: hemorrhagic cystitis — ensure 2–3 L/day fluids and give mesna to protect the bladder
  • Cisplatin: nephrotoxicity (hydration) and ototoxicity (assess hearing first); avoid concurrent aminoglycosides/furosemide

Antitumor antibiotics & other classes

Doxorubicin
  • Antitumor antibiotics (doxorubicin): cardiotoxicity — dysrhythmias acutely and cardiomyopathy/HF later; monitor ECG/echocardiogram; dexrazoxane is protective
  • Mitotic inhibitors (vincristine, paclitaxel): peripheral neuropathy; vincristine is a vesicant
  • Topoisomerase inhibitors (topotecan): interrupt DNA synthesis — bone marrow suppression

Managing Chemotherapy Toxicity

Bone marrow suppression, nausea, mucositis, and extravasation are the universal nursing priorities.

Bone marrow suppression

Nadir monitoring
  • Neutropenia (infection risk), thrombocytopenia (bleeding), and anemia — the dose-limiting toxicity
  • Monitor WBC/absolute neutrophil count, platelets, Hgb/Hct; assess for bruising and bleeding gums
  • Teach neutropenic precautions: avoid crowds and people with infections; report fever immediately

GI effects, mucositis & alopecia

Comfort & nutrition
  • Nausea/vomiting: give antiemetics (ondansetron + dexamethasone) before chemotherapy
  • Mucositis/stomatitis: gentle oral care with a soft brush and warm saline rinses; avoid alcohol-based mouthwash
  • Alopecia: hair loss begins 7–10 days after treatment and regrows after therapy ends; help the client prepare

Extravasation & safety

Vesicants
  • Extravasation of vesicants causes severe tissue damage — stop the infusion immediately; prefer central-line administration
  • Only specially trained personnel should give IV chemotherapy
  • Encourage 2–3 L/day fluids, monitor uric acid, and reinforce contraception during treatment

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has prostate cancer and a new prescription for monthly injections of leuprolide Im. What should the nurse teach this client about leuprolide? Use the atI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include two teaching points. on Exercises

Therapeutic Uses

Leuprolide is a gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist of luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormones. It is used instead of surgical ca

Complications

  • Hot flashes (or flashes), decreased libido, gynecomastia
  • Cardiac manifestations (dysrhythmias) and increased edema, which can lead
  • Decreased bone density, which can lead to fractures
  • Disease flare, which means manifestations of the client's prostate cancer can

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor prostate-specific antigen and testosterone levels, which should both
  • Bone density testing can be needed for some clients, as well as ECG if cardia

  • Increase calcium and vitamin D in diet.
  • Increase weight-bearing exercise to minimize bone loss.
  • Report a flare in prostate manifestations to the provider.
  • Report adverse effects (palpitations, edema, and hot flashes) to the provider.

Exercise 42.1

A nurse is caring for a client who has breast cancer and is receiving combination chemotherapy. The client asks why more than one medication is used. The nurse should explain that combination chemotherapy is used to do which of the following? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Decrease medication resistance
  2. Attack cancer cells at different stages of cell growth
  3. Block chemotherapy agent from entering healthy cells
  4. Stimulate immune system
  5. Decrease injury to normal body cells
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, E

  • A. Correct — Using multiple agents decreases the development of medication resistance.
  • B. Correct — Each medication can kill cancer cells at a different phase of the cell cycle.
  • C. Incorrect — Chemotherapy agents are not selectively blocked from healthy cells.
  • D. Incorrect — Combination chemotherapy does not work by stimulating the immune system.
  • E. Correct — Lower doses of each agent can reduce injury to normal body cells.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 42.2

A nurse is preparing to administer cyclophosphamide to a client. Which of the following medications should the nurse expect to administer concurrently to protect the client?

  1. Protectant agent, such as mesna
  2. Opioid, such as morphine
  3. Loop diuretic, such as furosemide
  4. H1 receptor antagonist, such as diphenhydramine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Mesna is a uroprotectant that prevents the hemorrhagic cystitis caused by cyclophosphamide.
  • B, C, D. An opioid, loop diuretic, and H1 antagonist are not given concurrently for this protective purpose.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 42.3

A nurse is preparing to administer leucovorin to a client who is receiving high-dose methotrexate. Which of the following responses should the nurse use when the client asks about the purpose of leucovorin?

  1. "Leucovorin reduces the risk of a transfusion reaction."
  2. "Leucovorin increases platelet production."
  3. "Leucovorin potentiates the cytotoxic effect."
  4. "Leucovorin protects healthy cells from the medication."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A, B, C. Leucovorin does not reduce transfusion reactions, increase platelets, or potentiate cytotoxicity.
  • D. Correct — Leucovorin (a folic acid derivative) is used as "rescue" therapy to protect healthy cells from methotrexate toxicity.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 42.4

A nurse is teaching a client who has breast cancer about tamoxifen. Which of the following adverse effects of tamoxifen should the nurse discuss with the client?

  1. Irregular heart beat
  2. Abnormal uterine bleeding
  3. Yellow sclera or dark-colored urine
  4. Difficulty swallowing
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Irregular heartbeat, jaundice, and dysphagia are not characteristic tamoxifen adverse effects to highlight here.
  • B. Correct — Tamoxifen can cause vaginal discharge and abnormal uterine bleeding (and raises endometrial cancer risk); report these.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 42.5

A nurse is caring for a client who is being treated with interferon alfa-2b for malignant melanoma. For which of the following adverse effects should the nurse monitor? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Tinnitus
  2. Muscle aches
  3. Peripheral neuropathy
  4. Bone loss
  5. Depression
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C, E

  • A. Incorrect — Tinnitus is not a characteristic adverse effect of interferon alfa-2b.
  • B. Correct — Muscle aches and other flu-like manifestations are common.
  • C. Correct — Peripheral neuropathy, dizziness, and fatigue can occur.
  • D. Incorrect — Bone loss is not a typical effect.
  • E. Correct — Depression and mental status changes can occur; monitor mood.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 42.6

A nurse is caring for a client who receives rituximab to treat non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and who asks the nurse how rituximab works. Which of the following should the nurse include?

  1. Blocks hormone receptors
  2. Increases immune response
  3. Binds with specific antigens on tumor cells
  4. Stops DNA replication during cell division
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Blocking hormone receptors describes agents like tamoxifen.
  • B. Increasing immune response describes agents like the interferons.
  • C. Correct — Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody that binds to specific antigens (CD20) on tumor cells.
  • D. Stopping DNA replication describes traditional cytotoxic chemotherapy.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 43

Principles of Antimicrobial Therapy

Antimicrobial principles include identifying causative organism (culture before starting), selecting narrow-spectrum when possible, avoiding superinfection and resistance, completing full course, and addressing hypersensitivity. Empiric vs targeted therapy.

Antimicrobial Therapy — Principles

Selective toxicity is the whole idea: kill the microbe, spare the host. Spectrum and lethality guide the choice.

Mechanisms of antimicrobial action

Selective toxicity
  • Antimicrobials use selective toxicity to kill or control microbes without destroying host cells
  • Mechanisms: destroy the bacterial cell wall, impair ribosomal protein synthesis, disrupt DNA/RNA, inhibit a unique enzyme, or inhibit viral replication

Spectrum & lethality

Bactericidal vs static
  • Narrow-spectrum antibiotics target few organisms; broad-spectrum target many
  • Bactericidal medications directly kill the organism; bacteriostatic slow growth so the immune system can clear it
  • Immunocompromised clients need bactericidal (not bacteriostatic) agents

Selecting & Monitoring Therapy

Culture before antibiotics, then match the drug to the bug, the site, and the host.

Choosing an antibiotic — culture first

Culture before antibiotics
  • Selection rests on three factors: identity of the organism, its sensitivity, and host factors
  • Obtain culture and sensitivity before starting antibiotics (the priority action) so therapy can be targeted
  • Broad-spectrum empiric therapy may start first in serious infection, then narrow once sensitivities return

Host factors

Site, age, pregnancy
  • Site of infection: CSF (meningitis), endocardium (endocarditis), and abscesses are hard for antibiotics to penetrate; drain abscesses
  • Age: infants and older adults develop toxicity more easily (reduced metabolism/excretion)
  • Pregnancy: sulfonamides → kernicterus, aminoglycosides → fetal hearing loss, tetracyclines → tooth discoloration

Resistance, Superinfection & Prophylaxis

Overuse breeds resistance and superinfection; prophylaxis has a few specific, important indications.

Resistance & superinfection

Stewardship
  • Antimicrobial resistance emerges as organisms change their DNA — complete the full prescribed course and avoid unnecessary antibiotics
  • Superinfection: antibiotics kill normal flora, allowing a new, hard-to-treat infection (e.g., C. difficile, candidiasis)
  • Report new diarrhea, white oral patches, or vaginal infection during therapy

Allergy & prophylaxis

Penicillin allergy
  • Screen for prior allergic reactions — do not give penicillin after a documented allergic reaction
  • Prophylactic antibiotics are indicated before some orthopedic/cardiac surgery and before dental work in clients with prosthetic heart valves
  • Also considered for recurrent UTIs and certain exposures — confirm indications with the provider

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Basic Concept.

Active Learning Scenario

Basic Concept

A staff educator is providing information to a group of nurses about ways to prevent the spread of micro-organisms. What information should the educator include? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: Basic Concept to complete this item.

  • RELATED CONTENT: Determine one related concept.
  • UNDERLYING PRINCIPLES: Describe one related to the concept.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Identify five related to the concept.

Related Content

Preventive nursing measures

Underlying Principles

Controlling the spread of infection to staff and clients in a health care setting

Nursing Interventions

  • Perform hand hygiene before and after each client contact to prevent the spread of infection.
  • Recognize invasive procedures that increase the risk of infection (indwelling urinary catheter, IV catheter, cardiac catheterization).
  • Encourage prevention by having clients maintain an up-to-date immunization status.
  • Instruct clients to take the full course of antimicrobials the provider prescribes to prevent medication resistance and recurrence of infection.
  • Use infection-control procedures to prevent transmission of resistant micro-organisms.
  • Evaluate the effectiveness of treatment.

Exercise 43.1

A nurse is implementing a plan of care for a client who has a wound infection. Which of the following actions is the nurse's priority?

  1. Administer antibiotic medication.
  2. Obtain a wound specimen for culture.
  3. Monitor the client for a superinfection.
  4. Teach the client about wound care.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Antibiotics are given, but a specimen should be obtained first.
  • B. Correct — Obtain a wound culture before starting antibiotics so the causative organism can be identified.
  • C. Monitoring for superinfection occurs during antibiotic therapy, not first.
  • D. Teaching wound care is important but not the immediate priority.

Exercise 43.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has manifestations of a urinary tract infection. The nurse should instruct the client that which of the following tests is needed to determine which microorganism is causing the infection?

  1. Blood WBC
  2. Blood creatinine
  3. Urine culture
  4. Urine specific gravity
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. An elevated blood WBC indicates infection but not the specific organism.
  • B. Blood creatinine evaluates kidney function.
  • C. Correct — A urine culture identifies the specific microorganism causing the infection.
  • D. Urine specific gravity evaluates concentration, not the organism.

NCLEX® Connection: Reduction of Risk Potential — Laboratory Values

Exercise 43.3

A nurse is teaching a group of nurses about antimicrobial therapy. The nurse should instruct that effective penetration of antibiotics can be impeded by which of the following conditions? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Meningitis
  2. An infected abscess
  3. Endocarditis
  4. Pneumonia
  5. Pyelonephritis
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C

  • A. Correct — The blood-brain barrier can impede antibiotic penetration in meningitis.
  • B. Correct — Purulent drainage and poor vascularity limit penetration into an abscess.
  • C. Correct — Vegetations in endocarditis impede penetration.
  • D. Incorrect — Pneumonia generally responds to appropriate antibiotics.
  • E. Incorrect — Pyelonephritis generally responds to appropriate antibiotics.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 43.4

A nurse is caring for a group of clients who are receiving antimicrobial therapy. The nurse should identify that which of the following clients is at risk for medication toxicity?

  1. A young adult client who has a sinus infection
  2. An older adult client who has prostatitis
  3. A client who is postpartum and has mastitis
  4. A middle adult client who has a urinary tract infection
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. These clients are not at heightened risk for antimicrobial toxicity.
  • B. Correct — Older adults often have reduced renal/hepatic function, increasing the risk of medication accumulation and toxicity.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 43.5

A nurse is teaching a group of nurses about the importance of prophylactic antimicrobial therapy. Which of the following information should the nurse include in the teaching? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Administer prophylactic antimicrobial therapy to clients who report exposure to a sexually transmitted infection.
  2. Administer prophylactic antimicrobial therapy to clients who are having orthopedic surgery.
  3. Instruct clients who have a prosthetic heart valve about the need for prophylactic antimicrobial therapy before dental work.
  4. Consult the provider for prophylactic antimicrobial therapy for clients who have recurrent urinary tract infections.
  5. Instruct clients to request prophylactic antimicrobial therapy immediately when they have an upper respiratory infection.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, D

  • A. Correct — Clients exposed to an STI may receive prophylaxis.
  • B. Correct — Orthopedic surgery clients receive surgical prophylaxis.
  • C. Correct — Clients with a prosthetic heart valve need prophylaxis before dental work (endocarditis prevention).
  • D. Correct — Recurrent UTIs may warrant provider-directed prophylaxis.
  • E. Incorrect — Upper respiratory infections are often viral; routine antibiotics are not appropriate.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 44

Antibiotics Affecting the Bacterial Cell Wall

Cell wall antibiotics include penicillins (penicillin G, amoxicillin, piperacillin), cephalosporins (cephalexin, cefazolin, ceftriaxone — generations), carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem), monobactams (aztreonam), and vancomycin. All bactericidal.

Cell-Wall Antibiotics — Overview

Beta-lactams and vancomycin kill bacteria by wrecking the cell wall — a structure host cells don’t have.

Cell-wall antibiotics — overview

Bactericidal beta-lactams
  • These antibiotics are bactericidal, destroying bacteria by weakening the cell wall
  • Includes penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams (beta-lactams), plus vancomycin

Penicillins

The original beta-lactam — allergy and cross-reactivity are the defining nursing concerns.

Penicillins — types & uses

Penicillin G
  • Prototype penicillin G; narrow (penicillin V), broad (amoxicillin, ampicillin, amoxicillin-clavulanate), antistaphylococcal (nafcillin, oxacillin), and antipseudomonal/extended (piperacillin-tazobactam)
  • Uses: gram-positive cocci (strep pneumonia, endocarditis, pharyngitis), N. meningitidis meningitis, and syphilis (Treponema pallidum)
  • Provide endocarditis prophylaxis before dental/other procedures in at-risk clients

Penicillins — allergy & complications

Anaphylaxis
  • Allergic reactions (rash, itching, hives, dyspnea, anaphylaxis) are the major risk — report immediately and screen for prior reactions
  • Cross-sensitivity with cephalosporins; observe after administration and keep emergency equipment available
  • Give IM cautiously to avoid nerve/artery injection

Penicillins — administration

Take the full course
  • Take penicillin V, amoxicillin, and amoxicillin-clavulanate with meals; take others with 8 oz water 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals
  • Complete the entire course even after symptoms resolve
  • Penicillins can decrease oral contraceptive effectiveness — use a backup method

Cephalosporins

Five generations, each broader — and the alcohol and ceftriaxone-calcium interactions are testable.

Cephalosporins — generations & uses

Cephalexin
  • Beta-lactams like penicillins; broad-spectrum bactericidal with a high therapeutic index (prototype cephalexin)
  • Each successive generation reaches CSF better, resists beta-lactamase more, and covers more gram-negative organisms
  • Ceftaroline (5th generation) is the only cephalosporin effective against MRSA

Cephalosporins — interactions & precautions

Disulfiram reaction
  • Do not give to clients with severe penicillin allergy (cross-reactivity); use cautiously in renal impairment/bleeding tendencies
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol + cefotetan or cefazolin — avoid alcohol
  • Do not mix ceftriaxone with calcium-containing solutions (precipitation); take oral forms with food, refrigerate suspensions

Carbapenems & Vancomycin

Reserve carbapenems for resistance; monitor vancomycin troughs and infuse it slowly.

Carbapenems

Imipenem / meropenem
  • Imipenem-cilastatin and meropenem are beta-lactams with a very broad spectrum for serious infections (pneumonia, peritonitis, UTI)
  • Effective against gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria
  • Reserve for clients who can’t use a narrower-spectrum antibiotic to delay resistance

Vancomycin

Red man syndrome
  • Inhibits cell-wall synthesis — used for serious gram-positive infections, including MRSA and C. difficile (oral for C. diff)
  • Red man syndrome (flushing, hypotension) from rapid infusion — infuse slowly over at least 60 min
  • Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity — monitor renal function and trough levels

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is administering vancomycin IV to a client who has a serious wound infection. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for vancomycin for this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two nursing actions for clients receiving vancomycin.

Therapeutic Uses

Vancomycin is an antibiotic that kills bacteria by disrupting their cell wall. The IV form treats serious infections due to methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, and streptococci.

Complications

  • Infusion reactions (red man syndrome: rashes, flushing, tachycardia, and hypotension)
  • Ototoxicity (rare and reversible)
  • Renal toxicity
  • Thrombophlebitis at the IV site
  • Im and IV injection-site pain

Nursing Interventions

  • Infuse vancomycin over at least 60 min/dose to prevent an infusion reaction.
  • Monitor the IV site for redness, pain, or other manifestations of thrombophlebitis.
  • Monitor I&O, and notify the provider for oliguria or other findings of acute renal injury.
  • Monitor for hearing loss.
  • Ask the client about allergy to antibiotics before administering the medication. Watch for allergic manifestations during and after the infusion.

Exercise 44.1

A nurse is preparing to administer nafcillin IM to an adult client who has an infection. Which of the following actions should the nurse plan to take? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Select a 25-gauge, ½-inch needle for the injection.
  2. Administer the medication deeply into the ventrogluteal muscle.
  3. Ask the client about an allergy to penicillin before administering the medication.
  4. Monitor the client for 30 min following the injection.
  5. Tell the client to expect a temporary rash to develop following the injection.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C, D

  • A. Incorrect — A 25-gauge, ½-inch needle is too small/short for a deep IM injection in an adult.
  • B. Correct — Administer nafcillin IM deeply into the ventrogluteal muscle.
  • C. Correct — Ask about penicillin allergy before administering (nafcillin is a penicillin).
  • D. Correct — Monitor for 30 min after a penicillin for signs of an allergic reaction.
  • E. Incorrect — A rash is not an expected reaction; a rash could indicate an allergic response.

A nurse is obtaining a medication history from a client who is to receive imipenem-cilastatin IV to treat an infection. Which of the following medications the client also receives increases the risk for a medication interaction?

  2. Furosemide

  4. Ferrous sulfate

Exercise 44.4

A nurse is caring for a client who has a cerebrospinal fluid infection with gram-negative bacteria. Which of the following cephalosporin antibiotics should the nurse expect to administer IV to treat this infection?

  1. Cefaclor
  2. Cefazolin
  3. Cefepime
  4. Cephalexin
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Cefaclor (2nd gen), cefazolin (1st gen), and cephalexin (1st gen) do not penetrate the CSF well.
  • C. Correct — Cefepime (a fourth-generation cephalosporin) crosses the blood-brain barrier and treats gram-negative CNS infections.

A nurse is preparing to administer penicillin V to a client who has a streptococcal infection. The nurse should request a prescription for which of the following medications?

  2. Amoxicillin

Answer: C

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 45

Antibiotics Affecting Protein Synthesis

Protein synthesis inhibitors include tetracyclines (doxycycline), macrolides (azithromycin, erythromycin), aminoglycosides (gentamicin — narrow TI, nephro/ototoxic), and others (clindamycin, linezolid). Mostly bacteriostatic except aminoglycosides.

Protein-Synthesis Antibiotics — Overview

These hit the bacterial ribosome — mostly bacteriostatic, with aminoglycosides the bactericidal exception.

Protein-synthesis antibiotics — overview

Ribosome-targeting
  • Inhibit bacterial protein synthesis at the ribosome — bacteriostatic (tetracyclines, macrolides) or bactericidal (aminoglycosides)
  • Treat respiratory, GI, urinary, and reproductive tract infections

Tetracyclines

Broad-spectrum, but chelation, teeth, and sun exposure dominate the teaching.

Tetracyclines — action & uses

Doxycycline
  • Broad-spectrum bacteriostatic agents (tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline) that inhibit protein synthesis
  • Uses: acne, rickettsial infections (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), chlamydia, Lyme disease, anthrax, H. pylori, and mycoplasma pneumonia

Tetracyclines — complications

Teeth & sun
  • Tooth discoloration/enamel hypoplasia — avoid in children <8 years and in pregnancy
  • Photosensitivity — wear protective clothing and SPF 30+ sunscreen
  • GI/esophageal ulceration (don’t take at bedtime) and hepatotoxicity with high IV doses

Tetracyclines — interactions & administration

Chelation
  • Chelation with milk/dairy, calcium, iron, magnesium laxatives, and antacids blocks absorption — separate by 1 hr after or 2 hr before
  • Take on an empty stomach with 8 oz water (minocycline may be taken with food)
  • Decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness (use backup) and increases digoxin toxicity risk

Macrolides, Aminoglycosides & Clindamycin

Macrolide interactions, aminoglycoside peaks/troughs, and clindamycin’s C. diff risk.

Macrolides

Erythromycin / azithromycin
  • Bacteriostatic (erythromycin, azithromycin); alternatives for penicillin-allergic clients
  • Erythromycin inhibits drug metabolism — raises levels of theophylline, carbamazepine, warfarin, and digoxin (toxicity); QT prolongation risk
  • Give oral forms on an empty stomach (except azithromycin); monitor warfarin PT/INR and LFTs with prolonged therapy

Aminoglycosides

Gentamicin
  • Bactericidal (gentamicin) for serious gram-negative infections
  • Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are the key dangers — monitor renal function and hearing
  • Monitor peak and trough levels; avoid concurrent nephrotoxic/ototoxic drugs

Clindamycin

C. difficile risk
  • Treats serious anaerobic and gram-positive infections
  • High risk of C. difficile-associated diarrhea/colitis — report watery/bloody diarrhea immediately
  • Discontinue and treat if severe diarrhea develops

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for oral erythromycin every 6 hr to treat pneumonia. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for erythromycin in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects the client should monitor for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two diagnostic tests to monitor for clients taking erythromycin.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include two teaching points for clients taking erythromycin.

Therapeutic Uses

Erythromycin inhibits protein synthesis in the cells of susceptible micro-organisms, usually gram-positive bacteria. Erythromycin can be either bacteriostatic or bactericidal, depending on the organism and on the medication's dosage. It also treats infections for clients who are allergic to penicillin.

Complications

  • The most common adverse effects of erythromycin are GI manifestations, including abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.
  • Hepatotoxicity with abdominal pain, anorexia, fatigue, and possibly jaundice can occur after 1 to 2 weeks of erythromycin therapy.
  • Erythromycin can cause a prolonged QT interval on ECG, which can lead to potentially fatal tachydysrhythmias.
  • Ototoxicity can occur with high doses, especially after prolonged periods.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor liver function tests for clients who take erythromycin over a period of several weeks.
  • If the client is concurrently taking warfarin or digoxin with erythromycin, carefully monitor PT and INR or digoxin levels.
  • Monitor WBC counts for effectiveness of erythromycin treatment.

Client Education

  • Take erythromycin on an empty stomach, 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals with 8 oz of water.
  • Observe for adverse effects, and call the provider for severe GI distress, manifestations of liver toxicity, and ototoxicity.
  • Take the entire course of the medication and not to stop when feeling better.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 45.1

A nurse is teaching a client about taking tetracycline to treat a GI infection due to Helicobacter pylori. Which of the following statements should the nurse identify as an indication that the client understands the instructions?

  1. "I will take this medication with 8 ounces of milk."
  2. "I will let my doctor know if I start having diarrhea."
  3. "I can stop taking this medication when I feel completely well."
  4. "I can take this medication just before bedtime."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Tetracycline forms a nonabsorbable chelate with milk/dairy; avoid taking it with milk.
  • B. Correct — Diarrhea can indicate a superinfection; the client should report it.
  • C. Take the full prescribed course, even after feeling well.
  • D. Take it in the morning (with water) and remain upright to prevent esophageal irritation.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 45.2

A nurse is administering gentamicin by IV infusion at 0900. The medication will take 1 hr to infuse. When should the nurse plan to obtain a blood sample for a peak blood level of gentamicin?

  1. 1000
  2. 1030
  3. 1100
  4. 1130
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. The infusion ends at 1000, but the peak is drawn after completion, not at the end.
  • B. Correct — Obtain the peak level about 30 min after the infusion completes (infusion 0900-1000 → peak at 1030).
  • C, D. Collecting at 1100 or 1130 is too late for an accurate peak level.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 45.3

A nurse is caring for a client who is starting a course of gentamicin IV for a serious respiratory infection. For which of the following manifestations should the nurse monitor as an adverse effect of this medication? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Pruritus
  2. Hematuria
  3. Muscle weakness
  4. Difficulty swallowing
  5. Vertigo
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C, E

  • A. Correct — Pruritus, paresthesias, and urticaria can occur (hypersensitivity).
  • B. Correct — Hematuria can indicate acute nephrotoxicity, an aminoglycoside risk.
  • C. Correct — Muscle weakness/respiratory effects can occur from neuromuscular blockade.
  • D. Incorrect — Difficulty swallowing is not an adverse effect of gentamicin.
  • E. Correct — Vertigo, ataxia, and hearing loss indicate ototoxicity.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 45.4

A nurse is caring for a client who has subacute bacterial endocarditis and is receiving several antibiotics, including streptomycin IM. For which of the following manifestations should the nurse monitor as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Ataxia
  2. Urinary retention
  3. Constipation
  4. Complex partial seizures
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A

  • A. Correct — Streptomycin (an aminoglycoside) is ototoxic/vestibulotoxic; ataxia and impaired balance can occur.
  • B, C, D. Urinary retention, constipation, and complex partial seizures are not adverse effects of streptomycin.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 45.5

A nurse is caring for a client who is undergoing preparation for extensive colorectal surgery. Which of the following oral antibiotics should the nurse expect to administer specifically to suppress normal flora in the GI tract?

  1. Kanamycin
  2. Gentamicin
  3. Neomycin
  4. Tobramycin
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A, B, D. Kanamycin, gentamicin, and tobramycin are aminoglycosides but are not the standard oral agent for bowel prep.
  • C. Correct — Oral neomycin is used to suppress normal GI flora before colorectal surgery.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 46

Urinary Tract Infections

UTIs are treated with TMP/SMX (Bactrim), nitrofurantoin for uncomplicated cystitis, fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) for complicated UTI/pyelonephritis, and urinary tract analgesics (phenazopyridine — turns urine red-orange).

Urinary Tract Infections — Overview

TMP-SMX and nitrofurantoin handle uncomplicated UTIs; fluoroquinolones step in when those fail.

UTI medications — overview

Match drug to severity
  • Treated with sulfonamides/trimethoprim, urinary antiseptics, fluoroquinolones, and others; regimens range from a single dose to 14 days
  • TMP-SMX and nitrofurantoin treat uncomplicated cystitis; fluoroquinolones treat resistant UTIs; fosfomycin is a single-dose option for adherence issues

Sulfonamides & Trimethoprim

Folic-acid blockers — the sulfa allergy and Stevens-Johnson risk are paramount.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole — action & uses

TMP-SMX
  • Inhibit synthesis of folic acid (tetrahydrofolate), which bacteria need for DNA/RNA/protein production
  • Uses: UTIs (most often E. coli), otitis media, and Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia
  • Take on an empty stomach with 8 oz water; complete the full course; increase fluid intake

Sulfonamides — allergy & interactions

Stevens-Johnson
  • Hypersensitivity including Stevens-Johnson syndrome — avoid with sulfa allergy; cross-reactivity with thiazide diuretics and sulfonylureas
  • Increases the effects of warfarin, phenytoin, and sulfonylureas — monitor PT/INR, phenytoin levels, and blood glucose
  • Decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness — use a backup method

Urinary Antiseptics & Fluoroquinolones

Nitrofurantoin’s lung risk and ciprofloxacin’s tendon and dairy cautions are the standouts.

Urinary antiseptics

Nitrofurantoin
  • Nitrofurantoin damages bacterial DNA — for acute UTIs and prophylaxis of recurrent lower UTIs; take with milk or food
  • Pulmonary hypersensitivity (fever, chills, dyspnea, cough) — stop the drug and report; do not take again
  • Methenamine is another urinary antiseptic; report GI upset and blood dyscrasias

Fluoroquinolones — action & uses

Ciprofloxacin
  • Bactericidal (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — inhibit an enzyme needed for DNA replication
  • Broad-spectrum: urinary, respiratory, GI, bone/joint, and skin infections; prevention of inhaled anthrax
  • An oral alternative to parenteral antibiotics in severe infection

Fluoroquinolones — complications

Tendon rupture
  • Achilles tendon rupture — report tendon pain/swelling, stop the drug, and avoid exercise until resolved
  • Phototoxicity (severe sunburn even with sunscreen) — avoid sun exposure; superinfection (thrush, vaginal yeast)
  • Take with food but not dairy; separate from antacids, iron, and calcium (chelation)

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A client who has a UTI has a prescription for phenazopyridine. What information should the nurse review? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • EXPECTED PHARMACOLOGICAL ACTION THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe four.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Include three teaching points.

Expected Pharmacological Action

Phenazopyridine is an azo dye, which acts as a local anesthetic on the mucosa of the urinary tract. It is not an antibiotic.

Therapeutic Uses

Relieves urinary burning, urgency, pain, and frequency

Client Education

  • Acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease are contraindications.
  • It changes urine to an orange-red color.
  • Tell clients that the urine can stain clothes.
  • Instruct clients to take it with or after meals to minimize GI discomfort.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 46.1

A nurse reviewing a client's medication history notes an allergy to sulfonamides. This allergy is a contraindication for taking which of the following medications? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Hydrochlorothiazide
  2. Metoprolol
  3. Acetaminophen
  4. Glipizide
  5. Furosemide
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Hydrochlorothiazide is a sulfonamide derivative; a sulfa allergy is a contraindication.
  • B. Incorrect — Metoprolol is not a sulfonamide.
  • C. Incorrect — Acetaminophen is not a sulfonamide.
  • D. Correct — Glipizide (a sulfonylurea) can cross-react with a sulfonamide allergy.
  • E. Correct — Furosemide is a sulfonamide derivative; a sulfa allergy is a contraindication.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 46.2

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for nitrofurantoin. Which of the following information should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Observe for bruising on the skin.
  2. Take the medication with milk or meals.
  3. Expect brown discoloration of urine.
  4. Crush the medication if it is difficult to swallow.
  5. Expect insomnia when taking it.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, C

  • A. Correct — Bruising can indicate a blood dyscrasia; report it.
  • B. Correct — Taking it with milk or meals minimizes GI upset.
  • C. Correct — Brown discoloration of the urine is an expected, harmless effect.
  • D. Incorrect — Do not crush the medication; it can stain the teeth.
  • E. Incorrect — Drowsiness, not insomnia, is more likely.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 46.3

A nurse is teaching a client who has a severe UTI about ciprofloxacin. Which of the following information about adverse reactions should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Observe for pain and swelling of the Achilles tendon.
  2. Watch for a vaginal yeast infection.
  3. Expect excessive nighttime perspiration.
  4. Inspect the mouth for cottage cheese-like lesions.
  5. Take the medication with a dairy product.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, B, D

  • A. Correct — Fluoroquinolones can cause tendon pain/rupture (e.g., Achilles); report it.
  • B. Correct — A vaginal yeast infection is a possible superinfection.
  • C. Incorrect — Altered perspiration is not an adverse effect.
  • D. Correct — Cottage cheese-like mouth lesions indicate oral candidiasis (superinfection).
  • E. Incorrect — Avoid dairy; calcium chelates ciprofloxacin and reduces absorption.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 46.4

A nurse is planning discharge teaching for a female client who has a new prescription for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Which of the following information should the nurse include?

  1. Take the medication even if pregnant.
  2. Maintain a fluid restriction while taking it.
  3. Take it on an empty stomach.
  4. Stop taking it when manifestations subside.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can cause birth defects/fetal kernicterus; avoid in pregnancy, especially first trimester and near term.
  • B. Increase fluids (at least eight 8 oz glasses daily) to prevent crystalluria; do not restrict fluids.
  • C. Correct — The medication can be taken with or without food, so taking it on an empty stomach is acceptable.
  • D. Take the entire prescribed course to fully eradicate the bacteria and prevent rebound infection.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 46.5

A nurse is planning to administer ciprofloxacin IV to a client who has cystitis. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?

  1. Administer a concentrated solution.
  2. Infuse the medication over 60 min.
  3. Infuse the solution through the primary IV fluid's tubing.
  4. Choose a small peripheral vein for administration.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Administer IV ciprofloxacin in a dilute solution, not concentrated.
  • B. Correct — Infuse IV ciprofloxacin slowly over 60 min to reduce vein irritation.
  • C. Do not infuse ciprofloxacin with any other IV medication in the same line.
  • D. Use a large vein to minimize irritation, not a small peripheral vein.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 47

Mycobacterial, Fungal, and Parasitic Infections

Mycobacterial, fungal, and parasitic infections require specialized therapy. TB: 4-drug RIPE regimen (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol). Fungal: amphotericin B (nephrotoxic), azoles, echinocandins. Parasitic: metronidazole.

Mycobacterial, Fungal & Parasitic — Overview

TB needs months and multiple drugs; fungal and parasitic infections each have their signature agents.

Overview

Long, combination therapy
  • Tuberculosis is slow-growing and requires long-term therapy with at least two effective drugs to limit resistance
  • Metronidazole is the drug of choice for many parasitic/anaerobic infections; antifungals treat systemic and superficial mycoses

Antituberculosis Drugs

Isoniazid and rifampin anchor therapy — hepatotoxicity, B6, and orange secretions are the high-yield points.

Isoniazid (INH)

Mycolic acid
  • Prototype antituberculosis drug; inhibits mycolic acid synthesis in the mycobacterial cell wall; used for latent and active TB
  • Peripheral neuropathy — give vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) to prevent it; hepatotoxicity (avoid alcohol; monitor LFTs)
  • Inhibits phenytoin metabolism (toxicity); take 1 hr before or 2 hr after meals; avoid tyramine foods

Rifampin

Orange secretions
  • Bactericidal; broad-spectrum, part of active-TB regimens
  • Harmless orange-red discoloration of body fluids (urine, sweat, tears) — can stain contact lenses; hepatotoxicity
  • Decreases oral contraceptive effectiveness — use a non-hormonal method; take on an empty stomach

Other TB drugs & regimen principles

Adherence
  • Ethambutol: optic neuritis — report vision/color changes; pyrazinamide: hepatotoxicity and hyperuricemia
  • Active TB uses a four-drug regimen (induction then continuation phase) over months
  • Directly observed therapy supports adherence; treatment is monitored with sputum cultures (goal: three negative cultures)

Antifungals & Antiprotozoals

Amphotericin B is ‘ampho-terrible’; metronidazole means no alcohol.

Metronidazole (antiprotozoal)

No alcohol
  • Broad-spectrum, bactericidal against anaerobes; treats protozoal infections (amebiasis, giardiasis, trichomoniasis), C. difficile, and H. pylori
  • GI upset/metallic taste and harmless darkening of urine; neurotoxicity (numbness, ataxia, seizures) with high/prolonged doses
  • Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol — avoid all alcohol during and after therapy

Amphotericin B

Systemic antifungal
  • For serious systemic mycoses — potent but toxic (“ampho-terrible”)
  • Infusion reactions (fever, chills, rigors) — premedicate; nephrotoxicity (hydrate, monitor renal function) and hypokalemia
  • Monitor electrolytes and kidney function throughout therapy

Azoles & topical antifungals

Fluconazole / nystatin
  • Azoles (fluconazole, ketoconazole): for systemic and mucosal fungal infections — hepatotoxicity and many CYP drug interactions
  • Nystatin: oral (swish-and-swallow) or topical for candidiasis (thrush)
  • Monitor LFTs with systemic azoles; teach full course completion

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse in a public health department is teaching a client who has latent tuberculosis (TB) and a new prescription for isoniazid twice weekly for 6 months. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Describe the therapeutic use for isoniazid in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: List two adverse effects the client should watch for.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe one test to monitor for clients taking isoniazid.
  • CLIENT EDUCATION: Describe two teaching points for clients taking isoniazid.

Therapeutic Uses

A client who has latent tuberculosis has been infected by Mycobacterium tuberculosis and is at risk for (but has not yet developed) active tuberculosis. Some clients who have latent tuberculosis (those who are immunocompromised or who have recently immigrated to the U.S. from a country where active TB is common) can require treatment with isoniazid, with or without rifapentine, in order to prevent the onset of active TB. The client who has latent TB has a positive tuberculin test but a negative sputum culture and negative chest x-ray for TB. The client cannot infect others with tuberculosis unless the infection becomes active.

Complications

  • Paresthesias in the extremities caused by vitamin B6 deficiency
  • Hepatotoxicity
  • Hyperglycemia (if client has diabetes mellitus)

Nursing Interventions

The client who starts isoniazid should have baseline liver function testing and be tested periodically throughout treatment.

Client Education

  • Teach the client to watch for paresthesias, and to take pyridoxine daily to reverse the effect if they occur.
  • Teach the client about indications of hepatitis (anorexia, fatigue, nausea, jaundice) and to notify the provider if these occur.
  • Teach the client to take isoniazid as prescribed, and not to stop until the entire course of treatment is completed.
  • The client who has latent tuberculosis does not feel ill. The nurse should be sure that the client understands why it is important to continue with treatment.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 47.1

A nurse is caring for a client who has diabetes mellitus, pulmonary tuberculosis, and a new prescription for isoniazid. Which of the following supplements should the nurse expect to administer to prevent an adverse effect of INH?

  1. Ascorbic acid
  2. Pyridoxine
  3. Folic acid
  4. Cyanocobalamin
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Ascorbic acid, folic acid, and cyanocobalamin do not prevent INH's neuropathy.
  • B. Correct — Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) is given with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, a risk heightened in clients with diabetes.

Exercise 47.2

A nurse is infusing IV amphotericin B to a client who has a systemic fungal infection. The nurse should monitor the client for which of the following manifestations as an adverse effect of this medication?

  1. Hypoglycemia
  2. Constipation
  3. Fever
  4. Hyperkalemia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Amphotericin B can cause hyperglycemia, not hypoglycemia.
  • B. Diarrhea, not constipation, can occur.
  • C. Correct — Infusion reactions (fever, chills, nausea) are common with amphotericin B.
  • D. Amphotericin B causes hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia.

Exercise 47.3

A nurse is administering IV amphotericin B to a client who has a systemic fungal infection. The nurse should monitor which of the following laboratory values? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Blood albumin
  2. Blood amylase
  3. Blood potassium
  4. Hematocrit
  5. Blood creatinine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Amphotericin B does not affect blood albumin.
  • B. Incorrect — It does not cause pancreatitis (amylase elevation).
  • C. Correct — Hypokalemia is a serious adverse effect; monitor potassium.
  • D. Correct — Bone marrow suppression/anemia can occur; monitor hematocrit.
  • E. Correct — Nephrotoxicity can occur; monitor blood creatinine.

A nurse is teaching a client who is beginning a course of metronidazole to treat an infection. For which of the following findings of an adverse effect should the nurse instruct the client as a priority to stop taking metronidazole and notify the provider?

  1. Metallic taste
  2. Nausea
  3. Ataxia
  4. Dark-colored urine
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. A metallic taste is an expected (harmless) adverse effect.
  • B. Nausea is an expected adverse effect.
  • C. Correct — Ataxia can indicate neurotoxicity; this is the priority finding to stop the medication and notify the provider.
  • D. Dark-colored urine is an expected, harmless effect.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 47.5

A nurse is teaching a client who has active tuberculosis about the treatment regimen. The client asks why four different medications are necessary. Which of the following responses should the nurse make?

  1. "Four medications decrease the risk for a severe allergic reaction."
  2. "Four medications reduce the chance that the bacteria will become resistant."
  3. "Four medications reduce the risk for adverse reactions."
  4. "Four medications decrease the chance of having a positive tuberculin skin test."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Multidrug therapy does not reduce allergic reactions, lower adverse effects, or alter skin-test results.
  • B. Correct — Using several antituberculosis medications together reduces the chance that the bacteria will develop resistance.
