Unit 12 · Infection · Chapter 48

Viral Infections, HIV, and AIDS

Viral infections: HIV uses multi-class HAART (NRTIs like zidovudine, NNRTIs, protease inhibitors like ritonavir, integrase inhibitors, entry inhibitors like maraviroc). Herpes: acyclovir, valacyclovir. Influenza: oseltamivir. Hepatitis: interferons, direct-acting antivirals.

Viral Infections, HIV & AIDS — Overview

Antivirals only work while the virus replicates; antiretrovirals control HIV but never cure it.

Antivirals & HIV — overview

Replication-dependent
  • Antivirals act by altering viral replication and are ineffective when the virus is dormant
  • HIV is a retrovirus (uses reverse transcriptase); antiretrovirals reduce viral load and transmission but do not eradicate the virus

Antiviral Agents

Acyclovir for herpes, ganciclovir for CMV — hydration and bone marrow are the watch points.

Acyclovir

Herpes
  • Treats herpes simplex and varicella-zoster infections by inhibiting viral DNA synthesis
  • Nephrotoxicity with rapid IV infusion, dehydration, or renal impairment — ensure adequate hydration
  • No sexual activity while lesions are present; use a condom; complete the full course

Ganciclovir

CMV / bone marrow
  • Treats cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections, especially in immunocompromised clients
  • Bone marrow suppression (neutropenia, thrombocytopenia) — monitor CBC; contraindicated with ANC <500 or platelets <25,000
  • Can cause infertility — use barrier contraception during and after treatment; give with food

HIV Antiretroviral Therapy

Combination therapy (HAART) and strict adherence are what keep resistance at bay.

Antiretroviral classes

Multiple targets
  • Entry/fusion inhibitors (enfuvirtide — subcutaneous) and CCR5 antagonists (maraviroc — hepatotoxicity) block cell entry
  • Enzyme inhibitors: NRTIs (zidovudine), NNRTIs, protease inhibitors, and integrase inhibitors
  • Each class interrupts a different step of HIV replication

HAART & adherence

CD4 & viral load
  • Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) combines three or more drugs to reduce viral load and raise CD4 counts
  • Strict adherence is critical — missed/reduced doses promote resistance and treatment failure
  • Continue transmission-prevention education even with an undetectable viral load

Active Learning Scenario

Case-based reasoning using the ATI Active Learning Template: Medication.

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is caring for a client who is immunocompromised and has a new prescription for ganciclovir iV twice per day to prevent cytomegalovirus. What should the nurse teach the client about this medication? Use the ati active learning template: Medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USES: Identify for ganciclovir in this client.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify two adverse effects.
  • NURSING INTERVENTIONS: Describe two for clients taking ganciclovir, and two tests the nurse should monitor.

Therapeutic Uses

Ganciclovir prevents reproduction of viral dna and thus prevents viral cell replication. it is used is to prevent or treat cytomegalovirus in clients who are immunocompromised.

Complications

  • Minor discomforts (fever, headache, and nausea)
  • Suppresses the bone marrow, causing a decrease in WBcs, especially granulocytes
  • Causes thrombocytopenia frequently
  • The client should report any discomforts and be sure to report new onset of fatigue, easy bruising, or sore throat.
  • Advise the client to report manifestations of infection or bleeding, and to avoid crowds or individuals who have respiratory infections.

Nursing Interventions

  • Monitor client blood counts, especially WBc, absolute neutrophil count, and thrombocyte count. expect ganciclovir therapy to be interrupted for an absolute neutrophil count less than 500/mm3 or a thrombocyte count less than 25,000/mm3.
  • Monitor blood counts.
  • Prepare to administer granulocyte colony-stimulating factors for a low absolute neutrophil count.
  • Monitor i&o, and encourage the client to increase fluid intake.
  • Avoid direct contact with the powder from oral ganciclovir or the iV solution, and wash well if contact occurs.
  • Advise clients to use a barrier contraception (condoms) during treatment and for 3 months following treatment.

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 48.1

A nurse is teaching a client who has a new prescription for combination oral NRTIs (abacavir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir) for treatment of HIV. Which of the following statements should the nurse include?

  1. "These medications work by blocking HIV entry into cells."
  2. "These medications work by weakening the cell wall of the HIV virus."
  3. "These medications work by inhibiting enzymes to prevent HIV replication."
  4. "These medications work by preventing protein synthesis within the HIV cell."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Blocking HIV entry describes fusion/entry inhibitors (e.g., enfuvirtide) and CCR5 antagonists.
  • B. "Cell wall" disruption describes some antibacterials, not antiretrovirals (and HIV has no cell wall).
  • C. Correct — NRTIs inhibit reverse transcriptase (an enzyme), preventing HIV replication.
  • D. Preventing bacterial protein synthesis describes certain antibiotics, not these antiretrovirals.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Expected Actions/Outcomes

Exercise 48.2

A nurse is caring for a client who takes several antiretroviral medications, including the NRTI zidovudine, to treat HIV infection. The nurse should monitor for which of the following adverse effects of zidovudine? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Fatigue
  2. Blurred vision
  3. Ataxia
  4. Hyperventilation
  5. Vomiting
Show answer & rationale

Answer: A, D, E

  • A. Correct — Fatigue can result from anemia, a hematologic adverse effect of zidovudine.
  • B. Incorrect — Zidovudine can cause hearing loss and photophobia, not blurred vision specifically.
  • C. Incorrect — Vertigo, rather than ataxia, can occur.
  • D. Correct — Hyperventilation can be a sign of lactic acidosis.
  • E. Correct — Vomiting and other GI effects can occur.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 48.3

A nurse is caring for a client who is taking ritonavir, a protease inhibitor, to treat HIV infection. The nurse should monitor for which of the following adverse effects of this medication?

  1. Increased TSH level
  2. Decreased ALT level
  3. Hypoglycemia
  4. Hyperlipidemia
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Increased TSH/T4 indicates a thyroid disorder, not a ritonavir effect.
  • B. Ritonavir increases (not decreases) liver enzymes such as ALT/AST.
  • C. Hyperglycemia (not hypoglycemia) can occur.
  • D. Correct — Protease inhibitors cause hyperlipidemia with increased cholesterol and triglycerides.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 48.4

A nurse is caring for a client who has a new prescription for enfuvirtide to treat HIV infection. The nurse should monitor the client for which of the following adverse reactions of this medication? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Bleeding
  2. Pneumonia
  3. Cerebral edema
  4. Localized erythema
  5. Hypotension
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, D, E

  • A. Incorrect — Bleeding is not an adverse effect of enfuvirtide.
  • B. Correct — Bacterial pneumonia (fever, cough) is an associated adverse reaction.
  • C. Incorrect — Cerebral edema is not an adverse reaction.
  • D. Correct — Enfuvirtide is given subcutaneously; localized erythema/injection-site reactions are common.
  • E. Correct — Hypotension can occur as part of a systemic allergic (hypersensitivity) reaction.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Adverse Effects/Contraindications/Side Effects/Interactions

Exercise 48.5

A nurse is administering IV acyclovir to a client who has varicella. Which of the following actions should the nurse take?

  1. Administer a stool softener.
  2. Decrease fluid intake following infusion.
  3. Infuse acyclovir over 1 hr.
  4. Monitor for hypotension.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Acyclovir can cause diarrhea; a stool softener is not indicated.
  • B. Increase fluids during and for 2 hr after infusion to protect the kidneys.
  • C. Correct — Infuse IV acyclovir slowly over at least 1 hr to reduce the risk of nephrotoxicity.
  • D. Hypotension is not the primary monitoring concern; nephrotoxicity is.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Exercise 48.6

A nurse is teaching a client who is beginning highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) for HIV infection about ways to prevent medication resistance. Which of the following information should the nurse teach the client about resistance?

  1. Taking low dosages of antiretroviral medication minimizes resistance.
  2. Taking one antiretroviral medication at a time minimizes resistance.
  3. Taking medication at the same times daily without missing doses minimizes resistance.
  4. Changing the medication regimen when adverse effects occur minimizes resistance.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Low (sub-therapeutic) dosing promotes resistance, not prevents it.
  • B. HAART uses a combination of medications; single-drug therapy promotes resistance.
  • C. Correct — Strict adherence — taking each dose on schedule without missing — minimizes resistance.
  • D. Self-changing the regimen for adverse effects does not prevent resistance; consult the provider.

NCLEX® Connection: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — Medication Administration

Unit 13 · Other Medications · Chapter 49

Complementary, Alternative, and Integrative Therapies

Complementary and alternative therapies include herbal supplements (echinacea, ginkgo, ginseng, St. John's wort, garlic, valerian, black cohosh, saw palmetto), megavitamins, glucosamine/chondroitin, and probiotics. Not FDA-regulated as drugs; many drug interactions.

Complementary & Alternative Therapies — Overview

Widely used, loosely regulated — the nurse’s job is to ask about use and flag interactions.

CAM — definitions & regulation

DSHEA 1994
  • Alternative = instead of conventional care; complementary = alongside it; integrative = coordinated, holistic, client-focused care
  • Supplements are less tested/standardized than drugs; under DSHEA (1994), labels must state the product is “not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease”
  • Always ask clients about supplement use — many interact with prescription medications

Common Herbal Products

The recurring danger is bleeding; kava and St. John’s wort are the standout hazards.

Aloe & echinacea

Skin & immune
  • Aloe: topical anti-inflammatory/analgesic for burns and skin; oral laxative effect
  • Echinacea: immune stimulation (common cold) — allergic reactions in clients allergic to ragweed/daisy family
  • Chronic echinacea use can reduce the effects of TB, HIV, and cancer medications

Feverfew, garlic & ginkgo

Bleeding risk
  • Feverfew: migraine prophylaxis (not for an acute migraine); discontinue 2 weeks before surgery
  • Garlic: lowers LDL/blood pressure and suppresses platelets; ginkgo: circulation/memory
  • All three increase bleeding risk with NSAIDs, heparin, and warfarin — ask about concurrent use

Kava & St. John’s wort

High-alert herbals
  • Kava: for anxiety/sleep (GABA) — causes liver injury; avoid with CNS depressants/alcohol and in liver disease
  • St. John’s wort: for mild depression — serotonin syndrome with antidepressants; photosensitivity
  • St. John’s wort decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, warfarin, digoxin, cyclosporine, and HIV protease inhibitors

Glucosamine & other supplements

Joint & more
  • Glucosamine (often with chondroitin): osteoarthritis — caution with shellfish allergy; bleeding risk with anticoagulants
  • Other common products: saw palmetto (BPH), ginseng, and melatonin (sleep)
  • Reinforce that “natural” does not mean safe — dosages are imprecise and quality varies

Active Learning Scenario

Medication

A nurse is educating a client about the use of the dietary herbal supplement St. John's Wort. What should the nurse include in the teaching? Use the ATI Active Learning Template: medication to complete this item.

  • THERAPEUTIC USE: Describe the potential uses of this supplement.
  • COMPLICATIONS: Identify four potential adverse effects of this supplement.
  • MEDICATION INTERACTIONS: Identify four medication interactions that can occur with this supplement.

Therapeutic Use

  • Affects serotonin, producing antidepressant effects
  • Mild depression
  • Oral analgesic to relieve pain and inflammation
  • Applied topically to treat infection

Complications

  • Mild adverse effects, including dry mouth, lightheadedness, constipation, GI discomfort
  • Skin rash with client exposure to sunlight

Interactions

  • Can cause serotonin syndrome when combined with other antidepressants, amphetamine, and cocaine
  • Decreases effectiveness of oral contraceptives, cyclosporine, warfarin, digoxin, calcium channel blockers, steroids, HIV protease inhibitors, and some anticancer medications

Application Exercises

Practice questions reflecting how this content appears on the NCLEX-RN. Rationales source the ATI Application Exercises Key.

Exercise 49.1

A nurse is caring for a client who has increased liver enzymes and is taking herbal supplements. Which of the following herbal supplements should the nurse report to the provider as the potential cause?

  1. Glucosamine
  2. Saw palmetto
  3. Kava
  4. St. John's Wort
Show answer & rationale

Answer: C

  • A. Glucosamine can increase bleeding risk.
  • B. Saw palmetto can cause mild GI effects.
  • C. Correct — Chronic use or high doses of kava can cause hepatotoxicity (increased liver enzymes); report it.
  • D. St. John's Wort is best known for numerous drug interactions rather than hepatotoxicity here.

Exercise 49.2

A nurse is caring for a client who requests information on the use of feverfew. Which of the following responses should the nurse make?

  1. "It is used to treat skin infections."
  2. "It can decrease the frequency of migraine headaches."
  3. "It can lessen the nasal congestion in the common cold."
  4. "It can relieve nausea of morning sickness during pregnancy."
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A. Aloe is used for tissue injury/skin.
  • B. Correct — Feverfew is used to decrease the frequency of migraine headaches.
  • C. Echinacea is associated with cold symptoms.
  • D. Ginger root is used for nausea; feverfew is not recommended in pregnancy.

Exercise 49.3

A nurse is reviewing a client's current medications. The client states, "I also take ginkgo biloba." Which of the following medications has the potential to interact with ginkgo biloba?

  1. Acetaminophen
  2. Warfarin
  3. Digoxin
  4. Lisinopril
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B

  • A, C, D. Acetaminophen, digoxin, and lisinopril do not have this significant interaction.
  • B. Correct — Ginkgo biloba suppresses coagulation; combined with warfarin it increases bleeding risk.

Exercise 49.4

A nurse is caring for a client who asks about the potential adverse effects of smoking cannabis. Which of the following manifestations should the nurse include in the response? (Select all that apply.)

  1. Decreased heart rate
  2. Dry mouth
  3. Hallucinations
  4. Hypertension
  5. Increased urination
Show answer & rationale

Answer: B, C

  • A. Incorrect — Cannabis tends to increase heart rate, not decrease it.
  • B. Correct — Dry mouth is a common adverse effect.
  • C. Correct — Hallucinations can occur.
  • D. Incorrect — Decreased blood pressure (not hypertension) can occur.
  • E. Incorrect — Decreased urination, not increased, can occur.

Exercise 49.5

A nurse is teaching about the use of medical marijuana with a group of newly licensed nurses. Which of the following statements indicates an understanding of the teaching?

  1. A health care provider must write a prescription for medical marijuana.
  2. Medical marijuana is a Schedule V controlled substance in the United States.
  3. Pharmacies must obtain certification prior to dispensing medical marijuana.
  4. The FDA does not recognize the marijuana plant as a form of medicine.
Show answer & rationale

Answer: D

  • A. Cannabis cannot be legally prescribed by health care providers (it is recommended/certified, not prescribed, where legal).
  • B. Marijuana is a Schedule I controlled substance federally, not Schedule V.
  • C. Cannabis cannot be legally dispensed from traditional pharmacies federally.
  • D. Correct — The FDA does not recognize or approve the marijuana plant as a form of medicine.
